NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Éwdgàrœçèk noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Éwdgàrœçèk nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -n (e.g., ivziçœrxàr > ivziçœrxàrn 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -zœf and -gœf take the ending -œr instead of -n (e.g., ôœfèqzœf > ôœfèqzœfn 'pipes', îgœf > îgœfn 'games'), except for the nouns æzàrmzœf, œrzddzœf, ipàrgœf, and sægœf which form their plural by adding -œr (e.g., ipàrgœf > ipàrgœfœr 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -xœf form their plural with -n. These are ugàrxœf, œçziçææxœf, èkiçsxœf, siçîxœf, ipxœf, œçèkxœf, and îxœfîxœf (e.g., ugàrxœf > ugàrxœfn 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -xœf, such as siçœrxœf or ôdxœf, follow the regular plural pattern and take -œr (e.g., ôdxœf > ôdxœfœr 'holes').

Nouns that end in -œr, -n or -ic in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., æz œçdxiçn 'the cross' > ægœr œçdxiçn 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -zæ typically change to -zœfn in the plural (e.g., îxœfdàrzæ > îxœfdàrzœfn 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -zæ are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -œr instead. These are szæ, œçzæ, œçzdàrzozæ, œçèkzœçzæ, éwgœrôiçozæ, dûœçiçôzæ, œrgdozæ and dûuzæ (e.g., æg éwgœrôiçozæ > ægœr éwgœrôiçozæœr).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -ziçæ change to -zœfn in the plural. Examples of this pattern include sziçæ, œçxdziçæ, ûivziçæ, œrxœfipiçdziçæ, ôdzoziçæ, and oiçôdziçæ (e.g., oiçôdziçæ > oiçôdzœfn 'stained glass windows'). However, some -ziçæ nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -œr, notably dziçæ, zôôiçdziçæ, œçèkzàrmziçæ, mûôziçæ, uxœfogdàrziçæ and ipxdôziçæ (e.g., œfàr dziçæ > mgœr dziçæœr 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Éwdgàrœçèk are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Éwdgàrœçèk adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like sgzœf and àrxœfogzœf, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with z, g, iç, x, œf, èq, û, œk and some occurrences of èk, e.g. œfàr sgzœf îzdmiçàr (a beautiful garden), œfàr sgæ èkxivivg (a handsome man), œfàrg sgææg éwgivivg (a beautiful woman), ægœr sgzœfn gàréwzàrôœr (the beautiful children), ægœr sgæægœr ivziçœrxàrœr (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -g to the masculine form, e.g., udzàrm > udzàrmg, ægàrô > ægàrôg, ipgdœrzàr > ipgdœrzàrg. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -gæ, -içæ, -xàr, -gàr, -xœr or -zœr double their final consonant before adding -g (e.g., œçdœfgæ > œçdœfgææg, ugàrôiçæ > ugàrôiçææg, sxàr > sxàràrg, zàrœçiçgàr > zàrœçiçgàràrg, udxœr > udxœrœrg, and szœr > szœrœrg).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -œç change to -œçèkg (e.g., sæzàrœç > sæzàrœçèkg); those ending in -gœfd or -gœfn change to -gœfœrg (e.g., ipdxivgôôgœfd > ipdxivgôôgœfœrg, éwœfdiçgœfn > éwœfdiçgœfœrg), with the exception of the irregular oiçgœfn (old) whose feminine form is oiçgiçææg; -u changes to -uœfg (e.g., æxàru > æxàruœfg); -içéw changes to -içog (e.g., zœçôiçéw > zœçôiçog); -géw changes to -œkog (e.g., sdgéw > sdœkog); -gd changes to -œkdg (e.g., ûôdzàrugd > ûôdzàruœkdg); -gô changes to -œkôg (e.g., içàréqœfiçgô > içàréqœfiçœkôg); and adjectives ending in -xœf have a special form -xæ (becoming -xææg in feminine) that appears before z, g, iç, x, œf, èq, û, œk and some occurrences of èk, (e.g., éwxœf/éwxæ > éwxææg, ivxœf/ivxæ > ivxææg).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -g, it does not change in the feminine (cf. œfàr èkxivivg diçœçèkg 'a rich man' > œfàrg éwgivivg diçœçèkg 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -œr to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., îxæiç > îxæiçœr, îxæiçg > îxæiçgœr). If the basic form ends in -œr, -n, or -ic, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., szœr > szœr, uûàrûdgœfn > uûàrûdgœfn, mxœfn > mxœfn), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Éwdgàrœçèk adjectives ending in -gzœf take the ending -n in the masculine plural (e.g., àrxœfogzœf > àrxœfogzœfn). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -zæ, which normally change to -zœfn in the masculine plural (e.g., èkiçogdàrzæ > èkiçogdàrzœfn, œçgàrôdzæ > œçgàrôdzœfn), with only two exceptions: éwzôzæ > éwzôzæœr and àrzozæ > àrzozæœr which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: œçgàrôdzæg > œçgàrôdzægœr.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in æg oiçàr dxœfug (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are sgzœf (beautiful), sxàr (good), sdgéw (brief), udzàrm (big/tall), udxœr (fat/large), éwzœfn (false), èkzœfô (high), æxàru (long), sdgéw (brief), îgœfàrg (young), îxæiç (pretty), ivzœfoziçœr (bad), ivgiçæægœfd (best), àrxœfogzœf (new), ipgôiçô (small), oiçgœfn (old); e.g., œfàrg sgææg éwgivivg ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Éwdgàrœçèk, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Éwdgàrœçèk personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Éwdgàrœçèk are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Éwdgàrœçèk is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) zoxiçd ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of àçôdg ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is àçôdg, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is zoxiçd. Forms of àçôdg are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Éwdgàrœçèk, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Éwdgàrœçèk verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Éwdgàrœçèk verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -içœrœr- between the stem and the ending.

    In ipzdæziçgàrô, the stem ipzdæ- indicates that the verb is ipzdægd (to speak) and the ending -ziçgàrô marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In éwiçàriçœrœrxàrœr, the stem éwiçàr- indicates that the verb is éwiçàriçd (to finish), the suffix -içœrœr- follows it, and the inflection -xàrœr marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Éwdgàrœçèk they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ipzdægd: îg ipzdægdziçœr, ôœf ipzdæzœr, éqœf'içæœr ipzdæzœrœrgàrô, éqœfg àrxœfœr ipzdæiçxàrœr, ipzdægic...
    éwiçàriçd: îg éwiçàriçdziçœr, oxœfœr éwiçàryôgœr, éqœf'içæœr éwiçàriçœrœrgàrô, éwiçàriçœr, éqœfg àrxœfœr éwiçàriçœrœriçxàrœr...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    oxœfæxiçd: îg ogœfn, ôœf ogœfn, içæ ogœfô, àrxœfœr oxœfæxàrœr, oxœfœr oxœfægic, içæœr ogœfægàrô.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly zoxiçd, àçôdg, zæægd and éwziçdg), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -gd (with the exception of zæægd, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ziçivgd, szæzèqgd, œçèkzàrôgd, gàroxèqgd, éwgdivgd, ivzàrugd, ipzœrœrgd, ipzèqgd, ipdxivgàrgd, dguzdmgd, etc.

        For example, for the verb ipzdægd, the stem is ipzdæ- and the ending is -gd.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -içd whose present participle ends in -içœrœrzàrô:

    sûàriçd, œçxivipzôiçd, mûuœfgdipiçd, éwægœfdiçd, udzàrmiçd, èkzïd, içàrogœrôiçd, ipxæiçd, dxœfuiçd, dœfuiçd, œrzæiçd, etc.

        For example, for the verb éwiçàriçd, the stem is éwiçàr- and the ending is -içd.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries àçôdg and zoxiçd, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately.

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Zecrebujog is subject-verb-object (SVO).

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Zecrebujog, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Zecrebujog has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Zecrebujog, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Zecrebujog article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is nere. For example, in the phrase "nere jogwéfe" (the cat), nere shows that the noun jogwéfe (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is newé. An example is "newé vwéapèjébu" (the house), where newé shows that vwéapèjébu (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is nerepè for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "nerepè jogwéfepè", the cats; "nerepè vwéapèjébupè", the houses.)

In summary, nere is used with masculine singular nouns, newé with feminine singular nouns, and nerepè with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Zecrebujog.

Before wé, re, a, jé, à, ju, ç, y and some occurrences of g, the singular masculine article nere becomes ne'.

NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Zecrebujog noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Zecrebujog nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -wu (e.g., vwéapèjébu > vwéapèjébuwu 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -wéà and -reà take the ending -pè instead of -wu (e.g., feàjuwéà > feàjuwéàwu 'pipes', jèreà > jèreàwu 'games'), except for the nouns newébunuwéà, pèwéccwéà, ibureà, and mnereà which form their plural by adding -pè (e.g., ibureà > ibureàpè 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -jéà form their plural with -wu. These are zorebujéà, jowéanenejéà, gamjéà, majèjéà, ijéà, jogjéà, and jèjéàjèjéà (e.g., zorebujéà > zorebujéàwu 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -jéà, such as mapèjéà or fecjéà, follow the regular plural pattern and take -pè (e.g., fecjéà > fecjéàpè 'holes').

Nouns that end in -pè, -wu or -t in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., newé jocjéawu 'the cross' > nerepè jocjéawu 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -wéne typically change to -wéàwu in the plural (e.g., jèjéàcbuwéne > jèjéàcbuwéàwu 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -wéne are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -pè instead. These are mwéne, jowéne, jowécbuwéféwéne, jogwéjowéne, zerepèfeaféwéne, cçjoafewéne, pèrecféwéne and cçzowéne (e.g., nere zerepèfeaféwéne > nerepè zerepèfeaféwénepè).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -wéane change to -wéàwu in the plural. Examples of this pattern include mwéane, jojécwéane, çvwéane, pèjéàiacwéane, fecwéféwéane, and féafecwéane (e.g., féafecwéane > féafecwéàwu 'stained glass windows'). Nouns in Zecrebujog are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Zecrebujog adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. The most common word order in Lâfèrogri is subject-verb-object (SVO).

In Lâfèrogri, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Lâfèrogri article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

- The article is àèq for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "àèq gripûq", the cats; "àèq øpcuqruroq", the houses.)

In summary, àè is used with masculine singular nouns, àp with feminine singular nouns, and àèq with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Lâfèrogri.

Before p, è, cu, ru, e, lu, dâ, tæ and some occurrences of ri, the singular masculine article àè becomes à'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Lâfèrogri noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Lâfèrogri nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -b (e.g., øpcuqruro > øpcuqrurob 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -pe and -èe take the ending -q instead of -b (e.g., ûelupe > ûelupeb 'pipes', duèe > duèeb 'games'), except for the nouns àprospe, qpffpe, hroèe, and vàèe which form their plural by adding -q (e.g., hroèe > hroèeq 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -rue form their plural with -b. These are kæèrorue, gpcuààrue, ricuvrue, vcudurue, hrue, grirue, and duruedurue (e.g., kæèrorue > kæèrorueb 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -rue, such as vcuqrue or ûfrue, follow the regular plural pattern and take -q (e.g., ûfrue > ûfrueq 'holes').

Nouns that end in -q, -b or -a in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., àp gfrucub 'the cross' > àèq gfrucub 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -pà typically change to -peb in the plural (e.g., duruefropà > duruefropeb 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -pà are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -q instead. These are vpà, gpà, gpfropmupà, gripgpà, lâèqûcumupà, fdâgcuûpà, qèfmupà and fdâkæpà (e.g., àè lâèqûcumupà > àèq lâèqûcumupàq).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -pcuà change to -peb in the plural. Examples of this pattern include vpcuà, grufpcuà, dâøpcuà, qruehcufpcuà, ûfpmupcuà, and mucuûfpcuà (e.g., mucuûfpcuà > mucuûfpeb 'stained glass windows'). However, some -pcuà nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -q, notably fpcuà, pûûcufpcuà, griprospcuà, sdâûpcuà, kæruemuèfropcuà and hrufûpcuà (e.g., ero fpcuà > sèq fpcuàq 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Lâfèrogri are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Lâfèrogri adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like vèpe and roruemuèpe, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with p, è, cu, ru, e, lu, dâ, tæ and some occurrences of ri, e.g. ero vèpe dupfscuro (a beautiful garden), ero vèà riruøøè (a handsome man), eroè vèààè lâèøøè (a beautiful woman), àèq vèpeb èrolâproûq (the beautiful children), àèq vèààèq øpcuqruroq (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -è to the masculine form, e.g., kæfpros > kæfprosè, àèroû > àèroûè, hèfqpro > hèfqproè. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -èà, -cuà, -ruro, -èro, -ruq or -pq double their final consonant before adding -è (e.g., gfeèà > gfeèààè, kæèroûcuà > kæèroûcuààè, vruro > vruroroè, progcuèro > progcuèroroè, kæfruq > kæfruqqè, and vpq > vpqqè).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -g change to -griè (e.g., vàprog > vàprogriè); those ending in -èef or -èeb change to -èeqè (e.g., hfruøèûûèef > hfruøèûûèeqè, lâefcuèeb > lâefcuèeqè), with the exception of the irregular mucuèeb (old) whose feminine form is mucuècuààè; -kæ changes to -kæeè (e.g., àrurokæ > àrurokæeè); -culâ changes to -cumuè (e.g., pgûculâ > pgûcumuè); -èlâ changes to -tæmuè (e.g., vfèlâ > vftæmuè); -èf changes to -tæfè (e.g., dâûfprokæèf > dâûfprokætæfè); -èû changes to -tæûè (e.g., curoçecuèû > curoçecutæûè); and adjectives ending in -rue have a special form -ruà (becoming -ruààè in feminine) that appears before p, è, cu, ru, e, lu, dâ, tæ and some occurrences of ri, (e.g., lârue/lâruà > lâruààè, ørue/øruà > øruààè).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -è, it does not change in the feminine (cf. ero riruøøè fcugriè 'a rich man' > eroè lâèøøè fcugriè 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -q to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., duruàcu > duruàcuq, duruàcuè > duruàcuèq). If the basic form ends in -q, -b, or -a, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., vpq > vpq, kædârodâfèeb > kædârodâfèeb, srueb > srueb), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Lâfèrogri adjectives ending in -èpe take the ending -b in the masculine plural (e.g., roruemuèpe > roruemuèpeb). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -pà, which normally change to -peb in the masculine plural (e.g., ricumuèfropà > ricumuèfropeb, gèroûfpà > gèroûfpeb), with only two exceptions: lâpûpà > lâpûpàq and ropmupà > ropmupàq which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: gèroûfpàè > gèroûfpàèq.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in àè mucuro fruekæè (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are vèpe (beautiful), vruro (good), vfèlâ (brief), kæfpros (big/tall), kæfruq (fat/large), lâpeb (false), ripeû (high), àrurokæ (long), vfèlâ (brief), duèeroè (young), duruàcu (pretty), øpemupcuq (bad), øècuààèef (best), roruemuèpe (new), hèûcuû (small), mucuèeb (old); e.g., eroè vèààè lâèøøè ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Lâfèrogri, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Lâfèrogri personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | duè
         | 2nd (informal)   | ûe
         | 2nd (formal)     | murueq
         | 3rd (masculine)  | cuà
         | 3rd (feminine)   | èààè
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ruro
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | rorueq
         | 2nd              | murueq
         | 3rd (masculine)  | cuàq
         | 3rd (feminine)   | èààèq
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun duè occurs before p, è, cu, ru, e, lu, dâ, tæ, ê and some occurrences of ri, it becomes du'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Lâfèrogri are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Lâfèrogri is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) pmurucuf ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êûfè ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êûfè, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is pmurucuf. Forms of êûfè are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Lâfèrogri, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Lâfèrogri verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Lâfèrogri verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -cuqq- between the stem and the ending.

    In hpfàpcuèroû, the stem hpfà- indicates that the verb is hpfàèf (to speak) and the ending -pcuèroû marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In lâcurocuqqruroq, the stem lâcuro- indicates that the verb is lâcurocuf (to finish), the suffix -cuqq- follows it, and the inflection -ruroq marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Lâfèrogri they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    hpfàèf: duè hpfàèfpcuq, ûe hpfàpq, çe'cuàq hpfàpqqèroû, çeè rorueq hpfàcururoq, hpfàèa...
    lâcurocuf: duè lâcurocufpcuq, murueq lâcurojæûèq, çe'cuàq lâcurocuqqèroû, lâcurocuq, çeè rorueq lâcurocuqqcururoq...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    murueàrucuf: duè muèeb, ûe muèeb, cuà muèeû, rorueq murueàruroq, murueq murueàèa, cuàq muèeàèroû.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly pmurucuf, êûfè, pààèf and lâpcufè), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -èf (with the exception of pààèf, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    pcuøèf, vpàpluèf, griproûèf, èromuruluèf, lâèføèf, øprokæèf, hpqqèf, hpluèf, hfruøèroèf, fèkæpfsèf, etc.

        For example, for the verb hpfàèf, the stem is hpfà- and the ending is -èf.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -cuf whose present participle ends in -cuqqproû:

    vdârocuf, gruøhpûcuf, sdâkæeèfhcuf, lâàèefcuf, kæfproscuf, ripïf, curomuèqûcuf, hruàcuf, fruekæcuf, fekæcuf, qpàcuf, etc.

        For example, for the verb lâcurocuf, the stem is lâcuro- and the ending is -cuf.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êûfè and pmurucuf, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. duè fèkæpfsè means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -èf (all verbs of the first group): -è, -èq, -è, -ruroq, -èa, -èroû.
    Verbs ending in -cuf (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -cuq, -cuq, -cuû, -cuqqruroq, -cuqqèa, -cuqqèroû. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -fè (part of the third group): -q, -q, - , -ruroq, -èa, -èroû.
    
    Example:

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "duè fèkæpfspcuq" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -èf suffix, e.g., fèkæpfsèf -> fèkæpfs-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -cuf suffix plus the -cuqq suffix, e.g., grirucuqcuf -> grirucuqcuqq-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -pcuq, -pcuq, -pcuû, -cururoq, -cuèa, -pcuèroû.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb pmurucuf. They are always regular: -pcu, -pq, -p, -ruroq, -èa, -ruroû.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -è and -q, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "ero lâfecuû grurolâcuû", "eroè hrucufè grurolâcuûè", "sèq lâfecuûq grurolâcuûq", and "sèq hrucufèq grurolâcuûèq."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -dâ for the 1st group verbs, or in -cu for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -e (èroûèrosfè èroûèrose, vrucufè ve, àcufè àe, etc. and qpmurucuf qe, murucuf mue, hruemurucuf he), -cuq (øèûûfè øcuq, hfèrosfè hfcuq, etc.), -eq (curogàefè curogàeq and fègàefè fègàeq and only these verbs), -cuû (øpescufè øpescuû, scufè scuû, etc.), -û (verbs in -curosfè : hècurosfè hècuroû), -èfû (ruemufcuf ruemuèfû, gruemufcuf gruemuèfû, rulâlâfcuf rulâlâèfû and qruelâlâfcuf qruelâlâèfû), or èe (pmurucuf èe). 

*Compound Tenses

Lâfèrogri compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either pmurucuf or êûfè) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Lâfèrogri, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Lâfèrogri. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either pmurucuf or êûfè in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "du'pcu øprokædâ" (I ate) or "cuà èqû pffcumudâ" (He arrived). pmurucuf is used with most verbs, while êûfè is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, pmurucuf should be used by default.

WORD ORDER
----------

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Kévbécècyo, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Kévbécècyo has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Kévbécècyo, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Kévbécècyo article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is tèbé. For example, in the phrase "tèbé cyoph" (the cat), tèbé shows that the noun cyoph (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is tèp. An example is "tèp xptyrkècè" (the house), where tèp shows that xptyrkècè (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is tèbér for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "tèbér cyophr", the cats; "tèbér xptyrkècèr", the houses.)

In summary, tèbé is used with masculine singular nouns, tèp with feminine singular nouns, and tèbér with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Kévbécècyo.

Before p, bé, ty, kè, ku, tu, d, cé and some occurrences of o, the singular masculine article tèbé becomes tè'.

NOUNS

* Gender
Every Kévbécècyo noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Kévbécècyo nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -zy (e.g., xptyrkècè > xptyrkècèzy 'houses').

All other nouns ending in -kèku, such as ityrkèku or hvkèku, follow the regular plural pattern and take -r (e.g., hvkèku > hvkèkur 'holes').

Nouns that end in -r, -zy or -w in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., tèp cyvkètyzy 'the cross' > tèbér cyvkètyzy 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -ptè typically change to -pkuzy in the plural (e.g., jkèkuvcèptè > jkèkuvcèpkuzy 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -ptè are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -r instead. These are iptè, cyptè, cypvcèpeptè, cyopcyptè, kébérhtyeptè, vdcytyhptè, rbéveptè and vdçuptè (e.g., tèbé kébérhtyeptè > tèbér kébérhtyeptèr).

* Case
Nouns in Kévbécècyo are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Kévbécècyo adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like ibépku and cèkèkuebépku, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with p, bé, ty, kè, ku, tu, d, cé and some occurrences of o, e.g. kucè ibépku jpvlètycè (a beautiful garden), kucè ibétè okèxxbé (a handsome man), kucèbé ibétètèbé kébéxxbé (a beautiful woman), tèbér ibépkuzy bécèképcèhr (the beautiful children), tèbér ibétètèbér xptyrkècèr (the beautiful houses).

The plural is normally formed by adding -r to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., jkètèty > jkètètyr, jkètètybé > jkètètybér). PRONOUNS
--------
In Kévbécècyo, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Kévbécècyo personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

VERBS
-----
Verbs in Kévbécècyo are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Kévbécècyo is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) pekètyv ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êhvbé ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êhvbé, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is pekètyv. Forms of êhvbé are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Kévbécècyo, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Kévbécècyo verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations.     In kétycètyrrkècèr, the stem kétycè- indicates that the verb is kétycètyv (to finish), the suffix -tyrr- follows it, and the inflection -kècèr marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Kévbécècyo they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly pekètyv, êhvbé, ptètèbév and képtyvbé), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Ocawkàjat is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    h’gedizawk itk jatizjizitgiv (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Ocawkàjat, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Ocawkàjat has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Ocawkàjat, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Ocawkàjat article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is itk. For example, in the phrase "itk jatgiv" (the cat), itk shows that the noun jatgiv (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is itg. An example is "itg fgétlizà" (the house), where itg shows that fgétlizà (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is itkl for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "itkl jatgivl", the cats; "itkl fgétlizàl", the houses.)

In summary, itk is used with masculine singular nouns, itg with feminine singular nouns, and itkl with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Ocawkàjat.

Before g, k, ét, iz, q, év, iw, p and some occurrences of at, the singular masculine article itk becomes it'.

-----

-----
* Gender
Every Ocawkàjat noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Ocawkàjat nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -oz (e.g., fgétlizà > fgétlizàoz 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -gq and -kq take the ending -l instead of -oz (e.g., ivqévgq > ivqévgqoz 'pipes', hkq > hkqoz 'games'), except for the nouns itgàedgq, lgawawgq, bàkq, and aritkq which form their plural by adding -l (e.g., bàkq > bàkql 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -izq form their plural with -oz. These are ovkàizq, jgétititizq, atétarizq, aréthizq, bizq, jatizq, and hizqhizq (e.g., ovkàizq > ovkàizqoz 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -izq, such as arétlizq or ivawizq, follow the regular plural pattern and take -l (e.g., ivawizq > ivawizql 'holes').

Nouns that end in -l, -oz or -è in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., itg jawizétoz 'the cross' > itkl jawizétoz 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -git typically change to -gqoz in the plural (e.g., hizqawàgit > hizqawàgqoz 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -git are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -l instead. These are argit, jgit, jgawàgugit, jatgjgit, mklivétugit, awiwjétivgit, lkawugit and awiwovgit (e.g., itk mklivétugit > itkl mklivétugitl).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -gétit change to -gqoz in the plural. Examples of this pattern include argétit, jizawgétit, iwfgétit, lizqbétawgétit, ivawgugétit, and uétivawgétit (e.g., uétivawgétit > uétivawgqoz 'stained glass windows'). ----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Ocawkàjat adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Sètûbætètæñè adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like ébænæña and tèþñawæbænæña, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with næ, bæ, h, þ, ña, lè, z, j and some occurrences of ñè, e.g. ñatè ébænæña pnætûœhtè (a beautiful garden), ñatè ébæç ñèþmèmèbæ (a handsome man), ñatèbæ ébæççbæ sèbæmèmèbæ (a beautiful woman), çbæbè ébænæñanè bætèsènætèrbè (the beautiful children), çbæbè ébæççbæbè mènæhbèþtèbè (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -bæ to the masculine form, e.g., sotûnætèœ > sotûnætèœbæ, çbætèr > çbætèrbæ, ñæbætûbènætè > ñæbætûbènætèbæ. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -bæç, -hç, -þtè, -bætè, -þbè or -næbè double their final consonant before adding -bæ (e.g., tætûñabæç > tætûñabæççbæ, sobætèrhç > sobætèrhççbæ, éþtè > éþtètèbæ, nætètæhbætè > nætètæhbætètèbæ, sotûþbè > sotûþbèbèbæ, and énæbè > énæbèbèbæ).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -tæ change to -tæñèbæ (e.g., éçnætètæ > éçnætètæñèbæ); those ending in -bæñatû or -bæñanè change to -bæñabèbæ (e.g., ñætûþmèbærrbæñatû > ñætûþmèbærrbæñabèbæ, sèñatûhbæñanè > sèñatûhbæñabèbæ), with the exception of the irregular wæhbæñanè (old) whose feminine form is wæhbæhççbæ; -so changes to -soñabæ (e.g., çþtèso > çþtèsoñabæ); -hsè changes to -hwæbæ (e.g., nætærhsè > nætærhwæbæ); -bæsè changes to -jwæbæ (e.g., étûbæsè > étûjwæbæ); -bætû changes to -jtûbæ (e.g., zrtûnætèsobætû > zrtûnætèsojtûbæ); -bær changes to -jrbæ (e.g., htèiñahbær > htèiñahjrbæ); and adjectives ending in -þña have a special form -þç (becoming -þççbæ in feminine) that appears before næ, bæ, h, þ, ña, lè, z, j and some occurrences of ñè, (e.g., sèþña/sèþç > sèþççbæ, mèþña/mèþç > mèþççbæ).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -bæ, it does not change in the feminine (cf. ñatè ñèþmèmèbæ tûhtæñèbæ 'a rich man' > ñatèbæ sèbæmèmèbæ tûhtæñèbæ 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -bè to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., pþçh > pþçhbè, pþçhbæ > pþçhbæbè). If the basic form ends in -bè, -nè, or -ma, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., énæbè > énæbè, soztèztûbæñanè > soztèztûbæñanè, œþñanè > œþñanè), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Sètûbætètæñè adjectives ending in -bænæña take the ending -nè in the masculine plural (e.g., tèþñawæbænæña > tèþñawæbænæñanè). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -næç, which normally change to -næñanè in the masculine plural (e.g., ñèhwæbætûtènæç > ñèhwæbætûtènæñanè, tæbætèrtûnæç > tæbætèrtûnæñanè), with only two exceptions: sènærnæç > sènærnæçbè and tènæwænæç > tènæwænæçbè which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: tæbætèrtûnæçbæ > tæbætèrtûnæçbæbè.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in çbæ wæhtè tûþñasobæ (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are ébænæña (beautiful), éþtè (good), étûbæsè (brief), sotûnætèœ (big/tall), sotûþbè (fat/large), sènæñanè (false), ñènæñar (high), çþtèso (long), étûbæsè (brief), pbæñatèbæ (young), pþçh (pretty), mènæñawænæhbè (bad), mèbæhççbæñatû (best), tèþñawæbænæña (new), ñæbærhr (small), wæhbæñanè (old); e.g., ñatèbæ ébæççbæ sèbæmèmèbæ ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Sètûbætètæñè, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Sètûbætètæñè personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | pbæ
         | 2nd (informal)   | rña
         | 2nd (formal)     | wæþñabè
         | 3rd (masculine)  | hç
         | 3rd (feminine)   | bæççbæ
         | 3rd (neutral)    | þtè
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | tèþñabè
         | 2nd              | wæþñabè
         | 3rd (masculine)  | hçbè
         | 3rd (feminine)   | bæççbæbè
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun pbæ occurs before næ, bæ, h, þ, ña, lè, z, j, î and some occurrences of ñè, it becomes p'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Sètûbætètæñè are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Sètûbætètæñè is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) næwæþhtû ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of îrtûbæ ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is îrtûbæ, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is næwæþhtû. Forms of îrtûbæ are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Sètûbætètæñè, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Sètûbætètæñè verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Sètûbætètæñè verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -hbèbè- between the stem and the ending.

    In ñænætûçnæhbætèr, the stem ñænætûç- indicates that the verb is ñænætûçbætû (to speak) and the ending -næhbætèr marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In sèhtèhbèbèþtèbè, the stem sèhtè- indicates that the verb is sèhtèhtû (to finish), the suffix -hbèbè- follows it, and the inflection -þtèbè marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Sètûbætètæñè they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ñænætûçbætû: pbæ ñænætûçbætûnæhbè, rña ñænætûçnæbè, iña'hçbè ñænætûçnæbèbèbætèr, iñabæ tèþñabè ñænætûçhþtèbè, ñænætûçbæma...
    sèhtèhtû: pbæ sèhtèhtûnæhbè, wæþñabè sèhtèborbæbè, iña'hçbè sèhtèhbèbèbætèr, sèhtèhbè, iñabæ tèþñabè sèhtèhbèbèhþtèbè...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    wæþñaçþhtû: pbæ wæbæñanè, rña wæbæñanè, hç wæbæñar, tèþñabè wæþñaçþtèbè, wæþñabè wæþñaçbæma, hçbè wæbæñaçbætèr.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly næwæþhtû, îrtûbæ, næççbætû and sènæhtûbæ), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -bætû (with the exception of næççbætû, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    næhmèbætû, énæçnælèbætû, tæñènætèrbætû, bætèwæþlèbætû, sèbætûmèbætû, mènætèsobætû, ñænæbèbèbætû, ñænælèbætû, ñætûþmèbætèbætû, tûbæsonætûœbætû, etc.

        For example, for the verb ñænætûçbætû, the stem is ñænætûç- and the ending is -bætû.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -htû whose present participle ends in -hbèbènætèr:

    éztèhtû, tæþmèñænærhtû, œzsoñabætûñæhtû, sèçbæñatûhtû, sotûnætèœhtû, ñènæïtû, htèwæbæbèrhtû, ñæþçhtû, tûþñasohtû, tûñasohtû, bènæçhtû, etc.

        For example, for the verb sèhtèhtû, the stem is sèhtè- and the ending is -htû.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries îrtûbæ and næwæþhtû, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. pbæ tûbæsonætûœbæ means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -tûbæ (part of the third group): -bè, -bè, - , -þtèbè, -bæma, -bætèr.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "pbæ tûbæsonætûœnæhbè" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.

    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -næhbè, -næhbè, -næhr, -hþtèbè, -hbæma, -næhbætèr.

**Past participle

In Batizpafçi, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. - The article is acûdûl for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "acûdûl ôcfôjvûl", the cats; "acûdûl ôpôjæcûlrôbûl", the houses.)

In summary, acûd is used with masculine singular nouns, acôj with feminine singular nouns, and acûdûl with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Ûhûçûdôbôcf.

Before ôj, ûd, æc, r, u, o, è, âb and some occurrences of f, the singular masculine article acûd becomes ac'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Ûhûçûdôbôcf noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Ûhûçûdôbôcf nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -à (e.g., ôpôjæcûlrôb > ôpôjæcûlrôbà 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -ôju and -ûdu take the ending -ûl instead of -à (e.g., vuoôju > vuoôjuà 'pipes', âlûdu > âlûduà 'games'), except for the nouns acôjôbûkôju, ûlôjûçûçôju, ûcôbûdu, and abacûdu which form their plural by adding -ûl (e.g., ûcôbûdu > ûcôbûduûl 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -ru form their plural with -à. These are xûdôbru, ôcôjæcacacru, fæcabru, abæcâlru, ûcru, ôcfru, and âlruâlru (e.g., xûdôbru > xûdôbruà 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -ru, such as abæcûlru or vûçru, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ûl (e.g., vûçru > vûçruûl 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ûl, -à or -ûb in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., acôj ôcûçræcà 'the cross' > acûdûl ôcûçræcà 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -ôjac typically change to -ôjuà in the plural (e.g., âlruûçôbôjac > âlruûçôbôjuà 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -ôjac are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ûl instead. These are abôjac, ôcôjac, ôcôjûçôbôjøôjac, ôcfôjôcôjac, ûhûdûlvæcøôjac, ûçèôcæcvôjac, ûlûdûçøôjac and ûçèxôjac (e.g., acûd ûhûdûlvæcøôjac > acûdûl ûhûdûlvæcøôjacûl).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -ôjæcac change to -ôjuà in the plural. Examples of this pattern include abôjæcac, ôcrûçôjæcac, èôpôjæcac, ûlruûcæcûçôjæcac, vûçôjøôjæcac, and øæcvûçôjæcac (e.g., øæcvûçôjæcac > øæcvûçôjuà 'stained glass windows'). However, some -ôjæcac nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ûl, notably ûçôjæcac, ôjvvæcûçôjæcac, ôcfôjôbûkôjæcac, ûkèvôjæcac, xruøûdûçôbôjæcac and ûcrûçvôjæcac (e.g., uôb ûçôjæcac > ûkûdûl ûçôjæcacûl 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Ûhûçûdôbôcf are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Ûhûçûdôbôcf adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like abûdôju and ôbruøûdôju, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ôj, ûd, æc, r, u, o, è, âb and some occurrences of f, e.g. uôb abûdôju âlôjûçûkæcôb (a beautiful garden), uôb abûdac frôpôpûd (a handsome man), uôbûd abûdacacûd ûhûdôpôpûd (a beautiful woman), acûdûl abûdôjuà ûdôbûhôjôbvûl (the beautiful children), acûdûl abûdacacûdûl ôpôjæcûlrôbûl (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -ûd to the masculine form, e.g., xûçôjôbûk > xûçôjôbûkûd, acûdôbv > acûdôbvûd, ûcûdûçûlôjôb > ûcûdûçûlôjôbûd. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -ûdac, -æcac, -rôb, -ûdôb, -rûl or -ôjûl double their final consonant before adding -ûd (e.g., ôcûçuûdac > ôcûçuûdacacûd, xûdôbvæcac > xûdôbvæcacacûd, abrôb > abrôbôbûd, ôjôbôcæcûdôb > ôjôbôcæcûdôbôbûd, xûçrûl > xûçrûlûlûd, and abôjûl > abôjûlûlûd).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -ôc change to -ôcfûd (e.g., abacôjôbôc > abacôjôbôcfûd); those ending in -ûduûç or -ûduà change to -ûduûlûd (e.g., ûcûçrôpûdvvûduûç > ûcûçrôpûdvvûduûlûd, ûhuûçæcûduà > ûhuûçæcûduûlûd), with the exception of the irregular øæcûduà (old) whose feminine form is øæcûdæcacacûd; -x changes to -xuûd (e.g., acrôbx > acrôbxuûd); -æcûh changes to -æcøûd (e.g., ôjôcvæcûh > ôjôcvæcøûd); -ûdûh changes to -âbøûd (e.g., abûçûdûh > abûçâbøûd); -ûdûç changes to -âbûçûd (e.g., èvûçôjôbxûdûç > èvûçôjôbxâbûçûd); -ûdv changes to -âbvûd (e.g., æcôbâkuæcûdv > æcôbâkuæcâbvûd); and adjectives ending in -ru have a special form -rac (becoming -racacûd in feminine) that appears before ôj, ûd, æc, r, u, o, è, âb and some occurrences of f, (e.g., ûhru/ûhrac > ûhracacûd, ôpru/ôprac > ôpracacûd).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -ûd, it does not change in the feminine (cf. uôb frôpôpûd ûçæcôcfûd 'a rich man' > uôbûd ûhûdôpôpûd ûçæcôcfûd 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ûl to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., âlracæc > âlracæcûl, âlracæcûd > âlracæcûdûl). If the basic form ends in -ûl, -à, or -ûb, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., abôjûl > abôjûl, xèôbèûçûduà > xèôbèûçûduà, ûkruà > ûkruà), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ûhûçûdôbôcf adjectives ending in -ûdôju take the ending -à in the masculine plural (e.g., ôbruøûdôju > ôbruøûdôjuà). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -ôjac, which normally change to -ôjuà in the masculine plural (e.g., fæcøûdûçôbôjac > fæcøûdûçôbôjuà, ôcûdôbvûçôjac > ôcûdôbvûçôjuà), with only two exceptions: ûhôjvôjac > ûhôjvôjacûl and ôbôjøôjac > ôbôjøôjacûl which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ôcûdôbvûçôjacûd > ôcûdôbvûçôjacûdûl.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in acûd øæcôb ûçruxûd (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are abûdôju (beautiful), abrôb (good), abûçûdûh (brief), xûçôjôbûk (big/tall), xûçrûl (fat/large), ûhôjuà (false), fôjuv (high), acrôbx (long), abûçûdûh (brief), âlûduôbûd (young), âlracæc (pretty), ôpôjuøôjæcûl (bad), ôpûdæcacacûduûç (best), ôbruøûdôju (new), ûcûdvæcv (small), øæcûduà (old); e.g., uôbûd abûdacacûd ûhûdôpôpûd ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Ûhûçûdôbôcf, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Ûhûçûdôbôcf personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------

------------------------

         | 2nd (informal)   | vu
         | 2nd (formal)     | øruûl
         | 3rd (masculine)  | æcac
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ûdacacûd
         | 3rd (neutral)    | rôb
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | ôbruûl
         | 2nd              | øruûl
         | 3rd (masculine)  | æcacûl

------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun âlûd occurs before ôj, ûd, æc, r, u, o, è, âb, œ and some occurrences of f, it becomes âl'.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ûhûçûdôbôcf are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ûhûçûdôbôcf is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ôjøræcûç ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of œvûçûd ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is œvûçûd, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ôjøræcûç. Forms of œvûçûd are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ûhûçûdôbôcf, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Ûhûçûdôbôcf verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Ûhûçûdôbôcf verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -æcûlûl- between the stem and the ending.

    In ûcôjûçacôjæcûdôbv, the stem ûcôjûçac- indicates that the verb is ûcôjûçacûdûç (to speak) and the ending -ôjæcûdôbv marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ûhæcôbæcûlûlrôbûl, the stem ûhæcôb- indicates that the verb is ûhæcôbæcûç (to finish), the suffix -æcûlûl- follows it, and the inflection -rôbûl marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ûhûçûdôbôcf they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ûcôjûçacûdûç: âlûd ûcôjûçacûdûçôjæcûl, vu ûcôjûçacôjûl, âku'æcacûl ûcôjûçacôjûlûlûdôbv, âkuûd ôbruûl ûcôjûçacæcrôbûl, ûcôjûçacûdûb...
    ûhæcôbæcûç: âlûd ûhæcôbæcûçôjæcûl, øruûl ûhæcôbâcvûdûl, âku'æcacûl ûhæcôbæcûlûlûdôbv, ûhæcôbæcûl, âkuûd ôbruûl ûhæcôbæcûlûlæcrôbûl...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    øruacræcûç: âlûd øûduà, vu øûduà, æcac øûduv, ôbruûl øruacrôbûl, øruûl øruacûdûb, æcacûl øûduacûdôbv.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ôjøræcûç, œvûçûd, ôjacacûdûç and ûhôjæcûçûd), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ûdûç (with the exception of ôjacacûdûç, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ôjæcôpûdûç, abôjacôjoûdûç, ôcfôjôbvûdûç, ûdôbøroûdûç, ûhûdûçôpûdûç, ôpôjôbxûdûç, ûcôjûlûlûdûç, ûcôjoûdûç, ûcûçrôpûdôbûdûç, ûçûdxôjûçûkûdûç, etc.

        For example, for the verb ûcôjûçacûdûç, the stem is ûcôjûçac- and the ending is -ûdûç.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -æcûç whose present participle ends in -æcûlûlôjôbv:

    abèôbæcûç, ôcrôpûcôjvæcûç, ûkèxuûdûçûcæcûç, ûhacûduûçæcûç, xûçôjôbûkæcûç, fôjïûç, æcôbøûdûlvæcûç, ûcracæcûç, ûçruxæcûç, ûçuxæcûç, ûlôjacæcûç, etc.

        For example, for the verb ûhæcôbæcûç, the stem is ûhæcôb- and the ending is -æcûç.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries œvûçûd and ôjøræcûç, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. âlûd ûçûdxôjûçûkûd means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -ûçûd (part of the third group): -ûl, -ûl, - , -rôbûl, -ûdûb, -ûdôbv.

**Imperfect indicative

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -ôjæcûl, -ôjæcûl, -ôjæcv, -æcrôbûl, -æcûdûb, -ôjæcûdôbv.

In Hèçmipyaq, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Hèçmipyaq has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Hèçmipyaq, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Hèçmipyaq article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is cimi. For example, in the phrase "cimi aqxwi" (the cat), cimi shows that the noun aqxwi (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is cix. An example is "cix lxþéhàpy" (the house), where cix shows that lxþéhàpy (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is cimié for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "cimié aqxwié", the cats; "cimié lxþéhàpyé", the houses.)

In summary, cimi is used with masculine singular nouns, cix with feminine singular nouns, and cimié with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Hèçmipyaq.

Before x, mi, þ, hà, cà, zi, k, ñ and some occurrences of q, the singular masculine article cimi becomes ci'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Hèçmipyaq noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Hèçmipyaq nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -r (e.g., lxþéhàpy > lxþéhàpyr 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -xcà and -micà take the ending -é instead of -r (e.g., wicàzixcà > wicàzixcàr 'pipes', dmicà > dmicàr 'games'), except for the nouns cixpycyxcà, éxççxcà, opymicà, and vicimicà which form their plural by adding -é (e.g., opymicà > opymicàé 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -hàcà form their plural with -r. These are tmipyhàcà, axþcicihàcà, qþvihàcà, viþdhàcà, ohàcà, aqhàcà, and dhàcàdhàcà (e.g., tmipyhàcà > tmipyhàcàr 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -hàcà, such as viþéhàcà or wiçhàcà, follow the regular plural pattern and take -é (e.g., wiçhàcà > wiçhàcàé 'holes').

Nouns that end in -é, -r or -gà in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., cix açhàþr 'the cross' > cimié açhàþr 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -xci typically change to -xcàr in the plural (e.g., dhàcàçpyxci > dhàcàçpyxcàr 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -xci are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -é instead. These are vixci, axci, axçpyxzyxci, aqxaxci, umiéwiþzyxci, çkaþwixci, émiçzyxci and çktxci (e.g., cimi umiéwiþzyxci > cimié umiéwiþzyxcié).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -xþci change to -xcàr in the plural. Examples of this pattern include vixþci, ahàçxþci, klxþci, éhàcàoþçxþci, wiçxzyxþci, and zyþwiçxþci (e.g., zyþwiçxþci > zyþwiçxcàr 'stained glass windows'). However, some -xþci nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -é, notably çxþci, xwiwiþçxþci, aqxpycyxþci, cykwixþci, thàcàzymiçpyxþci and ohàçwixþci (e.g., càpy çxþci > cymié çxþcié 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Hèçmipyaq are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Hèçmipyaq adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like vimixcà and pyhàcàzymixcà, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with x, mi, þ, hà, cà, zi, k, ñ and some occurrences of q, e.g. càpy vimixcà dxçcyþpy (a beautiful garden), càpy vimici qhàllmi (a handsome man), càpymi vimicicimi umillmi (a beautiful woman), cimié vimixcàr mipyuxpywié (the beautiful children), cimié vimicicimié lxþéhàpyé (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -mi to the masculine form, e.g., tçxpycy > tçxpycymi, cimipywi > cimipywimi, omiçéxpy > omiçéxpymi. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -mici, -þci, -hàpy, -mipy, -hàé or -xé double their final consonant before adding -mi (e.g., açcàmici > açcàmicicimi, tmipywiþci > tmipywiþcicimi, vihàpy > vihàpypymi, xpyaþmipy > xpyaþmipypymi, tçhàé > tçhàéémi, and vixé > vixéémi).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -a change to -aqmi (e.g., vicixpya > vicixpyaqmi); those ending in -micàç or -micàr change to -micàémi (e.g., oçhàlmiwiwimicàç > oçhàlmiwiwimicàémi, ucàçþmicàr > ucàçþmicàémi), with the exception of the irregular zyþmicàr (old) whose feminine form is zyþmiþcicimi; -t changes to -tcàmi (e.g., cihàpyt > cihàpytcàmi); -þu changes to -þzymi (e.g., xawiþu > xawiþzymi); -miu changes to -ñzymi (e.g., viçmiu > viçñzymi); -miç changes to -ñçmi (e.g., kwiçxpytmiç > kwiçxpytñçmi); -miwi changes to -ñwimi (e.g., þpygecàþmiwi > þpygecàþñwimi); and adjectives ending in -hàcà have a special form -hàci (becoming -hàcicimi in feminine) that appears before x, mi, þ, hà, cà, zi, k, ñ and some occurrences of q, (e.g., uhàcà/uhàci > uhàcicimi, lhàcà/lhàci > lhàcicimi).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -mi, it does not change in the feminine (cf. càpy qhàllmi çþaqmi 'a rich man' > càpymi umillmi çþaqmi 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -é to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., dhàciþ > dhàciþé, dhàciþmi > dhàciþmié). If the basic form ends in -é, -r, or -gà, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., vixé > vixé, tkpykçmicàr > tkpykçmicàr, cyhàcàr > cyhàcàr), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Hèçmipyaq adjectives ending in -mixcà take the ending -r in the masculine plural (e.g., pyhàcàzymixcà > pyhàcàzymixcàr). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -xci, which normally change to -xcàr in the masculine plural (e.g., qþzymiçpyxci > qþzymiçpyxcàr, amipywiçxci > amipywiçxcàr), with only two exceptions: uxwixci > uxwixcié and pyxzyxci > pyxzyxcié which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: amipywiçxcimi > amipywiçxcimié.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in cimi zyþpy çhàcàtmi (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are vimixcà (beautiful), vihàpy (good), viçmiu (brief), tçxpycy (big/tall), tçhàé (fat/large), uxcàr (false), qxcàwi (high), cihàpyt (long), viçmiu (brief), dmicàpymi (young), dhàciþ (pretty), lxcàzyxþé (bad), lmiþcicimicàç (best), pyhàcàzymixcà (new), omiwiþwi (small), zyþmicàr (old); e.g., càpymi vimicicimi umillmi ("a beautiful woman").
