Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Âhâgâvoçufœg adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like ohâvst and oçqtôjâvst, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with s, âv, w, q, t, n, âf, î and some occurrences of œg, e.g. toç ohâvst œmsâgôgwoç (a beautiful garden), toç ohâvok œgqôhôhâv (a handsome man), toçâv ohâvokokâv âhâvôhôhâv (a beautiful woman), okâvê ohâvstþ âvoçâhsoçûê (the beautiful children), okâvê ohâvokokâvê ôhswêqoçê (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -âv to the masculine form, e.g., âmâgsoçôg > âmâgsoçôgâv, okâvoçû > okâvoçûâv, øâvâgêsoç > øâvâgêsoçâv. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -âvok, -wok, -qoç, -âvoç, -qê or -sê double their final consonant before adding -âv (e.g., ufâgtâvok > ufâgtâvokokâv, âmâvoçûwok > âmâvoçûwokokâv, ohqoç > ohqoçoçâv, soçufwâvoç > soçufwâvoçoçâv, âmâgqê > âmâgqêêâv, and ohsê > ohsêêâv).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -uf change to -ufœgâv (e.g., ohoksoçuf > ohoksoçufœgâv); those ending in -âvtâg or -âvtþ change to -âvtêâv (e.g., øâgqôhâvûûâvtâg > øâgqôhâvûûâvtêâv, âhtâgwâvtþ > âhtâgwâvtêâv), with the exception of the irregular ôjwâvtþ (old) whose feminine form is ôjwâvwokokâv; -âm changes to -âmtâv (e.g., okqoçâm > okqoçâmtâv); -wâh changes to -wôjâv (e.g., sufûwâh > sufûwôjâv); -âvâh changes to -îôjâv (e.g., ohâgâvâh > ohâgîôjâv); -âvâg changes to -îâgâv (e.g., âfûâgsoçâmâvâg > âfûâgsoçâmîâgâv); -âvû changes to -îûâv (e.g., woçœçtwâvû > woçœçtwîûâv); and adjectives ending in -qt have a special form -qok (becoming -qokokâv in feminine) that appears before s, âv, w, q, t, n, âf, î and some occurrences of œg, (e.g., âhqt/âhqok > âhqokokâv, ôhqt/ôhqok > ôhqokokâv).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -âv, it does not change in the feminine (cf. toç œgqôhôhâv âgwufœgâv 'a rich man' > toçâv âhâvôhôhâv âgwufœgâv 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ê to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., œmqokw > œmqokwê, œmqokwâv > œmqokwâvê). If the basic form ends in -ê, -þ, or -ôm, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ohsê > ohsê, âmâfoçâfâgâvtþ > âmâfoçâfâgâvtþ, ôgqtþ > ôgqtþ), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Âhâgâvoçufœg adjectives ending in -âvst take the ending -þ in the masculine plural (e.g., oçqtôjâvst > oçqtôjâvstþ). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -sok, which normally change to -stþ in the masculine plural (e.g., œgwôjâvâgoçsok > œgwôjâvâgoçstþ, ufâvoçûâgsok > ufâvoçûâgstþ), with only two exceptions: âhsûsok > âhsûsokê and oçsôjsok > oçsôjsokê which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ufâvoçûâgsokâv > ufâvoçûâgsokâvê.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in okâv ôjwoç âgqtâmâv (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are ohâvst (beautiful), ohqoç (good), ohâgâvâh (brief), âmâgsoçôg (big/tall), âmâgqê (fat/large), âhstþ (false), œgstû (high), okqoçâm (long), ohâgâvâh (brief), œmâvtoçâv (young), œmqokw (pretty), ôhstôjswê (bad), ôhâvwokokâvtâg (best), oçqtôjâvst (new), øâvûwû (small), ôjwâvtþ (old); e.g., toçâv ohâvokokâv âhâvôhôhâv ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Âhâgâvoçufœg, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Âhâgâvoçufœg personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------

------------------------

         | 2nd (informal)   | ût
         | 2nd (formal)     | ôjqtê
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wok
         | 3rd (feminine)   | âvokokâv
         | 3rd (neutral)    | qoç
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | oçqtê
         | 2nd              | ôjqtê
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wokê
         | 3rd (feminine)   | âvokokâvê
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun œmâv occurs before s, âv, w, q, t, n, âf, î, âk and some occurrences of œg, it becomes œm'.

*Relative pronouns

Âhâgâvoçufœg, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, œçtw is ordinarily used: ok'œgqôhôhâv œçtw s ôjqokâf ôhs ohwufnufokâvûûâv ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that œçtw in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: okâvê ohwufnufokâvûûâvê œçtw qoçû âfûâf ôjqokâfâvê ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, œçtâv (or œçt' before s, âv, w, q, t, n, âf, î and some occurrences of œg) is ordinarily used: oks ohwufnufokâvûûâv œçt'wok s ôjqokâfâv ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like œçtw, œçtâv does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Âhâgâvoçufœg are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Âhâgâvoçufœg is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) sôjqwâg ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of âkûâgâv ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is âkûâgâv, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is sôjqwâg. Forms of âkûâgâv are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Âhâgâvoçufœg, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Âhâgâvoçufœg verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Âhâgâvoçufœg verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -wêê- between the stem and the ending.

    In øsâgokswâvoçû, the stem øsâgok- indicates that the verb is øsâgokâvâg (to speak) and the ending -swâvoçû marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In âhwoçwêêqoçê, the stem âhwoç- indicates that the verb is âhwoçwâg (to finish), the suffix -wêê- follows it, and the inflection -qoçê marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Âhâgâvoçufœg they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    øsâgokâvâg: œmâv øsâgokâvâgswê, ût øsâgoksê, œçt'wokê øsâgoksêêâvoçû, œçtâv oçqtê øsâgokwqoçê, øsâgokâvôm...
    âhwoçwâg: œmâv âhwoçwâgswê, ôjqtê âhwoçbûâvê, œçt'wokê âhwoçwêêâvoçû, âhwoçwê, œçtâv oçqtê âhwoçwêêwqoçê...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ôjqtokqwâg: œmâv ôjâvtþ, ût ôjâvtþ, wok ôjâvtû, oçqtê ôjqtokqoçê, ôjqtê ôjqtokâvôm, wokê ôjâvtokâvoçû.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly sôjqwâg, âkûâgâv, sokokâvâg and âhswâgâv), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -âvâg (with the exception of sokokâvâg, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    swôhâvâg, ohsoksnâvâg, ufœgsoçûâvâg, âvoçôjqnâvâg, âhâvâgôhâvâg, ôhsoçâmâvâg, øsêêâvâg, øsnâvâg, øâgqôhâvoçâvâg, âgâvâmsâgôgâvâg, etc.

        For example, for the verb øsâgokâvâg, the stem is øsâgok- and the ending is -âvâg.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -wâg whose present participle ends in -wêêsoçû:

    ohâfoçwâg, ufqôhøsûwâg, ôgâfâmtâvâgøwâg, âhokâvtâgwâg, âmâgsoçôgwâg, œgsïâg, woçôjâvêûwâg, øqokwâg, âgqtâmwâg, âgtâmwâg, êsokwâg, etc.

        For example, for the verb âhwoçwâg, the stem is âhwoç- and the ending is -wâg.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries âkûâgâv and sôjqwâg, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. œmâv âgâvâmsâgôgâv means "I watch".

    Verbs ending in -âvâg (all verbs of the first group): -âv, -âvê, -âv, -qoçê, -âvôm, -âvoçû.
    Verbs ending in -wâg (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -wê, -wê, -wû, -wêêqoçê, -wêêâvôm, -wêêâvoçû. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -âgâv (part of the third group): -ê, -ê, - , -qoçê, -âvôm, -âvoçû.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "œmâv âgâvâmsâgôgswê" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -âvâg suffix, e.g., âgâvâmsâgôgâvâg -> âgâvâmsâgôg-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -wâg suffix plus the -wêê suffix, e.g., ufœgqwêwâg -> ufœgqwêwêê-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -swê, -swê, -swû, -wqoçê, -wâvôm, -swâvoçû.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -àv (e.g., yñjcèvitàw > yñjcèvitàwàv 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -jèw and -dèw take the ending -èv instead of -àv (e.g., àzèwgjèw > àzèwgjèwàv 'pipes', edèw > edèwàv 'games'), except for the nouns bjàwévjèw, èvjininjèw, kàwdèw, and izbdèw which form their plural by adding -èv (e.g., kàwdèw > kàwdèwèv 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -itèw form their plural with -àv. These are éndàwitèw, ajcbbitèw, éçcizitèw, izceitèw, kitèw, aéçitèw, and eitèweitèw (e.g., éndàwitèw > éndàwitèwàv 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -itèw, such as izcèvitèw or àzinitèw, follow the regular plural pattern and take -èv (e.g., àzinitèw > àzinitèwèv 'holes').

Nouns that end in -èv, -àv or -q in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., bj ainitcàv 'the cross' > bdèv ainitcàv 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -jb typically change to -jèwàv in the plural (e.g., eitèwinàwjb > eitèwinàwjèwàv 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -jb are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -èv instead. These are izjb, ajb, ajinàwjhjb, aéçjajb, ymdèvàzchjb, inuacàzjb, èvdinhjb and inuénjb (e.g., bd ymdèvàzchjb > bdèv ymdèvàzchjbèv).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -jcb change to -jèwàv in the plural. Examples of this pattern include izjcb, aitinjcb, uyñjcb, èvitèwkcinjcb, àzinjhjcb, and hcàzinjcb (e.g., hcàzinjcb > hcàzinjèwàv 'stained glass windows'). However, some -jcb nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -èv, notably injcb, jàzàzcinjcb, aéçjàwévjcb, évuàzjcb, énitèwhdinàwjcb and kitinàzjcb (e.g., èwàw injcb > évdèv injcbèv 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Ymindàwaéç are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Ymindàwaéç adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like izdjèw and àwitèwhdjèw, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with j, d, c, it, èw, g, u, p and some occurrences of éç, e.g. èwàw izdjèw ejinévcàw (a beautiful garden), èwàw izdb éçityñyñd (a handsome man), èwàwd izdbbd ymdyñyñd (a beautiful woman), bdèv izdjèwàv dàwymjàwàzèv (the beautiful children), bdèv izdbbdèv yñjcèvitàwèv (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -d to the masculine form, e.g., éninjàwév > éninjàwévd, bdàwàz > bdàwàzd, kdinèvjàw > kdinèvjàwd. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -db, -cb, -itàw, -dàw, -itèv or -jèv double their final consonant before adding -d (e.g., ainèwdb > ainèwdbbd, éndàwàzcb > éndàwàzcbbd, izitàw > izitàwàwd, jàwacdàw > jàwacdàwàwd, éninitèv > éninitèvèvd, and izjèv > izjèvèvd).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -a change to -aéçd (e.g., izbjàwa > izbjàwaéçd); those ending in -dèwin or -dèwàv change to -dèwèvd (e.g., kinityñdàzàzdèwin > kinityñdàzàzdèwèvd, ymèwincdèwàv > ymèwincdèwèvd), with the exception of the irregular hcdèwàv (old) whose feminine form is hcdcbbd; -én changes to -énèwd (e.g., bitàwén > bitàwénèwd); -cym changes to -chd (e.g., jaàzcym > jaàzchd); -dym changes to -phd (e.g., izindym > izinphd); -din changes to -pind (e.g., uàzinjàwéndin > uàzinjàwénpind); -dàz changes to -pàzd (e.g., càwézèwcdàz > càwézèwcpàzd); and adjectives ending in -itèw have a special form -itb (becoming -itbbd in feminine) that appears before j, d, c, it, èw, g, u, p and some occurrences of éç, (e.g., ymitèw/ymitb > ymitbbd, yñitèw/yñitb > yñitbbd).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -d, it does not change in the feminine (cf. èwàw éçityñyñd incaéçd 'a rich man' > èwàwd ymdyñyñd incaéçd 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -èv to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., eitbc > eitbcèv, eitbcd > eitbcdèv). If the basic form ends in -èv, -àv, or -q, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., izjèv > izjèv, énuàwuindèwàv > énuàwuindèwàv, évitèwàv > évitèwàv), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Ymindàwaéç adjectives ending in -djèw take the ending -àv in the masculine plural (e.g., àwitèwhdjèw > àwitèwhdjèwàv). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -jb, which normally change to -jèwàv in the masculine plural (e.g., éçchdinàwjb > éçchdinàwjèwàv, adàwàzinjb > adàwàzinjèwàv), with only two exceptions: ymjàzjb > ymjàzjbèv and àwjhjb > àwjhjbèv which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: adàwàzinjbd > adàwàzinjbdèv.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in bd hcàw initèwénd (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are izdjèw (beautiful), izitàw (good), izindym (brief), éninjàwév (big/tall), éninitèv (fat/large), ymjèwàv (false), éçjèwàz (high), bitàwén (long), izindym (brief), edèwàwd (young), eitbc (pretty), yñjèwhjcèv (bad), yñdcbbdèwin (best), àwitèwhdjèw (new), kdàzcàz (small), hcdèwàv (old); e.g., èwàwd izdbbd ymdyñyñd ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Ymindàwaéç, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Ymindàwaéç personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | ed
         | 2nd (informal)   | àzèw
         | 2nd (formal)     | hitèwèv
         | 3rd (masculine)  | cb
         | 3rd (feminine)   | dbbd
         | 3rd (neutral)    | itàw
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | àwitèwèv
         | 2nd              | hitèwèv
         | 3rd (masculine)  | cbèv
         | 3rd (feminine)   | dbbdèv
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun ed occurs before j, d, c, it, èw, g, u, p, ê and some occurrences of éç, it becomes e'.

*Relative pronouns

Ymindàwaéç, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, ézèwc is ordinarily used: b'éçityñyñd ézèwc j hitbu yñj izcagabdàzàzd ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that ézèwc in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: bdèv izcagabdàzàzdèv ézèwc itàwàz uàzu hitbudèv ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, ézèwd (or ézèw' before j, d, c, it, èw, g, u, p and some occurrences of éç) is ordinarily used: bj izcagabdàzàzd ézèw'cb j hitbud ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like ézèwc, ézèwd does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Ymindàwaéç are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Ymindàwaéç is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) jhitcin ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êàzind ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êàzind, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is jhitcin. Forms of êàzind are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Ymindàwaéç, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Ymindàwaéç verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Ymindàwaéç verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -cèvèv- between the stem and the ending.

    In kjinbjcdàwàz, the stem kjinb- indicates that the verb is kjinbdin (to speak) and the ending -jcdàwàz marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In ymcàwcèvèvitàwèv, the stem ymcàw- indicates that the verb is ymcàwcin (to finish), the suffix -cèvèv- follows it, and the inflection -itàwèv marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Ymindàwaéç they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    kjinbdin: ed kjinbdinjcèv, àzèw kjinbjèv, ézèw'cbèv kjinbjèvèvdàwàz, ézèwd àwitèwèv kjinbcitàwèv, kjinbdq...
    ymcàwcin: ed ymcàwcinjcèv, hitèwèv ymcàwîàzdèv, ézèw'cbèv ymcàwcèvèvdàwàz, ymcàwcèv, ézèwd àwitèwèv ymcàwcèvèvcitàwèv...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    hitèwbitcin: ed hdèwàv, àzèw hdèwàv, cb hdèwàz, àwitèwèv hitèwbitàwèv, hitèwèv hitèwbdq, cbèv hdèwbdàwàz.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly jhitcin, êàzind, jbbdin and ymjcind), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -din (with the exception of jbbdin, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    jcyñdin, izjbjgdin, aéçjàwàzdin, dàwhitgdin, ymdinyñdin, yñjàwéndin, kjèvèvdin, kjgdin, kinityñdàwdin, indénjinévdin, etc.

        For example, for the verb kjinbdin, the stem is kjinb- and the ending is -din.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -cin whose present participle ends in -cèvèvjàwàz:

    izuàwcin, aityñkjàzcin, évuénèwdinkcin, ymbdèwincin, éninjàwévcin, éçjïin, càwhdèvàzcin, kitbcin, initèwéncin, inèwéncin, èvjbcin, etc.

        For example, for the verb ymcàwcin, the stem is ymcàw- and the ending is -cin.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êàzind and jhitcin, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. ed indénjinévd means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -din (all verbs of the first group): -d, -dèv, -d, -itàwèv, -dq, -dàwàz.
    Verbs ending in -cin (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -cèv, -cèv, -càz, -cèvèvitàwèv, -cèvèvdq, -cèvèvdàwàz. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -ind (part of the third group): -èv, -èv, - , -itàwèv, -dq, -dàwàz.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "ed indénjinévjcèv" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -din suffix, e.g., indénjinévdin -> indénjinév-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -cin suffix plus the -cèvèv suffix, e.g., aéçitcèvcin -> aéçitcèvcèvèv-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -jcèv, -jcèv, -jcàz, -citàwèv, -cdq, -jcdàwàz.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -d and -èv, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "èwàw yminèwcàz aitàwymcàz", "èwàwd kitcind aitàwymcàzd", "évdèv yminèwcàzèv aitàwymcàzèv", and "évdèv kitcindèv aitàwymcàzdèv."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -u for the 1st group verbs, or in -c for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -èw (dàwàzdàwévind dàwàzdàwévèw, izitcind izèw, bcind bèw, etc. and èvjhitcin èvèw, hitcin hèw, kitèwhitcin kèw), -cèv (yñdàzàzind yñcèv, kindàwévind kincèv, etc.), -èwèv (càwabèwind càwabèwèv and indabèwind indabèwèv and only these verbs), -càz (yñjèwévcind yñjèwévcàz, évcind évcàz, etc.), -àz (verbs in -càwévind : kdcàwévind kdcàwàz), -dinàz (itèwhincin itèwhdinàz, aitèwhincin aitèwhdinàz, itymymincin itymymdinàz and èvitèwymymincin èvitèwymymdinàz), or dèw (jhitcin dèw). 

*Compound Tenses

Ymindàwaéç compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either jhitcin or êàzind) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Ymindàwaéç, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Ymindàwaéç. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either jhitcin or êàzind in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "e'jc yñjàwénu" (I ate) or "cb dèvàz jininchu" (He arrived). jhitcin is used with most verbs, while êàzind is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, jhitcin should be used by default.

Example:

1st Group: indénjinévdin (to watch)

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Eleçimgokh is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    id’evuéeçim xim okhéokéxevom (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Eleçimgokh, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Eleçimgokh has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Eleçimgokh, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Eleçimgokh article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is xim. For example, in the phrase "xim okhevom" (the cat), xim shows that the noun okhevom (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is xev. An example is "xev akevqfég" (the house), where xev shows that akevqfég (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is ximf for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "ximf okhevomf", the cats; "ximf akevqfégf", the houses.)

In summary, xim is used with masculine singular nouns, xev with feminine singular nouns, and ximf with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Eleçimgokh.

Before ev, im, q, é, av, s, r, ot and some occurrences of h, the singular masculine article xim becomes x'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Eleçimgokh noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Eleçimgokh nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -b (e.g., akevqfég > akevqfégb 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -evav and -imav take the ending -f instead of -b (e.g., omavsevav > omavsevavb 'pipes', idimav > idimavb 'games'), except for the nouns xevguevav, feveçeçevav, pgimav, and azximav which form their plural by adding -f (e.g., pgimav > pgimavf 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -éav form their plural with -b. These are nimgéav, okevqxxéav, hqazéav, azqidéav, péav, okhéav, and idéavidéav (e.g., nimgéav > nimgéavb 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -éav, such as azqféav or omeçéav, follow the regular plural pattern and take -f (e.g., omeçéav > omeçéavf 'holes').

Nouns that end in -f, -b or -w in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., xev okeçéqb 'the cross' > ximf okeçéqb 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -evx typically change to -evavb in the plural (e.g., idéaveçgevx > idéaveçgevavb 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -evx are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -f instead. These are azevx, okevx, okeveçgevejevx, okhevokevx, cimfomqejevx, eçrokqomevx, fimeçejevx and eçrnevx (e.g., xim cimfomqejevx > ximf cimfomqejevxf).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -evqx change to -evavb in the plural. Examples of this pattern include azevqx, okéeçevqx, rakevqx, féavpqeçevqx, omeçevejevqx, and ejqomeçevqx (e.g., ejqomeçevqx > ejqomeçevavb 'stained glass windows'). However, some -evqx nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -f, notably eçevqx, evomomqeçevqx, okhevguevqx, uromevqx, néavejimeçgevqx and péeçomevqx (e.g., avg eçevqx > uimf eçevqxf 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Eleçimgokh are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Eleçimgokh adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like azimevav and géavejimevav, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ev, im, q, é, av, s, r, ot and some occurrences of h, e.g. avg azimevav ideveçuqg (a beautiful garden), avg azimx héakakim (a handsome man), avgim azimxxim cimakakim (a beautiful woman), ximf azimevavb imgcevgomf (the beautiful children), ximf azimxximf akevqfégf (the beautiful houses).

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -imx, -qx, -ég, -img, -éf or -evf double their final consonant before adding -im (e.g., okeçavimx > okeçavimxxim, nimgomqx > nimgomqxxim, azég > azéggim, evgokqimg > evgokqimggim, neçéf > neçéffim, and azevf > azevffim).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -im, it does not change in the feminine (cf. avg héakakim eçqokhim 'a rich man' > avgim cimakakim eçqokhim 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -f to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., idéxq > idéxqf, idéxqim > idéxqimf). If the basic form ends in -f, -b, or -w, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., azevf > azevf, nrgreçimavb > nrgreçimavb, uéavb > uéavb), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in xim ejqg eçéavnim (the red wine). In Eleçimgokh, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Eleçimgokh personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

Eleçimgokh, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, ozavq is ordinarily used: x'héakakim ozavq ev ejéxr akev azqoksokximomomim ("the man who stole my bike"). VERBS
-----
Verbs in Eleçimgokh are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). The most common word order in Àzbàpuxoràw is subject-verb-object (SVO).

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Àzbàpuxoràw, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
Àzbàpuxoràw has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Àzbàpuxoràw, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Àzbàpuxoràw article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is çàp. For example, in the phrase "çàp oràwléz" (the cat), çàp shows that the noun oràwléz (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is çl. An example is "çl clehdux" (the house), where çl shows that clehdux (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is çàph for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "çàph oràwlézh", the cats; "çàph clehduxh", the houses.)

In summary, çàp is used with masculine singular nouns, çl with feminine singular nouns, and çàph with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Àzbàpuxoràw.

Before l, àp, e, d, j, t, èk, us and some occurrences of àw, the singular masculine article çàp becomes ç'.

Every Àzbàpuxoràw noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

As in English, Àzbàpuxoràw nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -f (e.g., clehdux > clehduxf 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -lj and -àpj take the ending -h instead of -f (e.g., ézjtlj > ézjtljf 'pipes', énàpj > énàpjf 'games'), except for the nouns çluxmlj, hlbblj, auxàpj, and àxçàpj which form their plural by adding -h (e.g., auxàpj > auxàpjh 'tires').

Nouns that end in -h, -f or -uk in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., çl orbdef 'the cross' > çàph orbdef 'the crosses').

Nouns in Àzbàpuxoràw are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Àzbàpuxoràw adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like àxàplj and uxdjqàplj, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with l, àp, e, d, j, t, èk, us and some occurrences of àw, e.g. jux àxàplj énlbmeux (a beautiful garden), jux àxàpç àwdccàp (a handsome man), juxàp àxàpççàp yàpccàp (a beautiful woman), çàph àxàpljf àpuxyluxézh (the beautiful children), çàph àxàpççàph clehduxh (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -àp to the masculine form, e.g., ozbluxm > ozbluxmàp, çàpuxéz > çàpuxézàp, aàpbhlux > aàpbhluxàp. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -àpç, -eç, -dux, -àpux, -dh or -lh double their final consonant before adding -àp (e.g., orbjàpç > orbjàpççàp, ozàpuxézeç > ozàpuxézeççàp, àxdux > àxduxuxàp, luxoreàpux > luxoreàpuxuxàp, ozbdh > ozbdhhàp, and àxlh > àxlhhàp).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -or change to -oràwàp (e.g., àxçluxor > àxçluxoràwàp); those ending in -àpjb or -àpjf change to -àpjhàp (e.g., abdcàpézézàpjb > abdcàpézézàpjhàp, yjbeàpjf > yjbeàpjhàp), with the exception of the irregular qeàpjf (old) whose feminine form is qeàpeççàp; -oz changes to -ozjàp (e.g., çduxoz > çduxozjàp); -ey changes to -eqàp (e.g., lorézey > lorézeqàp); -àpy changes to -usqàp (e.g., àxbàpy > àxbusqàp); -àpb changes to -usbàp (e.g., èkézbluxozàpb > èkézbluxozusbàp); -àpéz changes to -usézàp (e.g., euxijeàpéz > euxijeusézàp); and adjectives ending in -dj have a special form -dç (becoming -dççàp in feminine) that appears before l, àp, e, d, j, t, èk, us and some occurrences of àw, (e.g., ydj/ydç > ydççàp, cdj/cdç > cdççàp).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -àp, it does not change in the feminine (cf. jux àwdccàp beoràwàp 'a rich man' > juxàp yàpccàp beoràwàp 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -h to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., éndçe > éndçeh, éndçeàp > éndçeàph). If the basic form ends in -h, -f, or -uk, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., àxlh > àxlh, ozèkuxèkbàpjf > ozèkuxèkbàpjf, mdjf > mdjf), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Àzbàpuxoràw adjectives ending in -àplj take the ending -f in the masculine plural (e.g., uxdjqàplj > uxdjqàpljf). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -lç, which normally change to -ljf in the masculine plural (e.g., àweqàpbuxlç > àweqàpbuxljf, oràpuxézblç > oràpuxézbljf), with only two exceptions: ylézlç > ylézlçh and uxlqlç > uxlqlçh which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: oràpuxézblçàp > oràpuxézblçàph.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in çàp qeux bdjozàp (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are àxàplj (beautiful), àxdux (good), àxbàpy (brief), ozbluxm (big/tall), ozbdh (fat/large), yljf (false), àwljéz (high), çduxoz (long), àxbàpy (brief), énàpjuxàp (young), éndçe (pretty), cljqleh (bad), càpeççàpjb (best), uxdjqàplj (new), aàpézeéz (small), qeàpjf (old); e.g., juxàp àxàpççàp yàpccàp ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Àzbàpuxoràw, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Àzbàpuxoràw personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | énàp
         | 2nd (informal)   | ézj
         | 2nd (formal)     | qdjh
         | 3rd (masculine)  | eç
         | 3rd (feminine)   | àpççàp
         | 3rd (neutral)    | dux
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | uxdjh
         | 2nd              | qdjh
         | 3rd (masculine)  | eçh
         | 3rd (feminine)   | àpççàph
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun énàp occurs before l, àp, e, d, j, t, èk, us, ê and some occurrences of àw, it becomes én'.

*Relative pronouns

Àzbàpuxoràw, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, ije is ordinarily used: ç'àwdccàp ije l qdçèk cl àxeortorçàpézézàp ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that ije in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: çàph àxeortorçàpézézàph ije duxéz èkézèk qdçèkàph ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, ijàp (or ij' before l, àp, e, d, j, t, èk, us and some occurrences of àw) is ordinarily used: çl àxeortorçàpézézàp ij'eç l qdçèkàp ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like ije, ijàp does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Àzbàpuxoràw are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Àzbàpuxoràw is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) lqdeb ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êézbàp ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êézbàp, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is lqdeb. Forms of êézbàp are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Àzbàpuxoràw, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Àzbàpuxoràw verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Àzbàpuxoràw verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -ehh- between the stem and the ending.

    In albçleàpuxéz, the stem albç- indicates that the verb is albçàpb (to speak) and the ending -leàpuxéz marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In yeuxehhduxh, the stem yeux- indicates that the verb is yeuxeb (to finish), the suffix -ehh- follows it, and the inflection -duxh marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Àzbàpuxoràw they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    albçàpb: énàp albçàpbleh, ézj albçlh, ij'eçh albçlhhàpuxéz, ijàp uxdjh albçeduxh, albçàpuk...
    yeuxeb: énàp yeuxebleh, qdjh yeuxîézàph, ij'eçh yeuxehhàpuxéz, yeuxeh, ijàp uxdjh yeuxehheduxh...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    qdjçdeb: énàp qàpjf, ézj qàpjf, eç qàpjéz, uxdjh qdjçduxh, qdjh qdjçàpuk, eçh qàpjçàpuxéz.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly lqdeb, êézbàp, lççàpb and ylebàp), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -àpb (with the exception of lççàpb, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    lecàpb, àxlçltàpb, oràwluxézàpb, àpuxqdtàpb, yàpbcàpb, cluxozàpb, alhhàpb, altàpb, abdcàpuxàpb, bàpozlbmàpb, etc.

        For example, for the verb albçàpb, the stem is albç- and the ending is -àpb.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -eb whose present participle ends in -ehhluxéz:

    àxèkuxeb, ordcalézeb, mèkozjàpbaeb, yçàpjbeb, ozbluxmeb, àwlïb, euxqàphézeb, adçeb, bdjozeb, bjozeb, hlçeb, etc.

        For example, for the verb yeuxeb, the stem is yeux- and the ending is -eb.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êézbàp and lqdeb, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. énàp bàpozlbmàp means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -àpb (all verbs of the first group): -àp, -àph, -àp, -duxh, -àpuk, -àpuxéz.
    Verbs ending in -eb (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -eh, -eh, -eéz, -ehhduxh, -ehhàpuk, -ehhàpuxéz. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -bàp (part of the third group): -h, -h, - , -duxh, -àpuk, -àpuxéz.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "énàp bàpozlbmleh" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -àpb suffix, e.g., bàpozlbmàpb -> bàpozlbm-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -eb suffix plus the -ehh suffix, e.g., oràwdeheb -> oràwdehehh-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -leh, -leh, -leéz, -eduxh, -eàpuk, -leàpuxéz.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -àp and -h, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "jux ybjeéz orduxyeéz", "juxàp adebàp orduxyeézàp", "màph ybjeézh orduxyeézh", and "màph adebàph orduxyeézàph."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -èk for the 1st group verbs, or in -e for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -j (àpuxézàpuxmbàp àpuxézàpuxmj, àxdebàp àxj, çebàp çj, etc. and hlqdeb hj, qdeb qj, adjqdeb aj), -eh (càpézézbàp ceh, abàpuxmbàp abeh, etc.), -jh (euxorçjbàp euxorçjh and bàporçjbàp bàporçjh and only these verbs), -eéz (cljmebàp cljmeéz, mebàp meéz, etc.), -éz (verbs in -euxmbàp : aàpeuxmbàp aàpeuxéz), -àpbéz (djqbeb djqàpbéz, ordjqbeb ordjqàpbéz, dyybeb dyyàpbéz and hdjyybeb hdjyyàpbéz), or àpj (lqdeb àpj). 

*Compound Tenses

Àzbàpuxoràw compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either lqdeb or êézbàp) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Àzbàpuxoràw, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Àzbàpuxoràw. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either lqdeb or êézbàp in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "én'le cluxozèk" (I ate) or "eç àphéz lbbeqèk" (He arrived). lqdeb is used with most verbs, while êézbàp is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, lqdeb should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Àzbàpuxoràw: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is lqdeb.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) àpççàph duxéz mdbce. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) orçlebàp l qj màpjf àxlçàpeuxàph. ("orçlebàp saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) eç t lqleéz màpjf àxlçàpeuxàph. orçlebàp çàph l qjàph. ("There were two whales. orçlebàp saw them.")

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

         | 3rd (feminine)   | îjttîj
         | 3rd (neutral)    | âéz

*Relative pronouns

Îwøpîjézaf, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, øcrec is ordinarily used: t'fâssîj øcrec év èâtêp sév îçecaœatîjbbîj ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that øcrec in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: tîjô îçecaœatîjbbîjô øcrec âézb êpbêp èâtêpîjô ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, øcrîj (or øcr' before év, îj, ec, â, r, œ, êp, û and some occurrences of f) is ordinarily used: tév îçecaœatîjbbîj øcr'ect év èâtêpîj ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like øcrec, øcrîj does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Îwøpîjézaf are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Îwøpîjézaf is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) évèâecøp ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of ønbøpîj ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is ønbøpîj, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is évèâecøp. Forms of ønbøpîj are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Îwøpîjézaf, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Îwøpîjézaf verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Îwøpîjézaf verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -ecôô- between the stem and the ending.

    In êzévøptévecîjézb, the stem êzévøpt- indicates that the verb is êzévøptîjøp (to speak) and the ending -évecîjézb marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In àecézecôôâézô, the stem àecéz- indicates that the verb is àecézecøp (to finish), the suffix -ecôô- follows it, and the inflection -âézô marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Îwøpîjézaf they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    êzévøptîjøp: gîj êzévøptîjøpévecô, br êzévøptévô, øcr'ectô êzévøptévôôîjézb, øcrîj ézârô êzévøptecâézô, êzévøptîji...
    àecézecøp: gîj àecézecøpévecô, èârô àecézøjbîjô, øcr'ectô àecézecôôîjézb, àecézecô, øcrîj ézârô àecézecôôecâézô...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    èârtâecøp: gîj èîjro, br èîjro, ect èîjrb, ézârô èârtâézô, èârô èârtîji, ectô èîjrtîjézb.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly évèâecøp, ønbøpîj, évttîjøp and àévecøpîj), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -îjøp (with the exception of évttîjøp, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    évecsîjøp, îçévtévœîjøp, afévézbîjøp, îjézèâœîjøp, àîjøpsîjøp, sévézkîjøp, êzévôôîjøp, êzévœîjøp, êzøpâsîjézîjøp, øpîjkévøpmîjøp, etc.

        For example, for the verb êzévøptîjøp, the stem is êzévøpt- and the ending is -îjøp.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ecøp whose present participle ends in -ecôôévézb:

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries ønbøpîj and évèâecøp, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately.

**Past participle

*Compound Tenses

Îwøpîjézaf compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either évèâecøp or ønbøpîj) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Îwøpîjézaf, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Îwøpîjézaf. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either évèâecøp or ønbøpîj in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "g'évec sévézkêp" (I ate) or "ect îjôb évøpøpecèêp" (He arrived). évèâecøp is used with most verbs, while ønbøpîj is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, évèâecøp should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Îwøpîjézaf: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is évèâecøp.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) îjttîjô âézb mâøpsec. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) atévecøpîj év èr mîjro îçévtîjecézîjô. ("atévecøpîj saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) ect œ évèévecb mîjro îçévtîjecézîjô. atévecøpîj tîjô év èrîjô. ("There were two whales. atévecøpîj saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) øcrîjttîjô îçévtîjecézîjô atévecøpîj év-b-îjttîj èrîjô ? ("Which whales did atévecøpîj see?")
        (relative clause introduced by øcrîj) tîjô mîjro îçévtîjecézîjô øcrîj atévecøpîj év èrîjô ("the two whales that atévecøpîj saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Îwøpîjézaf.

B. The auxiliary is ønbøpîj, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        îjttîjô ôâézb évøpøpecèêpîjô. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is ønbøpîj and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with évèâecøp in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears after the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) îjttîjô ôîj ôâézb ôraaêpmêp. ézârô ézârô ôâssîjô êzévøptêp. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object after verb) îjttîjô ôîj ôâézb êzâôêp mîjô øcrîjôbecâézô. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears before the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).
        (direct object pronoun) g'évec àévecb rézîj bévøpbîj. tîjô îjézàévézbô ôîj tév ôâézb êzévøpbévkêpîj. ("I made a pie. The children shared it.")
        (wh-question) øcrîjttîj bévøpbîj ôîj ôâézb-ectô êzévøpbévkêpîj ? ("Which pie did they share?")
        (øcrîj relative) tév bévøpbîj øcrîj tîjô îjézàévézbô ôîj ôâézb êzévøpbévkêpîj ("the pie that the children shared")

    The reflexive pronoun can itself be the direct object, in which case the participle agrees with it (and therefore with the subject). This also includes "inherently reflexive" verbs, for which the reflexive pronoun cannot be interpreted semantically as an object (direct or indirect) of the verb.
        (ordinary reflexive) îjttîjô ôîj ôâézb ôrecèecîjô. ézârô ézârô ôâssîjô ôévtrêpô. ("They (fem.) followed each other. We greeted each other.")
        (inherently reflexive) ectô ôîj ôâézb sâøcrêpô mîj sâec. ézârô ézârô ôâssîjô ôârèîjézrô mîj t'êpèêpézîjsîjézb. ("They made fun of me. We remembered the event.")

Pàydagolde has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Pàydagolde, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Pàydagolde article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is geda. For example, in the phrase "geda ldesvo" (the cat), geda shows that the noun ldesvo (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is ges. An example is "ges csiçhégo" (the house), where ges shows that csiçhégo (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is gedaç for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "gedaç ldesvoç", the cats; "gedaç csiçhégoç", the houses.)

In summary, geda is used with masculine singular nouns, ges with feminine singular nouns, and gedaç with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Pàydagolde.

Before s, da, i, hé, fé, bà, fo, dé and some occurrences of de, the singular masculine article geda becomes ge'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Pàydagolde noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Pàydagolde nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -r (e.g., csiçhégo > csiçhégor 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -sfé and -dafé take the ending -ç instead of -r (e.g., vofébàsfé > vofébàsfér 'pipes', zdafé > zdafér 'games'), except for the nouns gesgoqsfé, çsyysfé, jgodafé, and wgedafé which form their plural by adding -ç (e.g., jgodafé > jgodaféç 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -héfé form their plural with -r. These are bedagohéfé, lsigegehéfé, deiwhéfé, wizhéfé, jhéfé, ldehéfé, and zhéfézhéfé (e.g., bedagohéfé > bedagohéfér 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -héfé, such as wiçhéfé or voyhéfé, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ç (e.g., voyhéfé > voyhéféç 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ç, -r or -m in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., ges lyhéir 'the cross' > gedaç lyhéir 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -sge typically change to -sfér in the plural (e.g., zhéféygosge > zhéféygosfér 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -sge are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ç instead. These are wsge, lsge, lsygosksge, ldeslsge, pàdaçvoiksge, yfolivosge, çdayksge and yfobesge (e.g., geda pàdaçvoiksge > gedaç pàdaçvoiksgeç).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -sige change to -sfér in the plural. Examples of this pattern include wsige, lhéysige, focsige, çhéféjiysige, voysksige, and kivoysige (e.g., kivoysige > kivoysfér 'stained glass windows'). However, some -sige nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ç, notably ysige, svovoiysige, ldesgoqsige, qfovosige, behéfékdaygosige and jhéyvosige (e.g., fégo ysige > qdaç ysigeç 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Pàydagolde are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Pàydagolde adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like wdasfé and gohéfékdasfé, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with s, da, i, hé, fé, bà, fo, dé and some occurrences of de, e.g. fégo wdasfé zsyqigo (a beautiful garden), fégo wdage dehéccda (a handsome man), fégoda wdagegeda pàdaccda (a beautiful woman), gedaç wdasfér dagopàsgovoç (the beautiful children), gedaç wdagegedaç csiçhégoç (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -da to the masculine form, e.g., beysgoq > beysgoqda, gedagovo > gedagovoda, jdayçsgo > jdayçsgoda. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -dage, -ige, -hégo, -dago, -héç or -sç double their final consonant before adding -da (e.g., lyfédage > lyfédagegeda, bedagovoige > bedagovoigegeda, whégo > whégogoda, sgolidago > sgolidagogoda, beyhéç > beyhéççda, and wsç > wsççda).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -l change to -ldeda (e.g., wgesgol > wgesgoldeda); those ending in -daféy or -dafér change to -daféçda (e.g., jyhécdavovodaféy > jyhécdavovodaféçda, pàféyidafér > pàféyidaféçda), with the exception of the irregular kidafér (old) whose feminine form is kidaigegeda; -be changes to -beféda (e.g., gehégobe > gehégobeféda); -ipà changes to -ikda (e.g., slvoipà > slvoikda); -dapà changes to -dékda (e.g., wydapà > wydékda); -day changes to -déyda (e.g., fovoysgobeday > fovoysgobedéyda); -davo changes to -dévoda (e.g., igonoféidavo > igonoféidévoda); and adjectives ending in -héfé have a special form -hége (becoming -hégegeda in feminine) that appears before s, da, i, hé, fé, bà, fo, dé and some occurrences of de, (e.g., pàhéfé/pàhége > pàhégegeda, chéfé/chége > chégegeda).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -da, it does not change in the feminine (cf. fégo dehéccda yildeda 'a rich man' > fégoda pàdaccda yildeda 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ç to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., zhégei > zhégeiç, zhégeida > zhégeidaç). If the basic form ends in -ç, -r, or -m, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., wsç > wsç, befogofoydafér > befogofoydafér, qhéfér > qhéfér), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Pàydagolde adjectives ending in -dasfé take the ending -r in the masculine plural (e.g., gohéfékdasfé > gohéfékdasfér). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -sge, which normally change to -sfér in the masculine plural (e.g., deikdaygosge > deikdaygosfér, ldagovoysge > ldagovoysfér), with only two exceptions: pàsvosge > pàsvosgeç and gosksge > gosksgeç which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ldagovoysgeda > ldagovoysgedaç.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in geda kigo yhéfébeda (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are wdasfé (beautiful), whégo (good), wydapà (brief), beysgoq (big/tall), beyhéç (fat/large), pàsfér (false), desfévo (high), gehégobe (long), wydapà (brief), zdafégoda (young), zhégei (pretty), csféksiç (bad), cdaigegedaféy (best), gohéfékdasfé (new), jdavoivo (small), kidafér (old); e.g., fégoda wdagegeda pàdaccda ("a beautiful woman").
