*Compound Tenses

Ômiwîcîjr compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either émpâxèi or écékiw) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Ômiwîcîjr, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Ômiwîcîjr. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either émpâxèi or écékiw in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "g'émè ôtémîcàîk" (I ate) or "èâç wœék émiièpîk" (He arrived). émpâxèi is used with most verbs, while écékiw is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, émpâxèi should be used by default.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -çè (e.g., votlafeçe > votlafeçeçè 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -txà and -éxà take the ending -a instead of -çè (e.g., rxàbotxà > rxàbotxàçè 'pipes', yéxà > yéxàçè 'games'), except for the nouns zetçehtxà, atjjtxà, zèçeéxà, and szeéxà which form their plural by adding -a (e.g., zèçeéxà > zèçeéxàa 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -fexà form their plural with -çè. These are déçefexà, zotlzezefexà, plsfexà, slyfexà, zèfexà, zopfexà, and yfexàyfexà (e.g., déçefexà > déçefexàçè 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -fexà, such as slafexà or rjfexà, follow the regular plural pattern and take -a (e.g., rjfexà > rjfexàa 'holes').

Nouns that end in -a, -çè or -u in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., zet zojfelçè 'the cross' > zeéa zojfelçè 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -tze typically change to -txàçè in the plural (e.g., yfexàjçetze > yfexàjçetxàçè 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -tze are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -a instead. These are stze, zotze, zotjçetgotze, zoptzotze, ciéarlgotze, jmzolrtze, aéjgotze and jmdtze (e.g., zeé ciéarlgotze > zeéa ciéarlgotzea).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -tlze change to -txàçè in the plural. Examples of this pattern include stlze, zofejtlze, mvotlze, afexàzèljtlze, rjtgotlze, and golrjtlze (e.g., golrjtlze > golrjtxàçè 'stained glass windows'). However, some -tlze nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -a, notably jtlze, trrljtlze, zoptçehtlze, hmrtlze, dfexàgoéjçetlze and zèfejrtlze (e.g., xàçe jtlze > héa jtlzea 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Cijéçezop are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Cijéçezop adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like sétxà and çefexàgoétxà, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with t, é, l, fe, xà, bo, m, k and some occurrences of p, e.g. xàçe sétxà ytjhlçe (a beautiful garden), xàçe séze pfevovoé (a handsome man), xàçeé sézezeé ciévovoé (a beautiful woman), zeéa sétxàçè éçecitçera (the beautiful children), zeéa sézezeéa votlafeçea (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -é to the masculine form, e.g., djtçeh > djtçehé, zeéçer > zeéçeré, zèéjatçe > zèéjatçeé. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -éze, -lze, -feçe, -éçe, -fea or -ta double their final consonant before adding -é (e.g., zojxàéze > zojxàézezeé, déçerlze > déçerlzezeé, sfeçe > sfeçeçeé, tçezoléçe > tçezoléçeçeé, djfea > djfeaaé, and sta > staaé).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -zo change to -zopé (e.g., szetçezo > szetçezopé); those ending in -éxàj or -éxàçè change to -éxàaé (e.g., zèjfevoérréxàj > zèjfevoérréxàaé, cixàjléxàçè > cixàjléxàaé), with the exception of the irregular goléxàçè (old) whose feminine form is golélzezeé; -d changes to -dxàé (e.g., zefeçed > zefeçedxàé); -lci changes to -lgoé (e.g., tzorlci > tzorlgoé); -éci changes to -kgoé (e.g., sjéci > sjkgoé); -éj changes to -kjé (e.g., mrjtçedéj > mrjtçedkjé); -ér changes to -kré (e.g., lçebixàlér > lçebixàlkré); and adjectives ending in -fexà have a special form -feze (becoming -fezezeé in feminine) that appears before t, é, l, fe, xà, bo, m, k and some occurrences of p, (e.g., cifexà/cifeze > cifezezeé, vofexà/vofeze > vofezezeé).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -é, it does not change in the feminine (cf. xàçe pfevovoé jlzopé 'a rich man' > xàçeé ciévovoé jlzopé 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -a to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., yfezel > yfezela, yfezelé > yfezeléa). If the basic form ends in -a, -çè, or -u, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., sta > sta, dmçemjéxàçè > dmçemjéxàçè, hfexàçè > hfexàçè), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Cijéçezop adjectives ending in -étxà take the ending -çè in the masculine plural (e.g., çefexàgoétxà > çefexàgoétxàçè). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -tze, which normally change to -txàçè in the masculine plural (e.g., plgoéjçetze > plgoéjçetxàçè, zoéçerjtze > zoéçerjtxàçè), with only two exceptions: citrtze > citrtzea and çetgotze > çetgotzea which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: zoéçerjtzeé > zoéçerjtzeéa.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in zeé golçe jfexàdé (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are sétxà (beautiful), sfeçe (good), sjéci (brief), djtçeh (big/tall), djfea (fat/large), citxàçè (false), ptxàr (high), zefeçed (long), sjéci (brief), yéxàçeé (young), yfezel (pretty), votxàgotla (bad), voélzezeéxàj (best), çefexàgoétxà (new), zèérlr (small), goléxàçè (old); e.g., xàçeé sézezeé ciévovoé ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Cijéçezop, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Cijéçezop personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | yé
         | 2nd (informal)   | rxà
         | 2nd (formal)     | gofexàa
         | 3rd (masculine)  | lze
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ézezeé
         | 3rd (neutral)    | feçe
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | çefexàa
         | 2nd              | gofexàa
         | 3rd (masculine)  | lzea
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ézezeéa
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun yé occurs before t, é, l, fe, xà, bo, m, k, ê and some occurrences of p, it becomes y'.

*Relative pronouns

Cijéçezop, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, bixàl is ordinarily used: ze'pfevovoé bixàl t gofezem vot slzobozozeérré ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that bixàl in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: zeéa slzobozozeérréa bixàl feçer mrm gofezeméa ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, bixàé (or bixà' before t, é, l, fe, xà, bo, m, k and some occurrences of p) is ordinarily used: zet slzobozozeérré bixà'lze t gofezemé ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like bixàl, bixàé does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Cijéçezop are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Cijéçezop is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) tgofelj ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êrjé ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êrjé, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is tgofelj. Forms of êrjé are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Cijéçezop, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Cijéçezop verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Cijéçezop verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -laa- between the stem and the ending.

    In zètjzetléçer, the stem zètjze- indicates that the verb is zètjzeéj (to speak) and the ending -tléçer marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In cilçelaafeçea, the stem cilçe- indicates that the verb is cilçelj (to finish), the suffix -laa- follows it, and the inflection -feçea marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Cijéçezop they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    zètjzeéj: yé zètjzeéjtla, rxà zètjzeta, bixà'lzea zètjzetaaéçer, bixàé çefexàa zètjzelfeçea, zètjzeéu...
    cilçelj: yé cilçeljtla, gofexàa cilçeîréa, bixà'lzea cilçelaaéçer, cilçela, bixàé çefexàa cilçelaalfeçea...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    gofexàzefelj: yé goéxàçè, rxà goéxàçè, lze goéxàr, çefexàa gofexàzefeçea, gofexàa gofexàzeéu, lzea goéxàzeéçer.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly tgofelj, êrjé, tzezeéj and citljé), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -éj (with the exception of tzezeéj, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    tlvoéj, stzetboéj, zoptçeréj, éçegofeboéj, ciéjvoéj, votçedéj, zètaaéj, zètboéj, zèjfevoéçeéj, jédtjhéj, etc.

        For example, for the verb zètjzeéj, the stem is zètjze- and the ending is -éj.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -lj whose present participle ends in -laatçer:

    smçelj, zofevozètrlj, hmdxàéjzèlj, cizeéxàjlj, djtçehlj, ptïj, lçegoéarlj, zèfezelj, jfexàdlj, jxàdlj, atzelj, etc.

        For example, for the verb cilçelj, the stem is cilçe- and the ending is -lj.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êrjé and tgofelj, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. yé jédtjhé means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -éj (all verbs of the first group): -é, -éa, -é, -feçea, -éu, -éçer.
    Verbs ending in -lj (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -la, -la, -lr, -laafeçea, -laaéu, -laaéçer. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -jé (part of the third group): -a, -a, - , -feçea, -éu, -éçer.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "yé jédtjhtla" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -éj suffix, e.g., jédtjhéj -> jédtjh-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -lj suffix plus the -laa suffix, e.g., zopfelalj -> zopfelalaa-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -tla, -tla, -tlr, -lfeçea, -léu, -tléçer.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -é and -a, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "xàçe cijxàlr zofeçecilr", "xàçeé zèfeljé zofeçecilré", "héa cijxàlra zofeçecilra", and "héa zèfeljéa zofeçecilréa."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -m for the 1st group verbs, or in -l for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -xà (éçeréçehjé éçeréçehxà, sfeljé sxà, zeljé zexà, etc. and atgofelj axà, gofelj goxà, zèfexàgofelj zèxà), -la (voérrjé vola, zèjéçehjé zèjla, etc.), -xàa (lçezozexàjé lçezozexàa and jézozexàjé jézozexàa and only these verbs), -lr (votxàhljé votxàhlr, hljé hlr, etc.), -r (verbs in -lçehjé : zèélçehjé zèélçer), -éjr (fexàgojlj fexàgoéjr, zofexàgojlj zofexàgoéjr, fecicijlj feciciéjr and afexàcicijlj afexàciciéjr), or éxà (tgofelj éxà). 

*Compound Tenses

Cijéçezop compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either tgofelj or êrjé) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Cijéçezop, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Cijéçezop. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either tgofelj or êrjé in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "y'tl votçedm" (I ate) or "lze éar tjjlgom" (He arrived). tgofelj is used with most verbs, while êrjé is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, tgofelj should be used by default.

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -teé, -noé, -às, -tes, -àje or -cje double their final consonant before adding -te (e.g., kzototeé > kzototeééte, çtesènoé > çtesènoééte, quàs > quàsste, csknotes > csknotesste, çzoàje > çzoàjejete, and qucje > qucjejete).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -k change to -kdte (e.g., quécsk > quécskdte); those ending in -tetozo or -tetox change to -tetojete (e.g., vzoàbteèètetozo > vzoàbteèètetojete, retozonotetox > retozonotetojete), with the exception of the irregular nanotetox (old) whose feminine form is nanotenoééte; -ç changes to -çtote (e.g., éàsç > éàsçtote); -nore changes to -nonate (e.g., ckènore > ckènonate); -tere changes to -tinate (e.g., quzotere > quzotinate); -tezo changes to -tizote (e.g., juèzocsçtezo > juèzocsçtizote); -teè changes to -tiète (e.g., nosytonoteè > nosytonotiète); and adjectives ending in -àto have a special form -àé (becoming -àééte in feminine) that appears before c, te, no, à, to, w, ju, ti and some occurrences of d, (e.g., reàto/reàé > reàééte, bàto/bàé > bàééte).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -te, it does not change in the feminine (cf. tos dàbbte zonokdte 'a rich man' > toste retebbte zonokdte 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -je to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., fuàéno > fuàénoje, fuàénote > fuàénoteje). If the basic form ends in -je, -x, or -ma, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., qucje > qucje, çjusjuzotetox > çjusjuzotetox, jiàtox > jiàtox), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Rezoteskd adjectives ending in -tecto take the ending -x in the masculine plural (e.g., sàtonatecto > sàtonatectox). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -cé, which normally change to -ctox in the masculine plural (e.g., dnonatezoscé > dnonatezosctox, ktesèzocé > ktesèzoctox), with only two exceptions: recècé > recècéje and scnacé > scnacéje which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ktesèzocéte > ktesèzocéteje.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in éte nanos zoàtoçte (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are qutecto (beautiful), quàs (good), quzotere (brief), çzocsji (big/tall), çzoàje (fat/large), rectox (false), dctoè (high), éàsç (long), quzotere (brief), futetoste (young), fuàéno (pretty), bctonacnoje (bad), btenoéétetozo (best), sàtonatecto (new), vteènoè (small), nanotetox (old); e.g., toste quteééte retebbte ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Rezoteskd, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Rezoteskd personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | fute
         | 2nd (informal)   | èto
         | 2nd (formal)     | naàtoje
         | 3rd (masculine)  | noé
         | 3rd (feminine)   | teééte
         | 3rd (neutral)    | às
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | sàtoje
         | 2nd              | naàtoje
         | 3rd (masculine)  | noéje
         | 3rd (feminine)   | teééteje
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun fute occurs before c, te, no, à, to, w, ju, ti, ê and some occurrences of d, it becomes fu'.

*Relative pronouns

Rezoteskd, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, ytono is ordinarily used: é'dàbbte ytono c naàéju bc qunokwkéteèète ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that ytono in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: éteje qunokwkéteèèteje ytono àsè juèju naàéjuteje ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, ytote (or yto' before c, te, no, à, to, w, ju, ti and some occurrences of d) is ordinarily used: éc qunokwkéteèète yto'noé c naàéjute ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like ytono, ytote does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Rezoteskd are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Rezoteskd is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) cnaànozo ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êèzote ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êèzote, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is cnaànozo. Forms of êèzote are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Rezoteskd, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Rezoteskd verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Rezoteskd verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -nojeje- between the stem and the ending.

    In vczoécnotesè, the stem vczoé- indicates that the verb is vczoétezo (to speak) and the ending -cnotesè marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In renosnojejeàsje, the stem renos- indicates that the verb is renosnozo (to finish), the suffix -nojeje- follows it, and the inflection -àsje marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Rezoteskd they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    vczoétezo: fute vczoétezocnoje, èto vczoécje, yto'noéje vczoécjejetesè, ytote sàtoje vczoénoàsje, vczoétema...
    renosnozo: fute renosnozocnoje, naàtoje renosîèteje, yto'noéje renosnojejetesè, renosnoje, ytote sàtoje renosnojejenoàsje...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    naàtoéànozo: fute natetox, èto natetox, noé natetoè, sàtoje naàtoéàsje, naàtoje naàtoétema, noéje natetoétesè.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly cnaànozo, êèzote, céétezo and recnozote), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -tezo (with the exception of céétezo, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    cnobtezo, qucécwtezo, kdcsètezo, tesnaàwtezo, retezobtezo, bcsçtezo, vcjejetezo, vcwtezo, vzoàbtestezo, zoteçczojitezo, etc.

        For example, for the verb vczoétezo, the stem is vczoé- and the ending is -tezo.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -nozo whose present participle ends in -nojejecsè:

    qujusnozo, kàbvcènozo, jijuçtotezovnozo, reétetozonozo, çzocsjinozo, dcïzo, nosnatejeènozo, vàénozo, zoàtoçnozo, zotoçnozo, jecénozo, etc.

        For example, for the verb renosnozo, the stem is renos- and the ending is -nozo.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êèzote and cnaànozo, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. fute zoteçczojite means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -tezo (all verbs of the first group): -te, -teje, -te, -àsje, -tema, -tesè.
    Verbs ending in -nozo (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -noje, -noje, -noè, -nojejeàsje, -nojejetema, -nojejetesè. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "fute zoteçczojicnoje" means "I was watching".

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -te and -je, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "tos rezotonoè kàsrenoè", "toste vànozote kàsrenoète", "jiteje rezotonoèje kàsrenoèje", and "jiteje vànozoteje kàsrenoèteje."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -ju for the 1st group verbs, or in -no for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -to (tesètesjizote tesètesjito, quànozote quto, énozote éto, etc. and jecnaànozo jeto, naànozo nato, vàtonaànozo vto), -noje (bteèèzote bnoje, vzotesjizote vzonoje, etc.), -toje (noskétozote noskétoje and zotekétozote zotekétoje and only these verbs), -noè (bctojinozote bctojinoè, jinozote jinoè, etc.), -è (verbs in -nosjizote : vtenosjizote vtenosè), -tezoè (àtonazonozo àtonatezoè, kàtonazonozo kàtonatezoè, àrerezonozo àreretezoè and jeàtorerezonozo jeàtoreretezoè), or teto (cnaànozo teto). 

*Compound Tenses

Rezoteskd compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either cnaànozo or êèzote) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Rezoteskd, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Rezoteskd. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either cnaànozo or êèzote in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "fu'cno bcsçju" (I ate) or "noé tejeè czozononaju" (He arrived). cnaànozo is used with most verbs, while êèzote is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, cnaànozo should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Rezoteskd: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is cnaànozo.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) teééteje àsè jiàzobno. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) kécnozote c nato jitetox qucétenosteje. ("kécnozote saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) noé w cnacnoè jitetox qucétenosteje. kécnozote éteje c natoteje. ("There were two whales. kécnozote saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) ytoteééteje qucétenosteje kécnozote c-è-teééte natoteje ? ("Which whales did kécnozote see?")
        (relative clause introduced by ytote) éteje jitetox qucétenosteje ytote kécnozote c natoteje ("the two whales that kécnozote saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Rezoteskd.

B. The auxiliary is êèzote, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        teééteje jeàsè czozononajuteje. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is êèzote and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with cnaànozo in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears after the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) teééteje jete jeàsè jetokkjujiju. sàtoje sàtoje jeàbbteje vczoéju. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object after verb) teééteje jete jeàsè vàjeju jiteje ytotejeènoàsje. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears before the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).
        (direct object pronoun) fu'cno recnoè toste èczoète. éteje tesrecsèje jete éc jeàsè vczoècçjute. ("I made a pie. The children shared it.")
        (wh-question) ytoteééte èczoète jete jeàsè-noéje vczoècçjute ? ("Which pie did they share?")

However, some -ufewag nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -iv, notably eçufewag, ufmmeweçufewag, éçéfufznufewag, nomufewag, awyiguçéveçzufewag and cyeçmufewag (e.g., igz eçufewag > néviv eçufewagiv 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Akeçévzéçéf are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Akeçévzéçéf adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like ikévufig and zyiguçévufig, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with uf, év, ew, y, ig, à, o, ul and some occurrences of éf, e.g. igz ikévufig sufeçnewz (a beautiful garden), igz ikévag éfyixixév (a handsome man), igzév ikévagagév dévixixév (a beautiful woman), agéviv ikévufigiç évzdufzmiv (the beautiful children), agéviv ikévagagéviv ixufewivyziv (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -év to the masculine form, e.g., aweçufzn > aweçufznév, agévzm > agévzmév, céveçivufz > céveçivufzév. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -évag, -ewag, -yz, -évz, -yiv or -ufiv double their final consonant before adding -év (e.g., éçeçigévag > éçeçigévagagév, awévzmewag > awévzmewagagév, ikyz > ikyzzév, ufzéçewévz > ufzéçewévzzév, aweçyiv > aweçyivivév, and ikufiv > ikufivivév).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -éç change to -éçéfév (e.g., ikagufzéç > ikagufzéçéfév); those ending in -évigeç or -évigiç change to -évigivév (e.g., ceçyixévmmévigeç > ceçyixévmmévigivév, digeçewévigiç > digeçewévigivév), with the exception of the irregular uçewévigiç (old) whose feminine form is uçewévewagagév; -aw changes to -awigév (e.g., agyzaw > agyzawigév); -ewd changes to -ewuçév (e.g., uféçmewd > uféçmewuçév); -évd changes to -uluçév (e.g., ikeçévd > ikeçuluçév); -éveç changes to -uleçév (e.g., omeçufzawéveç > omeçufzawuleçév); -évm changes to -ulmév (e.g., ewzrigewévm > ewzrigewulmév); and adjectives ending in -yig have a special form -yag (becoming -yagagév in feminine) that appears before uf, év, ew, y, ig, à, o, ul and some occurrences of éf, (e.g., dyig/dyag > dyagagév, ixyig/ixyag > ixyagagév).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -év, it does not change in the feminine (cf. igz éfyixixév eçewéçéfév 'a rich man' > igzév dévixixév eçewéçéfév 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -iv to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., syagew > syagewiv, syagewév > syagewéviv). If the basic form ends in -iv, -iç, or -al, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ikufiv > ikufiv, awozoeçévigiç > awozoeçévigiç, nyigiç > nyigiç), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Akeçévzéçéf adjectives ending in -évufig take the ending -iç in the masculine plural (e.g., zyiguçévufig > zyiguçévufigiç). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -ufag, which normally change to -ufigiç in the masculine plural (e.g., éfewuçéveçzufag > éfewuçéveçzufigiç, éçévzmeçufag > éçévzmeçufigiç), with only two exceptions: dufmufag > dufmufagiv and zufuçufag > zufuçufagiv which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: éçévzmeçufagév > éçévzmeçufagéviv.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in agév uçewz eçyigawév (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are ikévufig (beautiful), ikyz (good), ikeçévd (brief), aweçufzn (big/tall), aweçyiv (fat/large), dufigiç (false), éfufigm (high), agyzaw (long), ikeçévd (brief), sévigzév (young), syagew (pretty), ixufiguçufewiv (bad), ixévewagagévigeç (best), zyiguçévufig (new), cévmewm (small), uçewévigiç (old); e.g., igzév ikévagagév dévixixév ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Akeçévzéçéf, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Akeçévzéçéf personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

------------------------

------------------------

         | 2nd (informal)   | mig
         | 2nd (formal)     | uçyigiv
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ewag
         | 3rd (feminine)   | évagagév
         | 3rd (neutral)    | yz
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | zyigiv
         | 2nd              | uçyigiv
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ewagiv
         | 3rd (feminine)   | évagagéviv
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun sév occurs before uf, év, ew, y, ig, à, o, ul, ê and some occurrences of éf, it becomes s'.

*Relative pronouns

Akeçévzéçéf, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, rigew is ordinarily used: ag'éfyixixév rigew uf uçyago ixuf ikewéçàéçagévmmév ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that rigew in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: agéviv ikewéçàéçagévmméviv rigew yzm omo uçyagoéviv ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, rigév (or rig' before uf, év, ew, y, ig, à, o, ul and some occurrences of éf) is ordinarily used: aguf ikewéçàéçagévmmév rig'ewag uf uçyagoév ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like rigew, rigév does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Akeçévzéçéf are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Akeçévzéçéf is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ufuçyeweç ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êmeçév ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êmeçév, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ufuçyeweç. Forms of êmeçév are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Akeçévzéçéf, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Akeçévzéçéf verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Akeçévzéçéf verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -ewiviv- between the stem and the ending.

    In cufeçagufewévzm, the stem cufeçag- indicates that the verb is cufeçagéveç (to speak) and the ending -ufewévzm marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In dewzewivivyziv, the stem dewz- indicates that the verb is dewzeweç (to finish), the suffix -ewiviv- follows it, and the inflection -yziv marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Akeçévzéçéf they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    cufeçagéveç: sév cufeçagéveçufewiv, mig cufeçagufiv, rig'ewagiv cufeçagufivivévzm, rigév zyigiv cufeçagewyziv, cufeçagéval...
    dewzeweç: sév dewzeweçufewiv, uçyigiv dewzîméviv, rig'ewagiv dewzewivivévzm, dewzewiv, rigév zyigiv dewzewivivewyziv...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    uçyigagyeweç: sév uçévigiç, mig uçévigiç, ewag uçévigm, zyigiv uçyigagyziv, uçyigiv uçyigagéval, ewagiv uçévigagévzm.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ufuçyeweç, êmeçév, ufagagéveç and dufeweçév), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -éveç (with the exception of ufagagéveç, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ufewixéveç, ikufagufàéveç, éçéfufzméveç, évzuçyàéveç, déveçixéveç, ixufzawéveç, cufivivéveç, cufàéveç, ceçyixévzéveç, eçévawufeçnéveç, etc.

        For example, for the verb cufeçagéveç, the stem is cufeçag- and the ending is -éveç.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -eweç whose present participle ends in -ewivivufzm:

    ikozeweç, éçyixcufmeweç, noawigéveçceweç, dagévigeçeweç, aweçufzneweç, éfufïeç, ewzuçévivmeweç, cyageweç, eçyigaweweç, eçigaweweç, ivufageweç, etc.

        For example, for the verb dewzeweç, the stem is dewz- and the ending is -eweç.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êmeçév and ufuçyeweç, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. sév eçévawufeçnév means "I watch".

**Past participle

*Compound Tenses

Akeçévzéçéf compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either ufuçyeweç or êmeçév) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Akeçévzéçéf, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Akeçévzéçéf. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either ufuçyeweç or êmeçév in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "s'ufew ixufzawo" (I ate) or "ewag évivm ufeçeçewuço" (He arrived). ufuçyeweç is used with most verbs, while êmeçév is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, ufuçyeweç should be used by default.

Wèxybépn has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Wèxybépn, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Wèxybépn article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is gay. For example, in the phrase "gay pnrèh" (the cat), gay shows that the noun pnrèh (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is garè. An example is "garè burèmreibé" (the house), where garè shows that burèmreibé (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is gayre for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "gayre pnrèhre", the cats; "gayre burèmreibére", the houses.)

In summary, gay is used with masculine singular nouns, garè with feminine singular nouns, and gayre with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Wèxybépn.

Before rè, y, m, i, ge, o, ç, k and some occurrences of n, the singular masculine article gay becomes ga'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Wèxybépn noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Wèxybépn nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -ca (e.g., burèmreibé > burèmreibéca 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -rège and -yge take the ending -re instead of -ca (e.g., hgeorège > hgeorègeca 'pipes', rayge > raygeca 'games'), except for the nouns garèbéjrège, rerèxxrège, lèbéyge, and dagayge which form their plural by adding -re (e.g., lèbéyge > lèbéygere 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -ige form their plural with -ca. These are wuybéige, prèmgagaige, nmdaige, damraige, lèige, pnige, and raigeraige (e.g., wuybéige > wuybéigeca 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -ige, such as damreige or hxige, follow the regular plural pattern and take -re (e.g., hxige > hxigere 'holes').

Nouns that end in -re, -ca or -s in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., garè pximca 'the cross' > gayre pximca 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -règa typically change to -règeca in the plural (e.g., raigexbérèga > raigexbérègeca 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -règa are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -re instead. These are darèga, prèga, prèxbérèlérèga, pnrèprèga, àyrehmlérèga, xçpmhrèga, reyxlérèga and xçwurèga (e.g., gay àyrehmlérèga > gayre àyrehmlérègare).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -rèmga change to -règeca in the plural. Examples of this pattern include darèmga, pixrèmga, çburèmga, reigelèmxrèmga, hxrèlérèmga, and lémhxrèmga (e.g., lémhxrèmga > lémhxrègeca 'stained glass windows'). However, some -rèmga nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -re, notably xrèmga, rèhhmxrèmga, pnrèbéjrèmga, jçhrèmga, wuigeléyxbérèmga and lèixhrèmga (e.g., gebé xrèmga > jyre xrèmgare 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Wèxybépn are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Wèxybépn adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like dayrège and béigeléyrège, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with rè, y, m, i, ge, o, ç, k and some occurrences of n, e.g. gebé dayrège rarèxjmbé (a beautiful garden), gebé dayga nibubuy (a handsome man), gebéy daygagay àybubuy (a beautiful woman), gayre dayrègeca ybéàrèbéhre (the beautiful children), gayre daygagayre burèmreibére (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -y to the masculine form, e.g., wuxrèbéj > wuxrèbéjy, gaybéh > gaybéhy, lèyxrerèbé > lèyxrerèbéy. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -yga, -mga, -ibé, -ybé, -ire or -rère double their final consonant before adding -y (e.g., pxgeyga > pxgeygagay, wuybéhmga > wuybéhmgagay, daibé > daibébéy, rèbépmybé > rèbépmybébéy, wuxire > wuxirerey, and darère > darèrerey).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -p change to -pny (e.g., dagarèbép > dagarèbépny); those ending in -ygex or -ygeca change to -ygerey (e.g., lèxibuyhhygex > lèxibuyhhygerey, àgexmygeca > àgexmygerey), with the exception of the irregular lémygeca (old) whose feminine form is lémymgagay; -wu changes to -wugey (e.g., gaibéwu > gaibéwugey); -mà changes to -mléy (e.g., rèphmà > rèphmléy); -yà changes to -kléy (e.g., daxyà > daxkléy); -yx changes to -kxy (e.g., çhxrèbéwuyx > çhxrèbéwukxy); -yh changes to -khy (e.g., mbéfgemyh > mbéfgemkhy); and adjectives ending in -ige have a special form -iga (becoming -igagay in feminine) that appears before rè, y, m, i, ge, o, ç, k and some occurrences of n, (e.g., àige/àiga > àigagay, buige/buiga > buigagay).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -y, it does not change in the feminine (cf. gebé nibubuy xmpny 'a rich man' > gebéy àybubuy xmpny 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -re to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., raigam > raigamre, raigamy > raigamyre). If the basic form ends in -re, -ca, or -s, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., darère > darère, wuçbéçxygeca > wuçbéçxygeca, jigeca > jigeca), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Wèxybépn adjectives ending in -yrège take the ending -ca in the masculine plural (e.g., béigeléyrège > béigeléyrègeca). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -règa, which normally change to -règeca in the masculine plural (e.g., nmléyxbérèga > nmléyxbérègeca, pybéhxrèga > pybéhxrègeca), with only two exceptions: àrèhrèga > àrèhrègare and bérèlérèga > bérèlérègare which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: pybéhxrègay > pybéhxrègayre.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in gay lémbé xigewuy (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are dayrège (beautiful), daibé (good), daxyà (brief), wuxrèbéj (big/tall), wuxire (fat/large), àrègeca (false), nrègeh (high), gaibéwu (long), daxyà (brief), raygebéy (young), raigam (pretty), burègelérèmre (bad), buymgagaygex (best), béigeléyrège (new), lèyhmh (small), lémygeca (old); e.g., gebéy daygagay àybubuy ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Wèxybépn, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Wèxybépn personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | ray
         | 2nd (informal)   | hge
         | 2nd (formal)     | léigere
         | 3rd (masculine)  | mga
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ygagay
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ibé
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | béigere
         | 2nd              | léigere
         | 3rd (masculine)  | mgare
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ygagayre
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun ray occurs before rè, y, m, i, ge, o, ç, k, ê and some occurrences of n, it becomes ra'.

*Relative pronouns

Wèxybépn, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, fgem is ordinarily used: ga'nibubuy fgem rè léigaç burè dampopgayhhy ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that fgem in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: gayre dampopgayhhyre fgem ibéh çhç léigaçyre ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, fgey (or fge' before rè, y, m, i, ge, o, ç, k and some occurrences of n) is ordinarily used: garè dampopgayhhy fge'mga rè léigaçy ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like fgem, fgey does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Wèxybépn are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Wèxybépn is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) rèléimx ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êhxy ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êhxy, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is rèléimx. Forms of êhxy are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Wèxybépn, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Wèxybépn verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Wèxybépn verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -mrere- between the stem and the ending.

    In lèrèxgarèmybéh, the stem lèrèxga- indicates that the verb is lèrèxgayx (to speak) and the ending -rèmybéh marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In àmbémrereibére, the stem àmbé- indicates that the verb is àmbémx (to finish), the suffix -mrere- follows it, and the inflection -ibére marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Wèxybépn they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    lèrèxgayx: ray lèrèxgayxrèmre, hge lèrèxgarère, fge'mgare lèrèxgarèrereybéh, fgey béigere lèrèxgamibére, lèrèxgays...
    àmbémx: ray àmbémxrèmre, léigere àmbéîhyre, fge'mgare àmbémrereybéh, àmbémre, fgey béigere àmbémreremibére...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    léigegaimx: ray léygeca, hge léygeca, mga léygeh, béigere léigegaibére, léigere léigegays, mgare léygegaybéh.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly rèléimx, êhxy, règagayx and àrèmxy), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -yx (with the exception of règagayx, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    rèmbuyx, darègarèoyx, pnrèbéhyx, ybéléioyx, àyxbuyx, burèbéwuyx, lèrèrereyx, lèrèoyx, lèxibuybéyx, xywurèxjyx, etc.

        For example, for the verb lèrèxgayx, the stem is lèrèxga- and the ending is -yx.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -mx whose present participle ends in -mrererèbéh:

    daçbémx, pibulèrèhmx, jçwugeyxlèmx, àgaygexmx, wuxrèbéjmx, nrèïx, mbéléyrehmx, lèigamx, xigewumx, xgewumx, rerègamx, etc.

        For example, for the verb àmbémx, the stem is àmbé- and the ending is -mx.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êhxy and rèléimx, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. ray xywurèxjy means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -yx (all verbs of the first group): -y, -yre, -y, -ibére, -ys, -ybéh.
    Verbs ending in -mx (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -mre, -mre, -mh, -mrereibére, -mrereys, -mrereybéh. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -xy (part of the third group): -re, -re, - , -ibére, -ys, -ybéh.
    
    Example:

2nd person     | hge xywurèxjyre        | léigere xywurèxjys
3rd person     | mga/ygagay/ibé xywurèxjy | mgare/ygagayre xywurèxjybéh

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "ray xywurèxjrèmre" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -yx suffix, e.g., xywurèxjyx -> xywurèxj-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -mx suffix plus the -mrere suffix, e.g., pnimremx -> pnimremrere-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -rèmre, -rèmre, -rèmh, -mibére, -mys, -rèmybéh.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -y and -re, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "gebé àxgemh pibéàmh", "gebéy lèimxy pibéàmhy", "jyre àxgemhre pibéàmhre", and "jyre lèimxyre pibéàmhyre."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -ç for the 1st group verbs, or in -m for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -ge (ybéhybéjxy ybéhybéjge, daimxy dage, gamxy gage, etc. and rerèléimx rege, léimx lége, lèigeléimx lège), -mre (buyhhxy bumre, lèxybéjxy lèxmre, etc.), -gere (mbépgagexy mbépgagere and xypgagexy xypgagere and only these verbs), -mh (burègejmxy burègejmh, jmxy jmh, etc.), -h (verbs in -mbéjxy : lèymbéjxy lèymbéh), -yxh (igeléxmx igeléyxh, pigeléxmx pigeléyxh, iààxmx iààyxh and reigeààxmx reigeààyxh), or yge (rèléimx yge). 

*Compound Tenses

Wèxybépn compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either rèléimx or êhxy) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Wèxybépn, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Wèxybépn. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either rèléimx or êhxy in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "ra'rèm burèbéwuç" (I ate) or "mga yreh rèxxmléç" (He arrived). rèléimx is used with most verbs, while êhxy is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. All other nouns ending in -lén, such as ofvémlén or èciclén, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ém (e.g., èciclén > ècicléném 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ém, -t or -on in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., ws eziclvt 'the cross' > wqém eziclvt 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -sw typically change to -sént in the plural (e.g., éclénicèmsw > éclénicèmsént 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -sw are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ém instead. These are ofsw, ezsw, ezsicèmsksw, ezasezsw, çqémècvksw, icedezvècsw, émqicksw and icedbsw (e.g., wq çqémècvksw > wqém çqémècvkswém).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -svw change to -sént in the plural. Examples of this pattern include ofsvw, ezlicsvw, edozsvw, émléngvicsvw, ècicsksvw, and kvècicsvw (e.g., kvècicsvw > kvècicsént 'stained glass windows'). However, some -svw nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ém, notably icsvw, sècècvicsvw, ezasèmusvw, uedècsvw, blénkqicèmsvw and glicècsvw (e.g., énèm icsvw > uqém icsvwém 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Idicqèmeza are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Idicqèmeza adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like ofqsén and èmlénkqsén, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with s, q, v, l, én, ip, ed, x and some occurrences of a, e.g. énèm ofqsén écsicuvèm (a beautiful garden), énèm ofqw alozozq (a handsome man), énèmq ofqwwq çqozozq (a beautiful woman), wqém ofqsént qèmçsèmècém (the beautiful children), wqém ofqwwqém ozsvémlèmém (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -q to the masculine form, e.g., bicsèmu > bicsèmuq, wqèmèc > wqèmècq, gqicémsèm > gqicémsèmq. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -qw, -vw, -lèm, -qèm, -lém or -sém double their final consonant before adding -q (e.g., ezicénqw > ezicénqwwq, bqèmècvw > bqèmècvwwq, oflèm > oflèmèmq, sèmezvqèm > sèmezvqèmèmq, biclém > biclémémq, and ofsém > ofsémémq).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -ez change to -ezaq (e.g., ofwsèmez > ofwsèmezaq); those ending in -qénic or -qént change to -qénémq (e.g., giclozqècècqénic > giclozqècècqénémq, çénicvqént > çénicvqénémq), with the exception of the irregular kvqént (old) whose feminine form is kvqvwwq; -b changes to -bénq (e.g., wlèmb > wlèmbénq); -vç changes to -vkq (e.g., sezècvç > sezècvkq); -qç changes to -xkq (e.g., oficqç > oficxkq); -qic changes to -xicq (e.g., edècicsèmbqic > edècicsèmbxicq); -qèc changes to -xècq (e.g., vèmyénvqèc > vèmyénvxècq); and adjectives ending in -lén have a special form -lw (becoming -lwwq in feminine) that appears before s, q, v, l, én, ip, ed, x and some occurrences of a, (e.g., çlén/çlw > çlwwq, ozlén/ozlw > ozlwwq).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -q, it does not change in the feminine (cf. énèm alozozq icvezaq 'a rich man' > énèmq çqozozq icvezaq 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ém to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., éclwv > éclwvém, éclwvq > éclwvqém). If the basic form ends in -ém, -t, or -on, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ofsém > ofsém, bedèmedicqént > bedèmedicqént, ulént > ulént), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Idicqèmeza adjectives ending in -qsén take the ending -t in the masculine plural (e.g., èmlénkqsén > èmlénkqsént). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -sw, which normally change to -sént in the masculine plural (e.g., avkqicèmsw > avkqicèmsént, ezqèmècicsw > ezqèmècicsént), with only two exceptions: çsècsw > çsècswém and èmsksw > èmskswém which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ezqèmècicswq > ezqèmècicswqém.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in wq kvèm iclénbq (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are ofqsén (beautiful), oflèm (good), oficqç (brief), bicsèmu (big/tall), biclém (fat/large), çsént (false), asénèc (high), wlèmb (long), oficqç (brief), écqénèmq (young), éclwv (pretty), ozsénksvém (bad), ozqvwwqénic (best), èmlénkqsén (new), gqècvèc (small), kvqént (old); e.g., énèmq ofqwwq çqozozq ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Idicqèmeza, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Idicqèmeza personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | écq
         | 2nd (informal)   | ècén
         | 2nd (formal)     | kléném
         | 3rd (masculine)  | vw
         | 3rd (feminine)   | qwwq
         | 3rd (neutral)    | lèm
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | èmléném
         | 2nd              | kléném
         | 3rd (masculine)  | vwém
         | 3rd (feminine)   | qwwqém
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun écq occurs before s, q, v, l, én, ip, ed, x, ê and some occurrences of a, it becomes éc'.

*Relative pronouns

Idicqèmeza, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, yénv is ordinarily used: w'alozozq yénv s klwed ozs ofvezipezwqècècq ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that yénv in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: wqém ofvezipezwqècècqém yénv lèmèc edèced klwedqém ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, yénq (or yén' before s, q, v, l, én, ip, ed, x and some occurrences of a) is ordinarily used: ws ofvezipezwqècècq yén'vw s klwedq ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like yénv, yénq does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Idicqèmeza are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Idicqèmeza is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) sklvic ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êècicq ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êècicq, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is sklvic. Forms of êècicq are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Idicqèmeza, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Idicqèmeza verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Idicqèmeza verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -vémém- between the stem and the ending.

    In gsicwsvqèmèc, the stem gsicw- indicates that the verb is gsicwqic (to speak) and the ending -svqèmèc marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In çvèmvémémlèmém, the stem çvèm- indicates that the verb is çvèmvic (to finish), the suffix -vémém- follows it, and the inflection -lèmém marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Idicqèmeza they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    gsicwqic: écq gsicwqicsvém, ècén gsicwsém, yén'vwém gsicwsémémqèmèc, yénq èmléném gsicwvlèmém, gsicwqon...
    çvèmvic: écq çvèmvicsvém, kléném çvèmîècqém, yén'vwém çvèmvémémqèmèc, çvèmvém, yénq èmléném çvèmvémémvlèmém...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    klénwlvic: écq kqént, ècén kqént, vw kqénèc, èmléném klénwlèmém, kléném klénwqon, vwém kqénwqèmèc.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly sklvic, êècicq, swwqic and çsvicq), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -qic (with the exception of swwqic, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    svozqic, ofswsipqic, ezasèmècqic, qèmklipqic, çqicozqic, ozsèmbqic, gsémémqic, gsipqic, giclozqèmqic, icqbsicuqic, etc.

        For example, for the verb gsicwqic, the stem is gsicw- and the ending is -qic.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -vic whose present participle ends in -vémémsèmèc:

    ofedèmvic, ezlozgsècvic, uedbénqicgvic, çwqénicvic, bicsèmuvic, asïic, vèmkqémècvic, glwvic, iclénbvic, icénbvic, émswvic, etc.

        For example, for the verb çvèmvic, the stem is çvèm- and the ending is -vic.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êècicq and sklvic, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. écq icqbsicuq means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -qic (all verbs of the first group): -q, -qém, -q, -lèmém, -qon, -qèmèc.
    Verbs ending in -vic (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -vém, -vém, -vèc, -vémémlèmém, -vémémqon, -vémémqèmèc. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -icq (part of the third group): -ém, -ém, - , -lèmém, -qon, -qèmèc.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "écq icqbsicusvém" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -qic suffix, e.g., icqbsicuqic -> icqbsicu-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -vic suffix plus the -vémém suffix, e.g., ezalvémvic -> ezalvémvémém-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -svém, -svém, -svèc, -vlèmém, -vqon, -svqèmèc.
