The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is ébà. For example, in the phrase "ébà bucajcè" (the cat), ébà shows that the noun bucajcè (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is éj. An example is "éj bijpnikèo" (the house), where éj shows that bijpnikèo (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is ébàni for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "ébàni bucajcèni", the cats; "ébàni bijpnikèoni", the houses.)

In summary, ébà is used with masculine singular nouns, éj with feminine singular nouns, and ébàni with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Nèfubàobuca.

Before j, bà, p, kè, s, v, e, ç and some occurrences of ca, the singular masculine article ébà becomes é'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Nèfubàobuca noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Nèfubàobuca nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -tu (e.g., bijpnikèo > bijpnikèotu 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -js and -bàs take the ending -ni instead of -tu (e.g., cèsvjs > cèsvjstu 'pipes', rbàs > rbàstu 'games'), except for the nouns éjoyjs, nijfufujs, hèobàs, and xébàs which form their plural by adding -ni (e.g., hèobàs > hèobàsni 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -kès form their plural with -tu. These are mbàokès, bujpéékès, capxkès, xprkès, hèkès, bucakès, and rkèsrkès (e.g., mbàokès > mbàokèstu 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -kès, such as xpnikès or cèfukès, follow the regular plural pattern and take -ni (e.g., cèfukès > cèfukèsni 'holes').

Nouns that end in -ni, -tu or -wu in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., éj bufukèptu 'the cross' > ébàni bufukèptu 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -jé typically change to -jstu in the plural (e.g., rkèsfuojé > rkèsfuojstu 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -jé are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -ni instead. These are xjé, bujé, bujfuojzajé, bucajbujé, lbànicèpzajé, fuebupcèjé, nibàfuzajé and fuemjé (e.g., ébà lbànicèpzajé > ébàni lbànicèpzajéni).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -jpé change to -jstu in the plural. Examples of this pattern include xjpé, bukèfujpé, ebijpé, nikèshèpfujpé, cèfujzajpé, and zapcèfujpé (e.g., zapcèfujpé > zapcèfujstu 'stained glass windows'). However, some -jpé nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -ni, notably fujpé, jcècèpfujpé, bucajoyjpé, yecèjpé, mkèszabàfuojpé and hèkèfucèjpé (e.g., so fujpé > ybàni fujpéni 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Nèfubàobuca are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Nèfubàobuca adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like xbàjs and okèszabàjs, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with j, bà, p, kè, s, v, e, ç and some occurrences of ca, e.g. so xbàjs rjfuypo (a beautiful garden), so xbàé cakèbibibà (a handsome man), sobà xbàéébà lbàbibibà (a beautiful woman), ébàni xbàjstu bàoljocèni (the beautiful children), ébàni xbàéébàni bijpnikèoni (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -bà to the masculine form, e.g., mfujoy > mfujoybà, ébàocè > ébàocèbà, hèbàfunijo > hèbàfunijobà. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -bàé, -pé, -kèo, -bào, -kèni or -jni double their final consonant before adding -bà (e.g., bufusbàé > bufusbàéébà, mbàocèpé > mbàocèpéébà, xkèo > xkèoobà, jobupbào > jobupbàoobà, mfukèni > mfukèninibà, and xjni > xjninibà).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -bu change to -bucabà (e.g., xéjobu > xéjobucabà); those ending in -bàsfu or -bàstu change to -bàsnibà (e.g., hèfukèbibàcècèbàsfu > hèfukèbibàcècèbàsnibà, lsfupbàstu > lsfupbàsnibà), with the exception of the irregular zapbàstu (old) whose feminine form is zapbàpéébà; -m changes to -msbà (e.g., ékèom > ékèomsbà); -pl changes to -pzabà (e.g., jbucèpl > jbucèpzabà); -bàl changes to -çzabà (e.g., xfubàl > xfuçzabà); -bàfu changes to -çfubà (e.g., ecèfujombàfu > ecèfujomçfubà); -bàcè changes to -çcèbà (e.g., podspbàcè > podspçcèbà); and adjectives ending in -kès have a special form -kèé (becoming -kèéébà in feminine) that appears before j, bà, p, kè, s, v, e, ç and some occurrences of ca, (e.g., lkès/lkèé > lkèéébà, bikès/bikèé > bikèéébà).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -bà, it does not change in the feminine (cf. so cakèbibibà fupbucabà 'a rich man' > sobà lbàbibibà fupbucabà 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -ni to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., rkèép > rkèépni, rkèépbà > rkèépbàni). If the basic form ends in -ni, -tu, or -wu, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., xjni > xjni, meoefubàstu > meoefubàstu, ykèstu > ykèstu), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Nèfubàobuca adjectives ending in -bàjs take the ending -tu in the masculine plural (e.g., okèszabàjs > okèszabàjstu). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -jé, which normally change to -jstu in the masculine plural (e.g., capzabàfuojé > capzabàfuojstu, bubàocèfujé > bubàocèfujstu), with only two exceptions: ljcèjé > ljcèjéni and ojzajé > ojzajéni which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: bubàocèfujébà > bubàocèfujébàni.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in ébà zapo fukèsmbà (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are xbàjs (beautiful), xkèo (good), xfubàl (brief), mfujoy (big/tall), mfukèni (fat/large), ljstu (false), cajscè (high), ékèom (long), xfubàl (brief), rbàsobà (young), rkèép (pretty), bijszajpni (bad), bibàpéébàsfu (best), okèszabàjs (new), hèbàcèpcè (small), zapbàstu (old); e.g., sobà xbàéébà lbàbibibà ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Nèfubàobuca, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Nèfubàobuca personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | rbà
         | 2nd (informal)   | cès
         | 2nd (formal)     | zakèsni
         | 3rd (masculine)  | pé
         | 3rd (feminine)   | bàéébà
         | 3rd (neutral)    | kèo
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | okèsni
         | 2nd              | zakèsni
         | 3rd (masculine)  | péni
         | 3rd (feminine)   | bàéébàni
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun rbà occurs before j, bà, p, kè, s, v, e, ç, ê and some occurrences of ca, it becomes r'.

*Relative pronouns

Nèfubàobuca, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, dsp is ordinarily used: é'cakèbibibà dsp j zakèée bij xpbuvbuébàcècèbà ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that dsp in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: ébàni xpbuvbuébàcècèbàni dsp kèocè ecèe zakèéebàni ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, dsbà (or ds' before j, bà, p, kè, s, v, e, ç and some occurrences of ca) is ordinarily used: éj xpbuvbuébàcècèbà ds'pé j zakèéebà ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like dsp, dsbà does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Nèfubàobuca are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Nèfubàobuca is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) jzakèpfu ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êcèfubà ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êcèfubà, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is jzakèpfu. Forms of êcèfubà are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Nèfubàobuca, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Nèfubàobuca verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Nèfubàobuca verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -pnini- between the stem and the ending.

    In hèjfuéjpbàocè, the stem hèjfué- indicates that the verb is hèjfuébàfu (to speak) and the ending -jpbàocè marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In lpopninikèoni, the stem lpo- indicates that the verb is lpopfu (to finish), the suffix -pnini- follows it, and the inflection -kèoni marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Nèfubàobuca they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    hèjfuébàfu: rbà hèjfuébàfujpni, cès hèjfuéjni, ds'péni hèjfuéjninibàocè, dsbà okèsni hèjfuépkèoni, hèjfuébàwu...
    lpopfu: rbà lpopfujpni, zakèsni lpoîcèbàni, ds'péni lpopninibàocè, lpopni, dsbà okèsni lpopninipkèoni...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    zakèsékèpfu: rbà zabàstu, cès zabàstu, pé zabàscè, okèsni zakèsékèoni, zakèsni zakèsébàwu, péni zabàsébàocè.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly jzakèpfu, êcèfubà, jéébàfu and ljpfubà), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -bàfu (with the exception of jéébàfu, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    jpbibàfu, xjéjvbàfu, bucajocèbàfu, bàozakèvbàfu, lbàfubibàfu, bijombàfu, hèjninibàfu, hèjvbàfu, hèfukèbibàobàfu, fubàmjfuybàfu, etc.

        For example, for the verb hèjfuébàfu, the stem is hèjfué- and the ending is -bàfu.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -pfu whose present participle ends in -pninijocè:

    xeopfu, bukèbihèjcèpfu, yemsbàfuhèpfu, lébàsfupfu, mfujoypfu, cajïfu, pozabànicèpfu, hèkèépfu, fukèsmpfu, fusmpfu, nijépfu, etc.

        For example, for the verb lpopfu, the stem is lpo- and the ending is -pfu.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êcèfubà and jzakèpfu, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. rbà fubàmjfuybà means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -bàfu (all verbs of the first group): -bà, -bàni, -bà, -kèoni, -bàwu, -bàocè.
    Verbs ending in -pfu (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -pni, -pni, -pcè, -pninikèoni, -pninibàwu, -pninibàocè. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -fubà (part of the third group): -ni, -ni, - , -kèoni, -bàwu, -bàocè.
    
    Example:

Person         | Singular             | Plural
-------------------------------
1st person     | rbà fubàmjfuybà         | okèsni fubàmjfuykèoni
2nd person     | cès fubàmjfuybàni        | zakèsni fubàmjfuybàwu
3rd person     | pé/bàéébà/kèo fubàmjfuybà | péni/bàéébàni fubàmjfuybàocè
-------------------------------

2nd person     | cès bucakèpnipni         | zakèsni bucakèpnipninibàwu

    Verbs of the second group take an -pnini- in the plural conjugations.
        
        
**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "rbà fubàmjfuyjpni" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -bàfu suffix, e.g., fubàmjfuybàfu -> fubàmjfuy-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -pfu suffix plus the -pnini suffix, e.g., bucakèpnipfu -> bucakèpnipnini-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -jpni, -jpni, -jpcè, -pkèoni, -pbàwu, -jpbàocè.

2nd person     | cès fubàmjfuyjpni         | zakèsni fubàmjfuypbàwu

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb jzakèpfu. They are always regular: -jp, -jni, -j, -kèoni, -bàwu, -kèocè.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

        rbà bucakèpnipfujp ('I will choose'), cès fubàmjfuybàfujni ('you will watch'), bàéébà nikèfucèpfuj ('she will exit'), okèsni cèfujzajpéébàfukèoni ('we will work'), zakèsni fukèsmpfubàwu ('you will blush'), péni hèjfucèpfukèocè ('they will leave').

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -bà and -ni, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "so lfuspcè bukèolpcè", "sobà hèkèpfubà bukèolpcèbà", "ybàni lfuspcèni bukèolpcèni", and "ybàni hèkèpfubàni bukèolpcèbàni."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -e for the 1st group verbs, or in -p for the 2nd group verbs. PRONOUNS
--------
In Éhçidægivæs, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Éhçidægivæs personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | itid
         | 2nd (informal)   | èrû
         | 2nd (formal)     | ædègûj
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ñe
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ideeid
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ègæg
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | ægègûj
         | 2nd              | ædègûj
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ñej
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ideeidj
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun itid occurs before l, id, ñ, èg, û, æt, ig, y, â and some occurrences of æs, it becomes it'.

*Relative pronouns

Éhçidægivæs, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, éqûñ is ordinarily used: e'æsègèvèvid éqûñ l ædègeig èvl æfñivætiveidèrèrid ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that éqûñ in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: eidj æfñivætiveidèrèridj éqûñ ègægèr igèrig ædègeigidj ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, éqûid (or éqû' before l, id, ñ, èg, û, æt, ig, y and some occurrences of æs) is ordinarily used: el æfñivætiveidèrèrid éqû'ñe l ædègeigid ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like éqûñ, éqûid does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Éhçidægivæs are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Éhçidægivæs is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) lædègñç ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of âèrçid ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is âèrçid, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is lædègñç. Forms of âèrçid are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Éhçidægivæs, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Éhçidægivæs verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Éhçidægivæs verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -ñjj- between the stem and the ending.

    In ævlçelñidægèr, the stem ævlçe- indicates that the verb is ævlçeidç (to speak) and the ending -lñidægèr marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In bñægñjjègægj, the stem bñæg- indicates that the verb is bñægñç (to finish), the suffix -ñjj- follows it, and the inflection -ègægj marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Éhçidægivæs they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ævlçeidç: itid ævlçeidçlñj, èrû ævlçelj, éqû'ñej ævlçeljjidægèr, éqûid ægègûj ævlçeñègægj, ævlçeidà...
    bñægñç: itid bñægñçlñj, ædègûj bñægôèridj, éqû'ñej bñægñjjidægèr, bñægñj, éqûid ægègûj bñægñjjñègægj...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ædègûeègñç: itid ædidûþ, èrû ædidûþ, ñe ædidûèr, ægègûj ædègûeègægj, ædègûj ædègûeidà, ñej ædidûeidægèr.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly lædègñç, âèrçid, leeidç and blñçid), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -idç (with the exception of leeidç, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    lñèvidç, æflelætidç, ivæslægèridç, idægædègætidç, bidçèvidç, èvlægkidç, ævljjidç, ævlætidç, ævçègèvidægidç, çidklçzidç, etc.

        For example, for the verb ævlçeidç, the stem is ævlçe- and the ending is -idç.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ñç whose present participle ends in -ñjjlægèr:

    æfigægñç, ivègèvævlèrñç, zigkûidçævñç, beidûçñç, kçlægzñç, æslïç, ñægædidjèrñç, ævègeñç, çègûkñç, çûkñç, jleñç, etc.

        For example, for the verb bñægñç, the stem is bñæg- and the ending is -ñç.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries âèrçid and lædègñç, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. itid çidklçzid means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

*Compound Tenses

Éhçidægivæs compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either lædègñç or âèrçid) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Éhçidægivæs, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Éhçidægivæs. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either lædègñç or âèrçid in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "it'lñ èvlægkig" (I ate) or "ñe idjèr lççñædig" (He arrived). lædègñç is used with most verbs, while âèrçid is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, lædègñç should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Éhçidægivæs: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is lædègñç.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) ideeidj ègægèr zègçèvñ. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) ivelñçid l ædû zidûþ æfleidñægidj. ("ivelñçid saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) ñe æt lædlñèr zidûþ æfleidñægidj. ivelñçid eidj l ædûidj. ("There were two whales. ivelñçid saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) éqûideeidj æfleidñægidj ivelñçid l-èr-ideeid ædûidj ? ("Which whales did ivelñçid see?")
        (relative clause introduced by éqûid) eidj zidûþ æfleidñægidj éqûid ivelñçid l ædûidj ("the two whales that ivelñçid saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Éhçidægivæs.

B. The auxiliary is âèrçid, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        ideeidj jègægèr lççñædigidj. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is âèrçid and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with lædègñç in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears after the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) ideeidj jid jègægèr jûivivigzig. ægègûj ægègûj jègèvèvidj ævlçeig. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object after verb) ideeidj jid jègægèr ævègjig zidj éqûidjèrñègægj. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears before the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).
        (direct object pronoun) it'lñ blñèr ûægid èrlçèrid. eidj idægblægèrj jid el jègægèr ævlçèrlkigid. ("I made a pie. The children shared it.")
        (wh-question) éqûideeid èrlçèrid jid jègægèr-ñej ævlçèrlkigid ? ("Which pie did they share?")
        (éqûid relative) el èrlçèrid éqûid eidj idægblægèrj jid jègægèr ævlçèrlkigid ("the pie that the children shared")

    The reflexive pronoun can itself be the direct object, in which case the participle agrees with it (and therefore with the subject). This also includes "inherently reflexive" verbs, for which the reflexive pronoun cannot be interpreted semantically as an object (direct or indirect) of the verb.

In summary, êrêç is used with masculine singular nouns, êrj with feminine singular nouns, and êrêçen with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Anøêçàghem.

Before j, êç, êl, al, q, ên, û, b and some occurrences of em, the singular masculine article êrêç becomes êr'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Anøêçàghem noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Anøêçàghem nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -p (e.g., yjêlenalàg > yjêlenalàgp 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -jq and -êçq take the ending -en instead of -p (e.g., etqênjq > etqênjqp 'pipes', erêçq > erêçqp 'games'), except for the nouns êrjàgœrjq, enjøøjq, vàgêçq, and iêrêçq which form their plural by adding -en (e.g., vàgêçq > vàgêçqen 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -alq form their plural with -p. These are âêçàgalq, hjêlêrêralq, emêlialq, iêleralq, valq, hemalq, and eralqeralq (e.g., âêçàgalq > âêçàgalqp 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -alq, such as iêlenalq or etøalq, follow the regular plural pattern and take -en (e.g., etøalq > etøalqen 'holes').

Nouns that end in -en, -p or -æ in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., êrj høalêlp 'the cross' > êrêçen høalêlp 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -jêr typically change to -jqp in the plural (e.g., eralqøàgjêr > eralqøàgjqp 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -jêr are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -en instead. These are ijêr, hjêr, hjøàgjàsjêr, hemjhjêr, anêçenetêlàsjêr, øûhêletjêr, enêçøàsjêr and øûâjêr (e.g., êrêç anêçenetêlàsjêr > êrêçen anêçenetêlàsjêren).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -jêlêr change to -jqp in the plural. Examples of this pattern include ijêlêr, haløjêlêr, ûyjêlêr, enalqvêløjêlêr, etøjàsjêlêr, and àsêletøjêlêr (e.g., àsêletøjêlêr > àsêletøjqp 'stained glass windows'). However, some -jêlêr nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -en, notably øjêlêr, jetetêløjêlêr, hemjàgœrjêlêr, œrûetjêlêr, âalqàsêçøàgjêlêr and valøetjêlêr (e.g., qàg øjêlêr > œrêçen øjêlêren 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Anøêçàghem are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Anøêçàghem adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like iêçjq and àgalqàsêçjq, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with j, êç, êl, al, q, ên, û, b and some occurrences of em, e.g. qàg iêçjq erjøœrêlàg (a beautiful garden), qàg iêçêr emalyyêç (a handsome man), qàgêç iêçêrêrêç anêçyyêç (a beautiful woman), êrêçen iêçjqp êçàganjàgeten (the beautiful children), êrêçen iêçêrêrêçen yjêlenalàgen (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -êç to the masculine form, e.g., âøjàgœr > âøjàgœrêç, êrêçàget > êrêçàgetêç, vêçøenjàg > vêçøenjàgêç. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -êçêr, -êlêr, -alàg, -êçàg, -alen or -jen double their final consonant before adding -êç (e.g., høqêçêr > høqêçêrêrêç, âêçàgetêlêr > âêçàgetêlêrêrêç, ialàg > ialàgàgêç, jàghêlêçàg > jàghêlêçàgàgêç, âøalen > âøalenenêç, and ijen > ijenenêç).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -h change to -hemêç (e.g., iêrjàgh > iêrjàghemêç); those ending in -êçqø or -êçqp change to -êçqenêç (e.g., vøalyêçetetêçqø > vøalyêçetetêçqenêç, anqøêlêçqp > anqøêlêçqenêç), with the exception of the irregular àsêlêçqp (old) whose feminine form is àsêlêçêlêrêrêç; -â changes to -âqêç (e.g., êralàgâ > êralàgâqêç); -êlan changes to -êlàsêç (e.g., jhetêlan > jhetêlàsêç); -êçan changes to -bàsêç (e.g., iøêçan > iøbàsêç); -êçø changes to -bøêç (e.g., ûetøjàgâêçø > ûetøjàgâbøêç); -êçet changes to -betêç (e.g., êlàgwqêlêçet > êlàgwqêlbetêç); and adjectives ending in -alq have a special form -alêr (becoming -alêrêrêç in feminine) that appears before j, êç, êl, al, q, ên, û, b and some occurrences of em, (e.g., analq/analêr > analêrêrêç, yalq/yalêr > yalêrêrêç).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -êç, it does not change in the feminine (cf. qàg emalyyêç øêlhemêç 'a rich man' > qàgêç anêçyyêç øêlhemêç 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -en to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., eralêrêl > eralêrêlen, eralêrêlêç > eralêrêlêçen). If the basic form ends in -en, -p, or -æ, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ijen > ijen, âûàgûøêçqp > âûàgûøêçqp, œralqp > œralqp), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Anøêçàghem adjectives ending in -êçjq take the ending -p in the masculine plural (e.g., àgalqàsêçjq > àgalqàsêçjqp). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -jêr, which normally change to -jqp in the masculine plural (e.g., emêlàsêçøàgjêr > emêlàsêçøàgjqp, hêçàgetøjêr > hêçàgetøjqp), with only two exceptions: anjetjêr > anjetjêren and àgjàsjêr > àgjàsjêren which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: hêçàgetøjêrêç > hêçàgetøjêrêçen.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in êrêç àsêlàg øalqâêç (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are iêçjq (beautiful), ialàg (good), iøêçan (brief), âøjàgœr (big/tall), âøalen (fat/large), anjqp (false), emjqet (high), êralàgâ (long), iøêçan (brief), erêçqàgêç (young), eralêrêl (pretty), yjqàsjêlen (bad), yêçêlêrêrêçqø (best), àgalqàsêçjq (new), vêçetêlet (small), àsêlêçqp (old); e.g., qàgêç iêçêrêrêç anêçyyêç ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Anøêçàghem, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Anøêçàghem personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------

         | 2nd (informal)   | etq
         | 2nd (formal)     | àsalqen
         | 3rd (masculine)  | êlêr
         | 3rd (feminine)   | êçêrêrêç
         | 3rd (neutral)    | alàg
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | àgalqen
         | 2nd              | àsalqen
         | 3rd (masculine)  | êlêren
         | 3rd (feminine)   | êçêrêrêçen
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun erêç occurs before j, êç, êl, al, q, ên, û, b, el and some occurrences of em, it becomes er'.

*Relative pronouns

Anøêçàghem, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, wqêl is ordinarily used: êr'emalyyêç wqêl j àsalêrû yj iêlhênhêrêçetetêç ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that wqêl in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: êrêçen iêlhênhêrêçetetêçen wqêl alàget ûetû àsalêrûêçen ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, wqêç (or wq' before j, êç, êl, al, q, ên, û, b and some occurrences of em) is ordinarily used: êrj iêlhênhêrêçetetêç wq'êlêr j àsalêrûêç ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like wqêl, wqêç does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Anøêçàghem are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Anøêçàghem is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) jàsalêlø ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of eletøêç ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is eletøêç, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is jàsalêlø. Forms of eletøêç are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Anøêçàghem, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Anøêçàghem verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Anøêçàghem verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -êlenen- between the stem and the ending.

    In vjøêrjêlêçàget, the stem vjøêr- indicates that the verb is vjøêrêçø (to speak) and the ending -jêlêçàget marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In anêlàgêlenenalàgen, the stem anêlàg- indicates that the verb is anêlàgêlø (to finish), the suffix -êlenen- follows it, and the inflection -alàgen marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Anøêçàghem they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    vjøêrêçø: erêç vjøêrêçøjêlen, etq vjøêrjen, wq'êlêren vjøêrjenenêçàget, wqêç àgalqen vjøêrêlalàgen, vjøêrêçæ...
    anêlàgêlø: erêç anêlàgêløjêlen, àsalqen anêlàgesetêçen, wq'êlêren anêlàgêlenenêçàget, anêlàgêlen, wqêç àgalqen anêlàgêlenenêlalàgen...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    àsalqêralêlø: erêç àsêçqp, etq àsêçqp, êlêr àsêçqet, àgalqen àsalqêralàgen, àsalqen àsalqêrêçæ, êlêren àsêçqêrêçàget.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly jàsalêlø, eletøêç, jêrêrêçø and anjêløêç), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -êçø (with the exception of jêrêrêçø, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    jêlyêçø, ijêrjênêçø, hemjàgetêçø, êçàgàsalênêçø, anêçøyêçø, yjàgâêçø, vjenenêçø, vjênêçø, vøalyêçàgêçø, øêçâjøœrêçø, etc.

        For example, for the verb vjøêrêçø, the stem is vjøêr- and the ending is -êçø.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -êlø whose present participle ends in -êlenenjàget:

    iûàgêlø, halyvjetêlø, œrûâqêçøvêlø, anêrêçqøêlø, âøjàgœrêlø, emjïø, êlàgàsêçenetêlø, valêrêlø, øalqâêlø, øqâêlø, enjêrêlø, etc.

        For example, for the verb anêlàgêlø, the stem is anêlàg- and the ending is -êlø.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries eletøêç and jàsalêlø, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. erêç øêçâjøœrêç means "I watch".

Beginning of Quxràyqègè Grammar Book Excerpts

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Quxràyqègè is subject-verb-object (SVO).

    t’ðàguðaxrà erà qègèðaqèðaeðàc (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Quxràyqègè, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Quxràyqègè has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Quxràyqègè, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Quxràyqègè article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is erà. For example, in the phrase "erà qègèðàc" (the cat), erà shows that the noun qègèðàc (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is eðà. An example is "eðà sðàñèzèðay" (the house), where eðà shows that sðàñèzèðay (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is eràzè for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "eràzè qègèðàczè", the cats; "eràzè sðàñèzèðayzè", the houses.)

In summary, erà is used with masculine singular nouns, eðà with feminine singular nouns, and eràzè with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Quxràyqègè.

Before ðà, rà, ñè, ða, p, w, jà, zu and some occurrences of gè, the singular masculine article erà becomes e'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Quxràyqègè noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Quxràyqègè nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -d (e.g., sðàñèzèðay > sðàñèzèðayd 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -ðàp and -ràp take the ending -zè instead of -d (e.g., cpwðàp > cpwðàpd 'pipes', tràp > tràpd 'games'), except for the nouns eðàyguðàp, zèðàxxðàp, ðèyràp, and rèeràp which form their plural by adding -zè (e.g., ðèyràp > ðèyràpzè 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -ðap form their plural with -d. These are baràyðap, qèðàñèeeðap, gèñèrèðap, rèñètðap, ðèðap, qègèðap, and tðaptðap (e.g., baràyðap > baràyðapd 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -ðap, such as rèñèzèðap or cxðap, follow the regular plural pattern and take -zè (e.g., cxðap > cxðapzè 'holes').

Nouns that end in -zè, -d or -n in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., eðà qèxðañèd 'the cross' > eràzè qèxðañèd 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -ðàe typically change to -ðàpd in the plural (e.g., tðapxyðàe > tðapxyðàpd 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -ðàe are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -zè instead. These are rèðàe, qèðàe, qèðàxyðàzaðàe, qègèðàqèðàe, hràzècñèzaðàe, xjàqèñècðàe, zèràxzaðàe and xjàbaðàe (e.g., erà hràzècñèzaðàe > eràzè hràzècñèzaðàezè).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -ðàñèe change to -ðàpd in the plural. Examples of this pattern include rèðàñèe, qèðaxðàñèe, jàsðàñèe, zèðapðèñèxðàñèe, cxðàzaðàñèe, and zañècxðàñèe (e.g., zañècxðàñèe > zañècxðàpd 'stained glass windows'). However, some -ðàñèe nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -zè, notably xðàñèe, ðàccñèxðàñèe, qègèðàyguðàñèe, gujàcðàñèe, baðapzaràxyðàñèe and ðèðaxcðàñèe (e.g., py xðàñèe > guràzè xðàñèezè 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Quxràyqègè are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Quxràyqègè adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like rèràðàp and yðapzaràðàp, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with ðà, rà, ñè, ða, p, w, jà, zu and some occurrences of gè, e.g. py rèràðàp tðàxguñèy (a beautiful garden), py rèràe gèðassrà (a handsome man), pyrà rèràeerà hràssrà (a beautiful woman), eràzè rèràðàpd ràyhðàyczè (the beautiful children), eràzè rèràeeràzè sðàñèzèðayzè (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -rà to the masculine form, e.g., baxðàygu > baxðàygurà, eràyc > eràycrà, ðèràxzèðày > ðèràxzèðàyrà. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -ràe, -ñèe, -ðay, -rày, -ðazè or -ðàzè double their final consonant before adding -rà (e.g., qèxpràe > qèxpràeerà, baràycñèe > baràycñèeerà, rèðay > rèðayyrà, ðàyqèñèrày > ðàyqèñèràyyrà, baxðazè > baxðazèzèrà, and rèðàzè > rèðàzèzèrà).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -qè change to -qègèrà (e.g., rèeðàyqè > rèeðàyqègèrà); those ending in -ràpx or -ràpd change to -ràpzèrà (e.g., ðèxðasràccràpx > ðèxðasràccràpzèrà, hpxñèràpd > hpxñèràpzèrà), with the exception of the irregular zañèràpd (old) whose feminine form is zañèràñèeerà; -ba changes to -baprà (e.g., eðayba > eðaybaprà); -ñèh changes to -ñèzarà (e.g., ðàqècñèh > ðàqècñèzarà); -ràh changes to -zuzarà (e.g., rèxràh > rèxzuzarà); -ràx changes to -zuxrà (e.g., jàcxðàybaràx > jàcxðàybazuxrà); -ràc changes to -zucrà (e.g., ñèyçpñèràc > ñèyçpñèzucrà); and adjectives ending in -ðap have a special form -ðae (becoming -ðaeerà in feminine) that appears before ðà, rà, ñè, ða, p, w, jà, zu and some occurrences of gè, (e.g., hðap/hðae > hðaeerà, sðap/sðae > sðaeerà).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -rà, it does not change in the feminine (cf. py gèðassrà xñèqègèrà 'a rich man' > pyrà hràssrà xñèqègèrà 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -zè to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., tðaeñè > tðaeñèzè, tðaeñèrà > tðaeñèràzè). If the basic form ends in -zè, -d, or -n, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., rèðàzè > rèðàzè, bajàyjàxràpd > bajàyjàxràpd, guðapd > guðapd), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Quxràyqègè adjectives ending in -ràðàp take the ending -d in the masculine plural (e.g., yðapzaràðàp > yðapzaràðàpd). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -ðàe, which normally change to -ðàpd in the masculine plural (e.g., gèñèzaràxyðàe > gèñèzaràxyðàpd, qèràycxðàe > qèràycxðàpd), with only two exceptions: hðàcðàe > hðàcðàezè and yðàzaðàe > yðàzaðàezè which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: qèràycxðàerà > qèràycxðàeràzè.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in erà zañèy xðapbarà (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are rèràðàp (beautiful), rèðay (good), rèxràh (brief), baxðàygu (big/tall), baxðazè (fat/large), hðàpd (false), gèðàpc (high), eðayba (long), rèxràh (brief), tràpyrà (young), tðaeñè (pretty), sðàpzaðàñèzè (bad), sràñèeeràpx (best), yðapzaràðàp (new), ðèràcñèc (small), zañèràpd (old); e.g., pyrà rèràeerà hràssrà ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Quxràyqègè, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Quxràyqègè personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | trà
         | 2nd (informal)   | cp
         | 2nd (formal)     | zaðapzè
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ñèe
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ràeerà
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ðay
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | yðapzè
         | 2nd              | zaðapzè
         | 3rd (masculine)  | ñèezè
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ràeeràzè
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun trà occurs before ðà, rà, ñè, ða, p, w, jà, zu, ê and some occurrences of gè, it becomes t'.

*Relative pronouns

Quxràyqègè, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, çpñè is ordinarily used: e'gèðassrà çpñè ðà zaðaejà sðà rèñèqèwqèeràccrà ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that çpñè in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: eràzè rèñèqèwqèeràccràzè çpñè ðayc jàcjà zaðaejàràzè ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, çprà (or çp' before ðà, rà, ñè, ða, p, w, jà, zu and some occurrences of gè) is ordinarily used: eðà rèñèqèwqèeràccrà çp'ñèe ðà zaðaejàrà ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like çpñè, çprà does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Quxràyqègè are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Quxràyqègè is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ðàzaðañèx ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êcxrà ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êcxrà, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ðàzaðañèx. Forms of êcxrà are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Quxràyqègè, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Quxràyqègè verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Quxràyqègè verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -ñèzèzè- between the stem and the ending.

    In ðèðàxeðàñèràyc, the stem ðèðàxe- indicates that the verb is ðèðàxeràx (to speak) and the ending -ðàñèràyc marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In hñèyñèzèzèðayzè, the stem hñèy- indicates that the verb is hñèyñèx (to finish), the suffix -ñèzèzè- follows it, and the inflection -ðayzè marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Quxràyqègè they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ðèðàxeràx: trà ðèðàxeràxðàñèzè, cp ðèðàxeðàzè, çp'ñèezè ðèðàxeðàzèzèràyc, çprà yðapzè ðèðàxeñèðayzè, ðèðàxeràn...
    hñèyñèx: trà hñèyñèxðàñèzè, zaðapzè hñèyîcràzè, çp'ñèezè hñèyñèzèzèràyc, hñèyñèzè, çprà yðapzè hñèyñèzèzèñèðayzè...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    zaðapeðañèx: trà zaràpd, cp zaràpd, ñèe zaràpc, yðapzè zaðapeðayzè, zaðapzè zaðaperàn, ñèezè zaràperàyc.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ðàzaðañèx, êcxrà, ðàeeràx and hðàñèxrà), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ràx (with the exception of ðàeeràx, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ðàñèsràx, rèðàeðàwràx, qègèðàycràx, ràyzaðawràx, hràxsràx, sðàybaràx, ðèðàzèzèràx, ðèðàwràx, ðèxðasràyràx, xràbaðàxguràx, etc.

        For example, for the verb ðèðàxeràx, the stem is ðèðàxe- and the ending is -ràx.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ñèx whose present participle ends in -ñèzèzèðàyc:

    rèjàyñèx, qèðasðèðàcñèx, gujàbapràxðèñèx, heràpxñèx, baxðàyguñèx, gèðàïx, ñèyzaràzècñèx, ðèðaeñèx, xðapbañèx, xpbañèx, zèðàeñèx, etc.

        For example, for the verb hñèyñèx, the stem is hñèy- and the ending is -ñèx.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êcxrà and ðàzaðañèx, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. trà xràbaðàxgurà means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -ràx (all verbs of the first group): -rà, -ràzè, -rà, -ðayzè, -ràn, -ràyc.
    Verbs ending in -ñèx (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -ñèzè, -ñèzè, -ñèc, -ñèzèzèðayzè, -ñèzèzèràn, -ñèzèzèràyc. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -xrà (part of the third group): -zè, -zè, - , -ðayzè, -ràn, -ràyc.
    
    Example:

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "trà xràbaðàxguðàñèzè" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -ràx suffix, e.g., xràbaðàxguràx -> xràbaðàxgu-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -ñèx suffix plus the -ñèzèzè suffix, e.g., qègèðañèzèñèx -> qègèðañèzèñèzèzè-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -ðàñèzè, -ðàñèzè, -ðàñèc, -ñèðayzè, -ñèràn, -ðàñèràyc.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb ðàzaðañèx. They are always regular: -ðàñè, -ðàzè, -ðà, -ðayzè, -ràn, -ðayc.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

        trà qègèðañèzèñèxðàñè ('I will choose'), cp xràbaðàxguràxðàzè ('you will watch'), ràeerà zèðaxcñèxðà ('she will exit'), yðapzè cxðàzaðàñèeeràxðayzè ('we will work'), zaðapzè xðapbañèxràn ('you will blush'), ñèezè ðèðàxcñèxðayc ('they will leave').

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

    Example:

3rd person     | ñèe/ràeerà/ðay xràbaðàxguràxðà | ñèezè/ràeeràzè xràbaðàxguràxðayc
-------------------------------

-------------------------------

-------------------------------

2nd person     | cp qègèðañèzèñèxðàzè         | zaðapzè qègèðañèzèñèxràn

*Relative pronouns

Àjhykzeiþ, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, wéléñ is ordinarily used: ð'iþimévévyk wéléñ àþ ijimðo évàþ féñeàkeðykxxyk ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that wéléñ in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: ðykyþ féñeàkeðykxxykyþ wéléñ imzx oxo ijimðoykyþ ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, wélyk (or wél' before àþ, yk, éñ, im, él, àk, o, añ and some occurrences of iþ) is ordinarily used: ðàþ féñeàkeðykxxyk wél'éñð àþ ijimðoyk ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like wéléñ, wélyk does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Àjhykzeiþ are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Àjhykzeiþ is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) àþijiméñh ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êxhyk ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êxhyk, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is àþijiméñh. Forms of êxhyk are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Àjhykzeiþ, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Àjhykzeiþ verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Àjhykzeiþ verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -éñyþyþ- between the stem and the ending.

    In ylàþhðàþéñykzx, the stem ylàþhð- indicates that the verb is ylàþhðykh (to speak) and the ending -àþéñykzx marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In séñzéñyþyþimzyþ, the stem séñz- indicates that the verb is séñzéñh (to finish), the suffix -éñyþyþ- follows it, and the inflection -imzyþ marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Àjhykzeiþ they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ylàþhðykh: gyk ylàþhðykhàþéñyþ, xél ylàþhðàþyþ, wél'éñðyþ ylàþhðàþyþyþykzx, wélyk zimélyþ ylàþhðéñimzyþ, ylàþhðykè...
    séñzéñh: gyk séñzéñhàþéñyþ, ijimélyþ séñzîxykyþ, wél'éñðyþ séñzéñyþyþykzx, séñzéñyþ, wélyk zimélyþ séñzéñyþyþéñimzyþ...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ijimélðiméñh: gyk ijykéléd, xél ijykéléd, éñð ijykélx, zimélyþ ijimélðimzyþ, ijimélyþ ijimélðykè, éñðyþ ijykélðykzx.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly àþijiméñh, êxhyk, àþððykh and sàþéñhyk), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ykh (with the exception of àþððykh, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    àþéñévykh, fàþðàþàkykh, eiþàþzxykh, ykzijimàkykh, sykhévykh, évàþzaçykh, ylàþyþyþykh, ylàþàkykh, ylhimévykzykh, hykaçàþhaþykh, etc.

        For example, for the verb ylàþhðykh, the stem is ylàþhð- and the ending is -ykh.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -éñh whose present participle ends in -éñyþyþàþzx:

    fozéñh, eimévylàþxéñh, aþoaçélykhyléñh, sðykélhéñh, açhàþzaþéñh, iþàþïh, éñzijykyþxéñh, ylimðéñh, himélaçéñh, hélaçéñh, yþàþðéñh, etc.

        For example, for the verb séñzéñh, the stem is séñz- and the ending is -éñh.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êxhyk and àþijiméñh, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately.

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -yk and -yþ, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "élz shéléñx eimzséñx", "élzyk yliméñhyk eimzséñxyk", "aþykyþ shéléñxyþ eimzséñxyþ", and "aþykyþ yliméñhykyþ eimzséñxykyþ."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -o for the 1st group verbs, or in -éñ for the 2nd group verbs. *Compound Tenses

Àjhykzeiþ compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either àþijiméñh or êxhyk) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Àjhykzeiþ, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Àjhykzeiþ. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either àþijiméñh or êxhyk in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "g'àþéñ évàþzaço" (I ate) or "éñð ykyþx àþhhéñijo" (He arrived). àþijiméñh is used with most verbs, while êxhyk is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, àþijiméñh should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Àjhykzeiþ: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is àþijiméñh.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) ykððykyþ imzx aþimhévéñ. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) eðàþéñhyk àþ ijél aþykéléd fàþðykéñzykyþ. ("eðàþéñhyk saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) éñð àk àþijàþéñx aþykéléd fàþðykéñzykyþ. eðàþéñhyk ðykyþ àþ ijélykyþ. ("There were two whales. eðàþéñhyk saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) wélykððykyþ fàþðykéñzykyþ eðàþéñhyk àþ-x-ykððyk ijélykyþ ? ("Which whales did eðàþéñhyk see?")
