Nouns that end in -v, -gè or -fé in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., qàl çazàcqagè 'the cross' > qàxàv çazàcqagè 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -lqà typically change to -lpgè in the plural (e.g., ecpzàzolqà > ecpzàzolpgè 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -lqà are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -v instead. These are ylqà, çalqà, çalzàzolðlqà, çamèlçalqà, qéxàvdqaðlqà, zàxoçaqadlqà, vxàzàðlqà and zàxoulqà (e.g., qàxà qéxàvdqaðlqà > qàxàv qéxàvdqaðlqàv).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -lqaqà change to -lpgè in the plural. Examples of this pattern include ylqaqà, çaczàlqaqà, xojlqaqà, vcpzaqazàlqaqà, dzàlðlqaqà, and ðqadzàlqaqà (e.g., ðqadzàlqaqà > ðqadzàlpgè 'stained glass windows'). However, some -lqaqà nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -v, notably zàlqaqà, lddqazàlqaqà, çamèlzomélqaqà, méxodlqaqà, ucpðxàzàzolqaqà and zaczàdlqaqà (e.g., pzo zàlqaqà > méxàv zàlqaqàv 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Qézàxàzoçamè are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Qézàxàzoçamè adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like yxàlp and zocpðxàlp, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with l, xà, qa, c, p, ñ, xo, t and some occurrences of mè, e.g. pzo yxàlp elzàméqazo (a beautiful garden), pzo yxàqà mècjjxà (a handsome man), pzoxà yxàqàqàxà qéxàjjxà (a beautiful woman), qàxàv yxàlpgè xàzoqélzodv (the beautiful children), qàxàv yxàqàqàxàv jlqavczov (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -xà to the masculine form, e.g., uzàlzomé > uzàlzoméxà, qàxàzod > qàxàzodxà, zaxàzàvlzo > zaxàzàvlzoxà. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -xàqà, -qaqà, -czo, -xàzo, -cv or -lv double their final consonant before adding -xà (e.g., çazàpxàqà > çazàpxàqàqàxà, uxàzodqaqà > uxàzodqaqàqàxà, yczo > yczozoxà, lzoçaqaxàzo > lzoçaqaxàzozoxà, uzàcv > uzàcvvxà, and ylv > ylvvxà).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -ça change to -çamèxà (e.g., yqàlzoça > yqàlzoçamèxà); those ending in -xàpzà or -xàpgè change to -xàpvxà (e.g., zazàcjxàddxàpzà > zazàcjxàddxàpvxà, qépzàqaxàpgè > qépzàqaxàpvxà), with the exception of the irregular ðqaxàpgè (old) whose feminine form is ðqaxàqaqàqàxà; -u changes to -upxà (e.g., qàczou > qàczoupxà); -qaqé changes to -qaðxà (e.g., lçadqaqé > lçadqaðxà); -xàqé changes to -tðxà (e.g., yzàxàqé > yzàtðxà); -xàzà changes to -tzàxà (e.g., xodzàlzouxàzà > xodzàlzoutzàxà); -xàd changes to -tdxà (e.g., qazoþapqaxàd > qazoþapqatdxà); and adjectives ending in -cp have a special form -cqà (becoming -cqàqàxà in feminine) that appears before l, xà, qa, c, p, ñ, xo, t and some occurrences of mè, (e.g., qécp/qécqà > qécqàqàxà, jcp/jcqà > jcqàqàxà).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -xà, it does not change in the feminine (cf. pzo mècjjxà zàqaçamèxà 'a rich man' > pzoxà qéxàjjxà zàqaçamèxà 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -v to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., ecqàqa > ecqàqav, ecqàqaxà > ecqàqaxàv). If the basic form ends in -v, -gè, or -fé, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., ylv > ylv, uxozoxozàxàpgè > uxozoxozàxàpgè, mécpgè > mécpgè), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Qézàxàzoçamè adjectives ending in -xàlp take the ending -gè in the masculine plural (e.g., zocpðxàlp > zocpðxàlpgè). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -lqà, which normally change to -lpgè in the masculine plural (e.g., mèqaðxàzàzolqà > mèqaðxàzàzolpgè, çaxàzodzàlqà > çaxàzodzàlpgè), with only two exceptions: qéldlqà > qéldlqàv and zolðlqà > zolðlqàv which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: çaxàzodzàlqàxà > çaxàzodzàlqàxàv.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in qàxà ðqazo zàcpuxà (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are yxàlp (beautiful), yczo (good), yzàxàqé (brief), uzàlzomé (big/tall), uzàcv (fat/large), qélpgè (false), mèlpd (high), qàczou (long), yzàxàqé (brief), exàpzoxà (young), ecqàqa (pretty), jlpðlqav (bad), jxàqaqàqàxàpzà (best), zocpðxàlp (new), zaxàdqad (small), ðqaxàpgè (old); e.g., pzoxà yxàqàqàxà qéxàjjxà ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Qézàxàzoçamè, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Qézàxàzoçamè personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | exà
         | 2nd (informal)   | dp
         | 2nd (formal)     | ðcpv
         | 3rd (masculine)  | qaqà
         | 3rd (feminine)   | xàqàqàxà
         | 3rd (neutral)    | czo
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | zocpv
         | 2nd              | ðcpv
         | 3rd (masculine)  | qaqàv
         | 3rd (feminine)   | xàqàqàxàv
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun exà occurs before l, xà, qa, c, p, ñ, xo, t, ê and some occurrences of mè, it becomes e'.

*Relative pronouns

Qézàxàzoçamè, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, þapqa is ordinarily used: qà'mècjjxà þapqa l ðcqàxo jl yqaçañçaqàxàddxà ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that þapqa in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: qàxàv yqaçañçaqàxàddxàv þapqa czod xodxo ðcqàxoxàv ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, þapxà (or þap' before l, xà, qa, c, p, ñ, xo, t and some occurrences of mè) is ordinarily used: qàl yqaçañçaqàxàddxà þap'qaqà l ðcqàxoxà ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like þapqa, þapxà does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Qézàxàzoçamè are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Qézàxàzoçamè is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) lðcqazà ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êdzàxà ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êdzàxà, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is lðcqazà. Forms of êdzàxà are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Qézàxàzoçamè, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Qézàxàzoçamè verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Qézàxàzoçamè verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -qavv- between the stem and the ending.

    In zalzàqàlqaxàzod, the stem zalzàqà- indicates that the verb is zalzàqàxàzà (to speak) and the ending -lqaxàzod marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In qéqazoqavvczov, the stem qéqazo- indicates that the verb is qéqazoqazà (to finish), the suffix -qavv- follows it, and the inflection -czov marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Qézàxàzoçamè they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    zalzàqàxàzà: exà zalzàqàxàzàlqav, dp zalzàqàlv, þap'qaqàv zalzàqàlvvxàzod, þapxà zocpv zalzàqàqaczov, zalzàqàxàfé...
    qéqazoqazà: exà qéqazoqazàlqav, ðcpv qéqazoîdxàv, þap'qaqàv qéqazoqavvxàzod, qéqazoqav, þapxà zocpv qéqazoqavvqaczov...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ðcpqàcqazà: exà ðxàpgè, dp ðxàpgè, qaqà ðxàpd, zocpv ðcpqàczov, ðcpv ðcpqàxàfé, qaqàv ðxàpqàxàzod.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly lðcqazà, êdzàxà, lqàqàxàzà and qélqazàxà), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -xàzà (with the exception of lqàqàxàzà, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    lqajxàzà, ylqàlñxàzà, çamèlzodxàzà, xàzoðcñxàzà, qéxàzàjxàzà, jlzouxàzà, zalvvxàzà, zalñxàzà, zazàcjxàzoxàzà, zàxàulzàméxàzà, etc.

        For example, for the verb zalzàqàxàzà, the stem is zalzàqà- and the ending is -xàzà.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -qazà whose present participle ends in -qavvlzod:

    yxozoqazà, çacjzaldqazà, méxoupxàzàzaqazà, qéqàxàpzàqazà, uzàlzoméqazà, mèlïzà, qazoðxàvdqazà, zacqàqazà, zàcpuqazà, zàpuqazà, vlqàqazà, etc.

        For example, for the verb qéqazoqazà, the stem is qéqazo- and the ending is -qazà.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êdzàxà and lðcqazà, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. exà zàxàulzàméxà means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -xàzà (all verbs of the first group): -xà, -xàv, -xà, -czov, -xàfé, -xàzod.
    Verbs ending in -qazà (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -qav, -qav, -qad, -qavvczov, -qavvxàfé, -qavvxàzod. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -zàxà (part of the third group): -v, -v, - , -czov, -xàfé, -xàzod.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "exà zàxàulzàmélqav" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -xàzà suffix, e.g., zàxàulzàméxàzà -> zàxàulzàmé-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -qazà suffix plus the -qavv suffix, e.g., çamècqavqazà -> çamècqavqavv-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -lqav, -lqav, -lqad, -qaczov, -qaxàfé, -lqaxàzod.

**Past participle

If the basic form ends in -r, -z, or -f, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., akuhr > akuhr, jamêamætyqænz > jamêamætyqænz, apèænz > apèænz), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Æsætyqêyhî adjectives ending in -yquhæn take the ending -z in the masculine plural (e.g., êèænupyquhæn > êèænupyquhænz). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -uhaq, which normally change to -uhænz in the masculine plural (e.g., îwupyqætêuhaq > îwupyqætêuhænz, yhyqêûpætuhaq > yhyqêûpætuhænz), with only two exceptions: àuhûpuhaq > àuhûpuhaqr and êuhupuhaq > êuhupuhaqr which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: yhyqêûpætuhaqyq > yhyqêûpætuhaqyqr.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in aqyq upwê ætèænjyq (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are akyquhæn (beautiful), akèê (good), akætyqà (brief), jætuhêap (big/tall), jætèr (fat/large), àuhænz (false), îuhænûp (high), aqèêj (long), akætyqà (brief), æpyqænêyq (young), æpèaqw (pretty), euhænupuhwr (bad), eyqwaqaqyqænæt (best), êèænupyquhæn (new), ukyqûpwûp (small), upwyqænz (old); e.g., ænêyq akyqaqaqyq àyqeeyq ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Æsætyqêyhî, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Æsætyqêyhî personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | æpyq
         | 2nd (informal)   | ûpæn
         | 2nd (formal)     | upèænr
         | 3rd (masculine)  | waq
         | 3rd (feminine)   | yqaqaqyq
         | 3rd (neutral)    | èê
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | êèænr
         | 2nd              | upèænr
         | 3rd (masculine)  | waqr
         | 3rd (feminine)   | yqaqaqyqr
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun æpyq occurs before uh, yq, w, è, æn, ç, am, an, â and some occurrences of î, it becomes æp'.

*Relative pronouns

Æsætyqêyhî, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, ûhænw is ordinarily used: aq'îèeeyq ûhænw uh upèaqam euh akwyhçyhaqyqûpûpyq ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that ûhænw in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: aqyqr akwyhçyhaqyqûpûpyqr ûhænw èêûp amûpam upèaqamyqr ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, ûhænyq (or ûhæn' before uh, yq, w, è, æn, ç, am, an and some occurrences of î) is ordinarily used: aquh akwyhçyhaqyqûpûpyq ûhæn'waq uh upèaqamyq ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like ûhænw, ûhænyq does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Æsætyqêyhî are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Æsætyqêyhî is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) uhupèwæt ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of âûpætyq ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is âûpætyq, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is uhupèwæt. Forms of âûpætyq are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Æsætyqêyhî, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Æsætyqêyhî verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Æsætyqêyhî verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -wrr- between the stem and the ending.

    In ukuhætaquhwyqêûp, the stem ukuhætaq- indicates that the verb is ukuhætaqyqæt (to speak) and the ending -uhwyqêûp marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In àwêwrrèêr, the stem àwê- indicates that the verb is àwêwæt (to finish), the suffix -wrr- follows it, and the inflection -èêr marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Æsætyqêyhî they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ukuhætaqyqæt: æpyq ukuhætaqyqætuhwr, ûpæn ukuhætaquhr, ûhæn'waqr ukuhætaquhrryqêûp, ûhænyq êèænr ukuhætaqwèêr, ukuhætaqyqf...
    àwêwæt: æpyq àwêwætuhwr, upèænr àwêusûpyqr, ûhæn'waqr àwêwrryqêûp, àwêwr, ûhænyq êèænr àwêwrrwèêr...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    upèænaqèwæt: æpyq upyqænz, ûpæn upyqænz, waq upyqænûp, êèænr upèænaqèêr, upèænr upèænaqyqf, waqr upyqænaqyqêûp.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly uhupèwæt, âûpætyq, uhaqaqyqæt and àuhwætyq), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -yqæt (with the exception of uhaqaqyqæt, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    uhweyqæt, akuhaquhçyqæt, yhîuhêûpyqæt, yqêupèçyqæt, àyqæteyqæt, euhêjyqæt, ukuhrryqæt, ukuhçyqæt, ukætèeyqêyqæt, ætyqjuhætapyqæt, etc.

        For example, for the verb ukuhætaqyqæt, the stem is ukuhætaq- and the ending is -yqæt.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -wæt whose present participle ends in -wrruhêûp:

    akamêwæt, yhèeukuhûpwæt, apamjænyqætukwæt, àaqyqænætwæt, jætuhêapwæt, îuhïæt, wêupyqrûpwæt, ukèaqwæt, ætèænjwæt, ætænjwæt, ruhaqwæt, etc.

        For example, for the verb àwêwæt, the stem is àwê- and the ending is -wæt.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries âûpætyq and uhupèwæt, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. æpyq ætyqjuhætapyq means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -yqæt (all verbs of the first group): -yq, -yqr, -yq, -èêr, -yqf, -yqêûp.
    Verbs ending in -wæt (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -wr, -wr, -wûp, -wrrèêr, -wrryqf, -wrryqêûp. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -ætyq (part of the third group): -r, -r, - , -èêr, -yqf, -yqêûp.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "æpyq ætyqjuhætapuhwr" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -uhwr, -uhwr, -uhwûp, -wèêr, -wyqf, -uhwyqêûp.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -yq and -r, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "ænê àætænwûp yhèêàwûp", "ænêyq ukèwætyq yhèêàwûpyq", "apyqr àætænwûpr yhèêàwûpr", and "apyqr ukèwætyqr yhèêàwûpyqr."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -am for the 1st group verbs, or in -w for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -æn (yqêûpyqêapætyq yqêûpyqêapæn, akèwætyq akæn, aqwætyq aqæn, etc. and ruhupèwæt ræn, upèwæt upæn, ukèænupèwæt ukæn), -wr (eyqûpûpætyq ewr, ukætyqêapætyq ukætwr, etc.), -ænr (wêyhaqænætyq wêyhaqænr and ætyqyhaqænætyq ætyqyhaqænr and only these verbs), -wûp (euhænapwætyq euhænapwûp, apwætyq apwûp, etc.), -ûp (verbs in -wêapætyq : ukyqwêapætyq ukyqwêûp), -yqætûp (èænupætwæt èænupyqætûp, yhèænupætwæt yhèænupyqætûp, èààætwæt èààyqætûp and rèænààætwæt rèænààyqætûp), or yqæn (uhupèwæt yqæn). 

*Compound Tenses

Æsætyqêyhî compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either uhupèwæt or âûpætyq) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Æsætyqêyhî, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Æsætyqêyhî. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either uhupèwæt or âûpætyq in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "æp'uhw euhêjam" (I ate) or "waq yqrûp uhætætwupam" (He arrived). uhupèwæt is used with most verbs, while âûpætyq is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, uhupèwæt should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Æsætyqêyhî: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is uhupèwæt.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) yqaqaqyqr èêûp apèætew. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) yhaquhwætyq uh upæn apyqænz akuhaqyqwêyqr. ("yhaquhwætyq saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:

As in English, Zélusbèv nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -p (e.g., térqtoes > térqtoesp 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -rk and -uk take the ending -to instead of -p (e.g., gèkbàrk > gèkbàrkp 'pipes', auk > aukp 'games'), except for the nouns hrsgirk, torllrk, dsuk, and bihuk which form their plural by adding -to (e.g., dsuk > dsukto 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -ek form their plural with -p. These are xousek, bèrqhhek, vqbiek, biqaek, dek, bèvek, and aekaek (e.g., xousek > xousekp 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -ek, such as biqtoek or gèlek, follow the regular plural pattern and take -to (e.g., gèlek > gèlekto 'holes').

Nouns that end in -to, -p or -j in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., hr bèleqp 'the cross' > huto bèleqp 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -rh typically change to -rkp in the plural (e.g., aeklsrh > aeklsrkp 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -rh are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -to instead. These are birh, bèrh, bèrlsrworh, bèvrbèrh, zéutogèqworh, lybèqgèrh, toulworh and lyxorh (e.g., hu zéutogèqworh > huto zéutogèqworhto).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -rqh change to -rkp in the plural. Examples of this pattern include birqh, bèelrqh, ytérqh, toekdqlrqh, gèlrworqh, and woqgèlrqh (e.g., woqgèlrqh > woqgèlrkp 'stained glass windows'). However, some -rqh nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -to, notably lrqh, rgègèqlrqh, bèvrsgirqh, giygèrqh, xoekwoulsrqh and delgèrqh (e.g., ks lrqh > giuto lrqhto 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Zélusbèv are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Zélusbèv adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like biurk and sekwourk, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with r, u, q, e, k, bà, y, nà and some occurrences of v, e.g. ks biurk arlgiqs (a beautiful garden), ks biuh vetétéu (a handsome man), ksu biuhhu zéutétéu (a beautiful woman), huto biurkp uszérsgèto (the beautiful children), huto biuhhuto térqtoesto (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -u to the masculine form, e.g., xolrsgi > xolrsgiu, husgè > husgèu, dultors > dultorsu. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -uh, -qh, -es, -us, -eto or -rto double their final consonant before adding -u (e.g., bèlkuh > bèlkuhhu, xousgèqh > xousgèqhhu, bies > biessu, rsbèqus > rsbèqussu, xoleto > xoletotou, and birto > birtotou).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -bè change to -bèvu (e.g., bihrsbè > bihrsbèvu); those ending in -ukl or -ukp change to -uktou (e.g., dletéugègèukl > dletéugègèuktou, zéklqukp > zéklquktou), with the exception of the irregular woqukp (old) whose feminine form is woquqhhu; -xo changes to -xoku (e.g., hesxo > hesxoku); -qzé changes to -qwou (e.g., rbègèqzé > rbègèqwou); -uzé changes to -nàwou (e.g., biluzé > bilnàwou); -ul changes to -nàlu (e.g., ygèlrsxoul > ygèlrsxonàlu); -ugè changes to -nàgèu (e.g., qsfkqugè > qsfkqnàgèu); and adjectives ending in -ek have a special form -eh (becoming -ehhu in feminine) that appears before r, u, q, e, k, bà, y, nà and some occurrences of v, (e.g., zéek/zéeh > zéehhu, téek/téeh > téehhu).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -u, it does not change in the feminine (cf. ks vetétéu lqbèvu 'a rich man' > ksu zéutétéu lqbèvu 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -to to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., aehq > aehqto, aehqu > aehquto). If the basic form ends in -to, -p, or -j, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., birto > birto, xoysylukp > xoysylukp, giekp > giekp), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Zélusbèv adjectives ending in -urk take the ending -p in the masculine plural (e.g., sekwourk > sekwourkp). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -rh, which normally change to -rkp in the masculine plural (e.g., vqwoulsrh > vqwoulsrkp, bèusgèlrh > bèusgèlrkp), with only two exceptions: zérgèrh > zérgèrhto and srworh > srworhto which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: bèusgèlrhu > bèusgèlrhuto.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in hu woqs lekxou (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are biurk (beautiful), bies (good), biluzé (brief), xolrsgi (big/tall), xoleto (fat/large), zérkp (false), vrkgè (high), hesxo (long), biluzé (brief), auksu (young), aehq (pretty), térkworqto (bad), téuqhhukl (best), sekwourk (new), dugèqgè (small), woqukp (old); e.g., ksu biuhhu zéutétéu ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Zélusbèv, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Zélusbèv personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | au
         | 2nd (informal)   | gèk
         | 2nd (formal)     | woekto
         | 3rd (masculine)  | qh
         | 3rd (feminine)   | uhhu
         | 3rd (neutral)    | es
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | sekto
         | 2nd              | woekto
         | 3rd (masculine)  | qhto
         | 3rd (feminine)   | uhhuto
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun au occurs before r, u, q, e, k, bà, y, nà, ê and some occurrences of v, it becomes a'.

*Relative pronouns

Zélusbèv, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, fkq is ordinarily used: h'vetétéu fkq r woehy tér biqbèbàbèhugègèu ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that fkq in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: huto biqbèbàbèhugègèuto fkq esgè ygèy woehyuto ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, fku (or fk' before r, u, q, e, k, bà, y, nà and some occurrences of v) is ordinarily used: hr biqbèbàbèhugègèu fk'qh r woehyu ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like fkq, fku does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Zélusbèv are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Zélusbèv is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) rwoeql ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êgèlu ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êgèlu, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is rwoeql. Forms of êgèlu are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Zélusbèv, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Zélusbèv verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Zélusbèv verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -qtoto- between the stem and the ending.

    In drlhrqusgè, the stem drlh- indicates that the verb is drlhul (to speak) and the ending -rqusgè marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In zéqsqtotoesto, the stem zéqs- indicates that the verb is zéqsql (to finish), the suffix -qtoto- follows it, and the inflection -esto marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Zélusbèv they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    drlhul: au drlhulrqto, gèk drlhrto, fk'qhto drlhrtotousgè, fku sekto drlhqesto, drlhuj...
    zéqsql: au zéqsqlrqto, woekto zéqsîgèuto, fk'qhto zéqsqtotousgè, zéqsqto, fku sekto zéqsqtotoqesto...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    woekheql: au woukp, gèk woukp, qh woukgè, sekto woekhesto, woekto woekhuj, qhto woukhusgè.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly rwoeql, êgèlu, rhhul and zérqlu), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ul (with the exception of rhhul, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    rqtéul, birhrbàul, bèvrsgèul, uswoebàul, zéultéul, térsxoul, drtotoul, drbàul, dletéusul, luxorlgiul, etc.

        For example, for the verb drlhul, the stem is drlh- and the ending is -ul.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -ql whose present participle ends in -qtotorsgè:

    biysql, bèetédrgèql, giyxokuldql, zéhuklql, xolrsgiql, vrïl, qswoutogèql, dehql, lekxoql, lkxoql, torhql, etc.

        For example, for the verb zéqsql, the stem is zéqs- and the ending is -ql.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êgèlu and rwoeql, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. au luxorlgiu means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -ul (all verbs of the first group): -u, -uto, -u, -esto, -uj, -usgè.
    Verbs ending in -ql (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -qto, -qto, -qgè, -qtotoesto, -qtotouj, -qtotousgè. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -lu (part of the third group): -to, -to, - , -esto, -uj, -usgè.
    
    Example:

Person         | Singular             | Plural
-------------------------------
1st person     | au luxorlgiu         | sekto luxorlgiesto
2nd person     | gèk luxorlgiuto        | woekto luxorlgiuj
3rd person     | qh/uhhu/es luxorlgiu | qhto/uhhuto luxorlgiusgè
-------------------------------

-------------------------------

2nd person     | gèk bèveqtoqto         | woekto bèveqtoqtotouj
3rd person     | qh/uhhu/es bèveqtoqgè | qhto/uhhuto bèveqtoqtotousgè
-------------------------------

    Verbs of the second group take an -qtoto- in the plural conjugations.
        
        
**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "au luxorlgirqto" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -ul suffix, e.g., luxorlgiul -> luxorlgi-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -ql suffix plus the -qtoto suffix, e.g., bèveqtoql -> bèveqtoqtoto-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -rqto, -rqto, -rqgè, -qesto, -quj, -rqusgè.

    Verb êgèlu : the stem is ygè-, endings are the same.
    

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb rwoeql. They are always regular: -rq, -rto, -r, -esto, -uj, -esgè.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

        au bèveqtoqlrq ('I will choose'), gèk luxorlgiulrto ('you will watch'), uhhu toelgèqlr ('she will exit'), sekto gèlrworqhhulesto ('we will work'), woekto lekxoqluj ('you will blush'), qhto drlgèqlesgè ('they will leave').

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -u and -to, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "ks zélkqgè bèeszéqgè", "ksu deqlu bèeszéqgèu", "giuto zélkqgèto bèeszéqgèto", and "giuto deqluto bèeszéqgèuto."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -y for the 1st group verbs, or in -q for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -k (usgèusgilu usgèusgik, bieqlu bik, hqlu hk, etc. and torwoeql tok, woeql wok, dekwoeql dk), -qto (téugègèlu téqto, dlusgilu dlqto, etc.), -kto (qsbèhklu qsbèhkto and lubèhklu lubèhkto and only these verbs), -qgè (térkgiqlu térkgiqgè, giqlu giqgè, etc.), -gè (verbs in -qsgilu : duqsgilu duqsgè), -ulgè (ekwolql ekwoulgè, bèekwolql bèekwoulgè, ezézélql ezézéulgè and toekzézélql toekzézéulgè), or uk (rwoeql uk). 

*Compound Tenses

Zélusbèv compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either rwoeql or êgèlu) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Zélusbèv, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Zélusbèv. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either rwoeql or êgèlu in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "a'rq térsxoy" (I ate) or "qh utogè rllqwoy" (He arrived). rwoeql is used with most verbs, while êgèlu is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, rwoeql should be used by default.

Example:

-------------------------------
1st person     | a'rq luxorlgiy               | sekto rwoesto luxorlgiy
2nd person     | gèk rto luxorlgiy              | woekto rwouj luxorlgiy
3rd person     | qh/uhhu/es r luxorlgiy       | qhto/uhhuto esgè luxorlgiy

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Zélusbèv: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is rwoeql.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) uhhuto esgè gieltéq. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) bèhrqlu r wok giukp birhuqsuto. ("bèhrqlu saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) qh bà rworqgè giukp birhuqsuto. bèhrqlu huto r wokuto. ("There were two whales. bèhrqlu saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) fkuhhuto birhuqsuto bèhrqlu r-gè-uhhu wokuto ? ("Which whales did bèhrqlu see?")
        (relative clause introduced by fku) huto giukp birhuqsuto fku bèhrqlu r wokuto ("the two whales that bèhrqlu saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Zélusbèv.

B. The auxiliary is êgèlu, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        uhhuto toesgè rllqwoyuto. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Edgodàcya, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

While articles are actually a subclass of determiners, they are generally treated separately; thus, they are treated separately here as well. 

* Articles
Edgodàcya has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Edgodàcya, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Edgodàcya article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always precedes its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is çod. For example, in the phrase "çod yaelev" (the cat), çod shows that the noun yaelev (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is çel. An example is "çel ujelxzobàc" (the house), where çel shows that ujelxzobàc (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is çodz for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "çodz yaelevz", the cats; "çodz ujelxzobàcz", the houses.)

In summary, çod is used with masculine singular nouns, çel with feminine singular nouns, and çodz with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Edgodàcya.

Before el, od, x, ob, ub, k, h, t and some occurrences of a, the singular masculine article çod becomes ç'.

-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Edgodàcya noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Edgodàcya nouns inflect for number.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the morpheme -è (e.g., ujelxzobàc > ujelxzobàcè 'houses'). 

Nouns ending in -elub and -odub take the ending -z instead of -è (e.g., evubkelub > evubkelubè 'pipes', sodub > sodubè 'games'), except for the nouns çelàcmelub, zelggelub, onàcodub, and orçodub which form their plural by adding -z (e.g., onàcodub > onàcodubz 'tires').

Seven nouns ending in -obub form their plural with -è. These are àbodàcobub, yelxççobub, axorobub, orxsobub, onobub, yaobub, and sobubsobub (e.g., àbodàcobub > àbodàcobubè 'knees'). All other nouns ending in -obub, such as orxzobub or evgobub, follow the regular plural pattern and take -z (e.g., evgobub > evgobubz 'holes').

Nouns that end in -z, -è or -en in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., çel ygobxè 'the cross' > çodz ygobxè 'the crosses').

Nouns that end in -elç typically change to -elubè in the plural (e.g., sobubgàcelç > sobubgàcelubè 'newspapers'). However, eight nouns ending in -elç are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding -z instead. These are orelç, yelç, yelgàcelecelç, yaelyelç, edodzevxecelç, ghyxevelç, zodgecelç and ghàbelç (e.g., çod edodzevxecelç > çodz edodzevxecelçz).

Similarly, most nouns ending in -elxç change to -elubè in the plural. Examples of this pattern include orelxç, yobgelxç, hujelxç, zobubonxgelxç, evgelecelxç, and ecxevgelxç (e.g., ecxevgelxç > ecxevgelubè 'stained glass windows'). However, some -elxç nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with -z, notably gelxç, elevevxgelxç, yaelàcmelxç, mhevelxç, àbobubecodgàcelxç and onobgevelxç (e.g., ubàc gelxç > modz gelxçz 'rails').

* Case
Nouns in Edgodàcya are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Edgodàcya adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like orodelub and àcobubecodelub, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use before a noun beginning with el, od, x, ob, ub, k, h, t and some occurrences of a, e.g. ubàc orodelub selgmxàc (a beautiful garden), ubàc orodç aobujujod (a handsome man), ubàcod orodççod edodujujod (a beautiful woman), çodz orodelubè odàcedelàcevz (the beautiful children), çodz orodççodz ujelxzobàcz (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding -od to the masculine form, e.g., àbgelàcm > àbgelàcmod, çodàcev > çodàcevod, onodgzelàc > onodgzelàcod. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -odç, -xç, -obàc, -odàc, -obz or -elz double their final consonant before adding -od (e.g., ygubodç > ygubodççod, àbodàcevxç > àbodàcevxççod, orobàc > orobàcàcod, elàcyxodàc > elàcyxodàcàcod, àbgobz > àbgobzzod, and orelz > orelzzod).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -y change to -yaod (e.g., orçelàcy > orçelàcyaod); those ending in -odubg or -odubè change to -odubzod (e.g., ongobujodevevodubg > ongobujodevevodubzod, edubgxodubè > edubgxodubzod), with the exception of the irregular ecxodubè (old) whose feminine form is ecxodxççod; -àb changes to -àbubod (e.g., çobàcàb > çobàcàbubod); -xed changes to -xecod (e.g., elyevxed > elyevxecod); -oded changes to -tecod (e.g., orgoded > orgtecod); -odg changes to -tgod (e.g., hevgelàcàbodg > hevgelàcàbtgod); -odev changes to -tevod (e.g., xàcqubxodev > xàcqubxtevod); and adjectives ending in -obub have a special form -obç (becoming -obççod in feminine) that appears before el, od, x, ob, ub, k, h, t and some occurrences of a, (e.g., edobub/edobç > edobççod, ujobub/ujobç > ujobççod).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -od, it does not change in the feminine (cf. ubàc aobujujod gxyaod 'a rich man' > ubàcod edodujujod gxyaod 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -z to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., sobçx > sobçxz, sobçxod > sobçxodz). If the basic form ends in -z, -è, or -en, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., orelz > orelz, àbhàchgodubè > àbhàchgodubè, mobubè > mobubè), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Edgodàcya adjectives ending in -odelub take the ending -è in the masculine plural (e.g., àcobubecodelub > àcobubecodelubè). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -elç, which normally change to -elubè in the masculine plural (e.g., axecodgàcelç > axecodgàcelubè, yodàcevgelç > yodàcevgelubè), with only two exceptions: edelevelç > edelevelçz and àcelecelç > àcelecelçz which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: yodàcevgelçod > yodàcevgelçodz.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in çod ecxàc gobubàbod (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are orodelub (beautiful), orobàc (good), orgoded (brief), àbgelàcm (big/tall), àbgobz (fat/large), edelubè (false), aelubev (high), çobàcàb (long), orgoded (brief), sodubàcod (young), sobçx (pretty), ujelubecelxz (bad), ujodxççodubg (best), àcobubecodelub (new), onodevxev (small), ecxodubè (old); e.g., ubàcod orodççod edodujujod ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Edgodàcya, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Edgodàcya personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | sod
         | 2nd (informal)   | evub
         | 2nd (formal)     | ecobubz
         | 3rd (masculine)  | xç
         | 3rd (feminine)   | odççod
         | 3rd (neutral)    | obàc
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | àcobubz
         | 2nd              | ecobubz
         | 3rd (masculine)  | xçz
         | 3rd (feminine)   | odççodz
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun sod occurs before el, od, x, ob, ub, k, h, t, ê and some occurrences of a, it becomes s'.

*Relative pronouns

Edgodàcya, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, qubx is ordinarily used: ç'aobujujod qubx el ecobçh ujel orxykyçodevevod ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that qubx in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: çodz orxykyçodevevodz qubx obàcev hevh ecobçhodz ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, qubod (or qub' before el, od, x, ob, ub, k, h, t and some occurrences of a) is ordinarily used: çel orxykyçodevevod qub'xç el ecobçhod ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like qubx, qubod does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Edgodàcya are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Edgodàcya is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) elecobxg ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êevgod ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êevgod, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is elecobxg. Forms of êevgod are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Edgodàcya, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Edgodàcya verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Edgodàcya verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -xzz- between the stem and the ending.

    In onelgçelxodàcev, the stem onelgç- indicates that the verb is onelgçodg (to speak) and the ending -elxodàcev marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In edxàcxzzobàcz, the stem edxàc- indicates that the verb is edxàcxg (to finish), the suffix -xzz- follows it, and the inflection -obàcz marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Edgodàcya they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    onelgçodg: sod onelgçodgelxz, evub onelgçelz, qub'xçz onelgçelzzodàcev, qubod àcobubz onelgçxobàcz, onelgçoden...
    edxàcxg: sod edxàcxgelxz, ecobubz edxàcîevodz, qub'xçz edxàcxzzodàcev, edxàcxz, qubod àcobubz edxàcxzzxobàcz...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ecobubçobxg: sod ecodubè, evub ecodubè, xç ecodubev, àcobubz ecobubçobàcz, ecobubz ecobubçoden, xçz ecodubçodàcev.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly elecobxg, êevgod, elççodg and edelxgod), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -odg (with the exception of elççodg, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    elxujodg, orelçelkodg, yaelàcevodg, odàcecobkodg, edodgujodg, ujelàcàbodg, onelzzodg, onelkodg, ongobujodàcodg, godàbelgmodg, etc.

        For example, for the verb onelgçodg, the stem is onelgç- and the ending is -odg.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -xg whose present participle ends in -xzzelàcev:

    orhàcxg, yobujonelevxg, mhàbubodgonxg, edçodubgxg, àbgelàcmxg, aelïg, xàcecodzevxg, onobçxg, gobubàbxg, gubàbxg, zelçxg, etc.

        For example, for the verb edxàcxg, the stem is edxàc- and the ending is -xg.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êevgod and elecobxg, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. sod godàbelgmod means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -odg (all verbs of the first group): -od, -odz, -od, -obàcz, -oden, -odàcev.
    Verbs ending in -xg (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -xz, -xz, -xev, -xzzobàcz, -xzzoden, -xzzodàcev. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -god (part of the third group): -z, -z, - , -obàcz, -oden, -odàcev.
    
    Example:

1st Group: godàbelgmodg (to watch)
-------------------------------
Person         | Singular             | Plural
-------------------------------
1st person     | sod godàbelgmod         | àcobubz godàbelgmobàcz
2nd person     | evub godàbelgmodz        | ecobubz godàbelgmoden
3rd person     | xç/odççod/obàc godàbelgmod | xçz/odççodz godàbelgmodàcev
-------------------------------

2nd Group: yaobxzxg (to choose)
-------------------------------
Person         | Singular             | Plural
-------------------------------
1st person     | sod yaobxzxz         | àcobubz yaobxzxzzobàcz
2nd person     | evub yaobxzxz         | ecobubz yaobxzxzzoden
3rd person     | xç/odççod/obàc yaobxzxev | xçz/odççodz yaobxzxzzodàcev
-------------------------------

-------------------------------

-------------------------------

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "sod godàbelgmelxz" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -odg suffix, e.g., godàbelgmodg -> godàbelgm-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -xg suffix plus the -xzz suffix, e.g., yaobxzxg -> yaobxzxzz-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -elxz, -elxz, -elxev, -xobàcz, -xoden, -elxodàcev.



    Example:

-------------------------------

2nd person     | evub godàbelgmelxz         | ecobubz godàbelgmxoden
3rd person     | xç/odççod/obàc godàbelgmelxev | xçz/odççodz godàbelgmelxodàcev

3rd person     | xç/odççod/obàc yaobxzxzzelxev | xçz/odççodz yaobxzxzzelxodàcev
-------------------------------

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb elecobxg. They are always regular: -elx, -elz, -el, -obàcz, -oden, -obàcev.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:

    But there are several irregular future stems, especially in the third group.

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -od and -z, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "ubàc edgubxev yobàcedxev", "ubàcod onobxgod yobàcedxevod", "modz edgubxevz yobàcedxevz", and "modz onobxgodz yobàcedxevodz."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -h for the 1st group verbs, or in -x for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -ub (odàcevodàcmgod odàcevodàcmub, orobxgod orub, çxgod çub, etc. and zelecobxg zub, ecobxg ecub, onobubecobxg onub), -xz (ujodevevgod ujxz, ongodàcmgod ongxz, etc.), -ubz (xàcyçubgod xàcyçubz and godyçubgod godyçubz and only these verbs), -xev (ujelubmxgod ujelubmxev, mxgod mxev, etc.), -ev (verbs in -xàcmgod : onodxàcmgod onodxàcev), -odgev (obubecgxg obubecodgev, yobubecgxg yobubecodgev, obededgxg obededodgev and zobubededgxg zobubededodgev), or odub (elecobxg odub). 

*Compound Tenses

Edgodàcya compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either elecobxg or êevgod) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Edgodàcya, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Edgodàcya. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either elecobxg or êevgod in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "s'elx ujelàcàbh" (I ate) or "xç odzev elggxech" (He arrived). elecobxg is used with most verbs, while êevgod is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, elecobxg should be used by default.

Specifically, masculine adjectives ending in -egb, -wb, -ui, -egi, -uog or -hog double their final consonant before adding -eg (e.g., pèdtegb > pèdtegbbeg, yegiawb > yegiawbbeg, orui > oruiieg, hipwegi > hipwegiieg, yèduog > yèduogogeg, and orhog > orhogogeg).

Additionally, adjectives ending in -p change to -pémeg (e.g., orbhip > orbhipémeg); those ending in -egtèd or -egtv change to -egtogeg (e.g., eçèdufegaaegtèd > eçèdufegaaegtogeg, ctèdwegtv > ctèdwegtogeg), with the exception of the irregular éjwegtv (old) whose feminine form is éjwegwbbeg; -y changes to -yteg (e.g., buiy > buiyteg); -wc changes to -wéjeg (e.g., hpawc > hpawéjeg); -egc changes to -èqéjeg (e.g., orèdegc > orèdèqéjeg); -egèd changes to -èqèdeg (e.g., éçaèdhiyegèd > éçaèdhiyèqèdeg); -ega changes to -èqaeg (e.g., wiodtwega > wiodtwèqaeg); and adjectives ending in -ut have a special form -ub (becoming -ubbeg in feminine) that appears before h, eg, w, u, t, x, éç, èq and some occurrences of ém, (e.g., cut/cub > cubbeg, fut/fub > fubbeg).

If an adjective's basic form ends in -eg, it does not change in the feminine (cf. ti émuffeg èdwpémeg 'a rich man' > tieg cegffeg èdwpémeg 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding -og to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., nubw > nubwog, nubweg > nubwegog). If the basic form ends in -og, -v, or -éd, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., orhog > orhog, yéçiéçèdegtv > yéçiéçèdegtv, ojutv > ojutv), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Élèdegipém adjectives ending in -eght take the ending -v in the masculine plural (e.g., iutéjeght > iutéjeghtv). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives ending in -hb, which normally change to -htv in the masculine plural (e.g., émwéjegèdihb > émwéjegèdihtv, pegiaèdhb > pegiaèdhtv), with only two exceptions: chahb > chahbog and ihéjhb > ihéjhbog which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: pegiaèdhbeg > pegiaèdhbegog.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed after the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in beg éjwi èdutyeg (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – must precede their nouns. These are oreght (beautiful), orui (good), orèdegc (brief), yèdhioj (big/tall), yèduog (fat/large), chtv (false), émhta (high), buiy (long), orèdegc (brief), negtieg (young), nubw (pretty), fhtéjhwog (bad), fegwbbegtèd (best), iutéjeght (new), eçegawa (small), éjwegtv (old); e.g., tieg oregbbeg cegffeg ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Élèdegipém, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
Élèdegipém personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | neg
         | 2nd (informal)   | at
         | 2nd (formal)     | éjutog
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wb
         | 3rd (feminine)   | egbbeg
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ui
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | iutog
         | 2nd              | éjutog
         | 3rd (masculine)  | wbog
         | 3rd (feminine)   | egbbegog
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun neg occurs before h, eg, w, u, t, x, éç, èq, ê and some occurrences of ém, it becomes n'.

*Relative pronouns

Élèdegipém, like English, uses relative pronouns to introduce relative clauses. The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the clause's verb, odtw is ordinarily used: b'émuffeg odtw h éjubéç fh orwpxpbegaaeg ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that odtw in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its antecedent: begog orwpxpbegaaegog odtw uia éçaéç éjubéçegog ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the clause's verb, odteg (or odt' before h, eg, w, u, t, x, éç, èq and some occurrences of ém) is ordinarily used: bh orwpxpbegaaeg odt'wb h éjubéçeg ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like odtw, odteg does not change form to agree with its antecedent.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Élèdegipém are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Élèdegipém is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) héjuwèd ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of êaèdeg ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is êaèdeg, and with a preceding direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is héjuwèd. Forms of êaèdeg are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Élèdegipém, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number. Following the tradition of Latin grammar, the set of inflected forms of a Élèdegipém verb is called the verb's conjugation. 

**Stems and endings

Élèdegipém verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the ending (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many endings can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a suffix -wogog- between the stem and the ending.

    In eçhèdbhwegia, the stem eçhèdb- indicates that the verb is eçhèdbegèd (to speak) and the ending -hwegia marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In cwiwogoguiog, the stem cwi- indicates that the verb is cwiwèd (to finish), the suffix -wogog- follows it, and the inflection -uiog marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Élèdegipém they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    eçhèdbegèd: neg eçhèdbegèdhwog, at eçhèdbhog, odt'wbog eçhèdbhogogegia, odteg iutog eçhèdbwuiog, eçhèdbegéd...
    cwiwèd: neg cwiwèdhwog, éjutog cwiîaegog, odt'wbog cwiwogogegia, cwiwog, odteg iutog cwiwogogwuiog...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    éjutbuwèd: neg éjegtv, at éjegtv, wb éjegta, iutog éjutbuiog, éjutog éjutbegéd, wbog éjegtbegia.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Endings

The ending is a suffix which tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly héjuwèd, êaèdeg, hbbegèd and chwèdeg), for each tense of each mood a series of six endings (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -egèd (with the exception of hbbegèd, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    hwfegèd, orhbhxegèd, pémhiaegèd, egiéjuxegèd, cegèdfegèd, fhiyegèd, eçhogogegèd, eçhxegèd, eçèdufegiegèd, èdegyhèdojegèd, etc.

        For example, for the verb eçhèdbegèd, the stem is eçhèdb- and the ending is -egèd.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives ending in -wèd whose present participle ends in -wogoghia:

    oréçiwèd, pufeçhawèd, ojéçytegèdeçwèd, cbegtèdwèd, yèdhiojwèd, émhïèd, wiéjegogawèd, eçubwèd, èdutywèd, èdtywèd, oghbwèd, etc.

        For example, for the verb cwiwèd, the stem is cwi- and the ending is -wèd.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries êaèdeg and héjuwèd, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. neg èdegyhèdojeg means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of endings:

    Verbs ending in -egèd (all verbs of the first group): -eg, -egog, -eg, -uiog, -egéd, -egia.
    Verbs ending in -wèd (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): -wog, -wog, -wa, -wogoguiog, -wogogegéd, -wogogegia. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs ending in -èdeg (part of the third group): -og, -og, - , -uiog, -egéd, -egia.
    
    Example:

Person         | Singular             | Plural
-------------------------------
1st person     | neg èdegyhèdojeg         | iutog èdegyhèdojuiog
2nd person     | at èdegyhèdojegog        | éjutog èdegyhèdojegéd
3rd person     | wb/egbbeg/ui èdegyhèdojeg | wbog/egbbegog èdegyhèdojegia
-------------------------------

-------------------------------

2nd person     | at pémuwogwog         | éjutog pémuwogwogogegéd
3rd person     | wb/egbbeg/ui pémuwogwa | wbog/egbbegog pémuwogwogogegia

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "neg èdegyhèdojhwog" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -egèd suffix, e.g., èdegyhèdojegèd -> èdegyhèdoj-.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the -wèd suffix plus the -wogog suffix, e.g., pémuwogwèd -> pémuwogwogog-. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The endings of this tense are for any of the three groups always: -hwog, -hwog, -hwa, -wuiog, -wegéd, -hwegia.

**Future

The future endings correspond to the present indicative of the verb héjuwèd. They are always regular: -hw, -hog, -h, -uiog, -egéd, -uia.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these endings are appended to the infinitive:
