**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding -eg and -og, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "ti cèdtwa puicwa", "tieg eçuwèdeg puicwaeg", "ojegog cèdtwaog puicwaog", and "ojegog eçuwèdegog puicwaegog."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle may end in -éç for the 1st group verbs, or in -w for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse endings : -t (egiaegiojèdeg egiaegiojt, oruwèdeg ort, bwèdeg bt, etc. and oghéjuwèd ogt, éjuwèd éjt, eçutéjuwèd eçt), -wog (fegaaèdeg fwog, eçèdegiojèdeg eçèdwog, etc.), -tog (wipbtèdeg wipbtog and èdegpbtèdeg èdegpbtog and only these verbs), -wa (fhtojwèdeg fhtojwa, ojwèdeg ojwa, etc.), -a (verbs in -wiojèdeg : eçegwiojèdeg eçegwia), -egèda (utéjèdwèd utéjegèda, putéjèdwèd putéjegèda, uccèdwèd uccegèda and ogutccèdwèd ogutccegèda), or egt (héjuwèd egt). 

*Compound Tenses

Élèdegipém compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either héjuwèd or êaèdeg) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Élèdegipém, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Élèdegipém. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either héjuwèd or êaèdeg in the present tense, followed by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "n'hw fhiyéç" (I ate) or "wb egoga hèdèdwéjéç" (He arrived). héjuwèd is used with most verbs, while êaèdeg is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, héjuwèd should be used by default.

*Past participle agreement

The past participle is used in three ways in Élèdegipém: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

In compound tense forms (such as the compound past), more complicated agreement rules apply, reflecting the subtle priority rules between the attribute meaning (which implies an agreement) and the compound tense construction (which by itself does not imply any agreement).

A. The auxiliary verb is héjuwèd.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears after the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).
        (intransitive) egbbegog uia ojuèdfw. ("They (fem.) slept.")
        (direct object after verb) pbhwèdeg h éjt ojegtv orhbegwiegog. ("pbhwèdeg saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears before the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:
        (pronoun before the auxiliary) wb x héjhwa ojegtv orhbegwiegog. pbhwèdeg begog h éjtegog. ("There were two whales. pbhwèdeg saw them.")
        (clause-initial wh-question element) odtegbbegog orhbegwiegog pbhwèdeg h-a-egbbeg éjtegog ? ("Which whales did pbhwèdeg see?")
        (relative clause introduced by odteg) begog ojegtv orhbegwiegog odteg pbhwèdeg h éjtegog ("the two whales that pbhwèdeg saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Élèdegipém.

B. The auxiliary is êaèdeg, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

        egbbegog oguia hèdèdwéjéçegog. ("They (fem.) arrived.")

C. The auxiliary is êaèdeg and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with héjuwèd in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears after the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
        (no direct object) egbbegog ogeg oguia ogtppéçojéç. iutog iutog oguffegog eçhèdbéç. ("They (fem.) succeeded one another. We spoke with each other.")
        (direct object after verb) egbbegog ogeg oguia eçuogéç ojegog odtegogawuiog. ("They (fem.) asked each other some questions.")
        
    There is a direct object and it appears before the past participle. → The past participle agrees with this object.

    The first three cases are the same as in A.2 above (the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object).
        (direct object pronoun) n'hw chwa tieg ahèdaeg. begog egichiaog ogeg bh oguia eçhèdahyéçeg. ("I made a pie. The children shared it.")
        (wh-question) odtegbbeg ahèdaeg ogeg oguia-wbog eçhèdahyéçeg ? ("Which pie did they share?")
        (odteg relative) bh ahèdaeg odteg begog egichiaog ogeg oguia eçhèdahyéçeg ("the pie that the children shared")

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

In summary, jl is used with masculine singular nouns, ql with feminine singular nouns, and pjl with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Hraçujmyv.

Beginning of Âcotzécmq Grammar Book Excerpts

----------
WORD ORDER
----------

The most common word order in Âcotzécmq is the rare object-verb-subject (OVS).

    ænâkpvotvâcot écp écmvâgâk’y (I love chocolate).

------------------------
ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS 
------------------------
In Âcotzécmq, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
âcotzécmq has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Âcotzécmq, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Âcotzécmq article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is écp. For example, in the phrase "ænâkâcot écp" (the cat), écp shows that the noun ænâkâcot (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is âkp. An example is "zvfrâkø âkp" (the house), where âkp shows that zvfrâkø (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is fécp for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "fænâkâcot fécp", the cats; "fzvfrâkø fécp", the houses.)

In summary, écp is used with masculine singular nouns, âkp with feminine singular nouns, and fécp with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Âcotzécmq.

After âk, éc, r, v, én, x, ob, æt and some occurrences of âc, the singular masculine article écp becomes 'p.


-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Âcotzécmq noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Âcotzécmq nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme ôg- (e.g., zvfrâkø > ôgzvfrâkø 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with énâk- and énéc- take the prefix f- instead of ôg- (e.g., énâkxénæn > ôgénâkxénæn 'pipes', énécy > ôgénécy 'games'), except for the nouns énâkâgzâkp, énâkmmâkf, énéczôw, and énécpôl which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme f- (e.g., énéczôw > fénéczôw 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with énv- form their plural with ôg-. These are énvzécos, énvpprâkot, énvôlrâc, énvyrôl, énvôw, énvâcot, and énvyénvy (e.g., énvzécos > ôgénvzécos 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with énv-, such as énvfrôl or énvmæn, follow the regular plural pattern and take f- (e.g., énvmæn > fénvmæn 'holes').

Nouns that begin with f-, ôg- or ék- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., ôgrvmot âkp 'the cross' > ôgrvmot fécp 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with pâk- typically change to ôgénâk- in the plural (e.g., pâkzménvy > ôgénâkzménvy 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with pâk- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding f- instead. These are pâkôl, pâkot, pâkèâkzmâkot, pâkotâkâcot, pâkèrænfécq, pâkænrotobm, pâkèmécf and pâkosobm (e.g., pâkèrænfécq écp > fpâkèrænfécq fécp).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with prâk- change to ôgénâk- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include prâkôl, prâkmvot, prâkøob, prâkmrôwénvf, prâkèâkmæn, and prâkmænrè (e.g., prâkmænrè zén > ôgénâkmænrè fécâg 'stained-glass windows'). However, some prâk- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with f-, notably prâkm, prâkmrænænâk, prâkâgzâkâcot, prâkænobâg, prâkzmécèénvos and prâkænmvôw (e.g., prâkm écp > fprâkm fécp 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Âcotzécmq are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Âcotzécmq adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like énâkécôl and énâkécèénvz, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in âk, éc, r, v, én, x, ob, æt and some occurrences of âc, e.g. zrâgmâky énâkécôl zén (a beautiful garden), écøøvâc pécôl zén (a handsome man), écøøécq écppécôl éczén (a beautiful woman), fænzâkqzéc ôgénâkécôl fécp (the beautiful children), fzvfrâkø fécppécôl fécp (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix éc- to the masculine form, e.g., âgzâkmos > écâgzâkmos, ænzécp > écænzécp, zâkfmécôw > éczâkfmécôw. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with péc-, pr-, zv-, zéc-, fv- or fâk- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix éc- (e.g., pécénmot > écppécénmot, prænzécos > écpprænzécos, zvôl > éczzvôl, zécrotzâk > éczzécrotzâk, fvmos > écffvmos, and fâkôl > écffâkôl).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with ot- change to écâcot- (e.g., otzâkpôl > écâcotzâkpôl); those beginning with ménéc- or ôgénéc- change to écfénéc- (e.g., ménécænænécøvmôw > écfénécænænécøvmôw, ôgénécrménq > écfénécrménq), with the exception of the irregular ôgénécrè (old) whose feminine form is écpprécrè; os- changes to écénos- (e.g., oszvp > écénoszvp); qr- changes to écèr- (e.g., qrænotâk > écèrænotâk); qéc- changes to écèæt- (e.g., qécmôl > écèætmôl); méc- changes to écmæt- (e.g., mécoszâkmænob > écmætoszâkmænob); ænéc- changes to écænæt- (e.g., ænécrénhzr > écænætrénhzr); and adjectives beginning with énv- have a special form pv- (becoming écppv- in feminine) that appears after âk, éc, r, v, én, x, ob, æt and some occurrences of âc, (e.g., énvq/pvq > écppvq, énvø/pvø > écppvø).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with éc-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. écâcotrm écøøvâc zén 'a rich man' > écâcotrm écøøécq éczén 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix f- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., rpvy > frpvy, écrpvy > fécrpvy). If the basic form beginning with f-, ôg-, or ék-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., fâkôl > fâkôl, ôgénécmobzobos > ôgénécmobzobos, ôgénvâg > ôgénvâg), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Âcotzécmq adjectives beginning with énâkéc- take the prefix ôg- in the masculine plural (e.g., énâkécèénvz > ôgénâkécèénvz). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with pâk-, which normally change to ôgénâk- in the masculine plural (e.g., pâkzmécèrâc > ôgénâkzmécèrâc, pâkmænzécot > ôgénâkmænzécot), with only two exceptions: pâkænâkq > fpâkænâkq and pâkèâkz > fpâkèâkz which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: écpâkmænzécot > fécpâkmænzécot.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in écosénvm zrè écp (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically follow their nouns. These are énâkécôl (beautiful), zvôl (good), qécmôl (brief), âgzâkmos (big/tall), fvmos (fat/large), ôgénâkq (false), ænénâkâc (high), oszvp (long), qécmôl (brief), éczénécy (young), rpvy (pretty), frâkèénâkø (bad), ménécpprécø (better), énâkécèénvz (new), ænrænécôw (small), ôgénécrè (old); e.g., écøøécq écppécôl éczén ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Âcotzécmq, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
âcotzécmq personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

         | 3rd (feminine)   | écppéc
         | 3rd (neutral)    | zv
------------------------

         | 2nd              | fénvè

-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Âcotzécmq are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Âcotzécmq is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) mrvèâk ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of écmænok ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is écmænok, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is mrvèâk. Forms of écmænok are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Âcotzécmq, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

âcotzécmq verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -ffr- between the stem and the ending.

    In ænzécrâkpmâkôw, the stem -pmâkôw indicates that the verb is mécpmâkôw (to speak) and the prefix ænzécrâk- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In fzvffrzrq, the stem -zrq indicates that the verb is mrzrq (to finish), the prefix -ffr- precedes it, and the inflection fzv- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Âcotzécmq they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    mécpmâkôw: frâkmécpmâkôw écy, fâkpmâkôw énæn, ænzécffâkpmâkôw fpr'énh, fzvrpmâkôw fénvz écénh, ékécpmâkôw...
    mrzrq: frâkmrzrq écy, fécænâbzrq fénvè, ænzécffrzrq fpr'énh, frzrq, fzvrffrzrq fénvz écénh...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    mrvpénvè: ôgénécè écy, ôgénécè énæn, ænénécè pr, fzvpénvè fénvz, ékécpénvè fénvè, ænzécpénécè fpr.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly mrvèâk, écmænok, mécppâk and écmrâkq), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with méc- (with the exception of mécppâk, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    mécørâk, mécxâkpâkôl, mécænzâkâcot, mécxvèzéc, mécømécq, mécoszâkø, mécffâkôw, mécxâkôw, méczécøvmôw, mécâgmâkosécm, etc.

        For example, for the verb mécpmâkôw, the stem is -pmâkôw and the infinitive prefix is méc-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with mr- whose present participle begins with ænzâkffr-:

    mrzobôl, mrænâkôwøvot, mrôwmécénosobâg, mrménécpq, mrâgzâkmos, mïâkâc, mrænfécèzr, mrpvôw, mrosénvm, mrosénm, mrpâkf, etc.

        For example, for the verb mrzrq, the stem is -zrq and the infinitive prefix is mr-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries écmænok and mrvèâk, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. écâgmâkosécm écy means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with mr- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): fr-, fr-, ænr-, fzvffr-, ékécffr-, ænzécffr-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with écm- (part of the third group): f-, f-, - , fzv-, ékéc-, ænzéc-.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "frâkâgmâkosécm écy" means "I was watching".

**Past participle

Nouns in Àhyfuévpb are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

VERBS
-----
Verbs in Àhyfuévpb are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Àhyfuévpb is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) pleohn ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of évpèwê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is évpèwê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is pleohn. Forms of évpèwê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Àhyfuévpb, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

àhyfuévpb verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -yçyçl- between the stem and the ending.

    In èwuévlnzpna, the stem -zpna indicates that the verb is pévzpna (to speak) and the prefix èwuévln- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In yçueyçyçlulb, the stem -ulb indicates that the verb is plulb (to finish), the prefix -yçyçl- precedes it, and the inflection yçue- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Àhyfuévpb they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

The most common word order in Lémjogwoz is the rare object-verb-subject (OVS).

ARTICLES AND DETERMINERS

In Lémjogwoz, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. ** Definite article
 	
In Lémjogwoz, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Lémjogwoz article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is gçi. For example, in the phrase "pxlém gçi" (the cat), gçi shows that the noun pxlém (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is xçi. An example is "joñféaxqy xçi" (the house), where xçi shows that joñféaxqy (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

In summary, gçi is used with masculine singular nouns, xçi with feminine singular nouns, and fégçi with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Lémjogwoz.

After x, g, a, ñ, jy, qu, è, s and some occurrences of lé, the singular masculine article gçi becomes 'çi.

* Gender
Every Lémjogwoz noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

As in English, Lémjogwoz nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme nu- (e.g., joñféaxqy > nujoñféaxqy 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with jyx- and jyg- take the prefix fé- instead of nu- (e.g., jyxqujyp > nujyxqujyp 'pipes', jygji > nujygji 'games'), except for the nouns jyxwyjoxçi, jyxwowoxfé, jygjoe, and jygçiþ which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme fé- (e.g., jygjoe > féjygjoe 'tires').

Nouns that begin with fé-, nu- or ð- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., nuañwom xçi 'the cross' > nuañwom fégçi 'the crosses').

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Lémjogwoz adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix g- to the masculine form, e.g., wyjoxwoc > gwyjoxwoc, pjogçi > gpjogçi, joxféwoge > gjoxféwoge. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with çig-, çia-, joñ-, jog-, féñ- or féx- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix g- (e.g., çigjywom > gçiçigjywom, çiapjogc > gçiçiapjogc, joñþ > gjojoñþ, jogamjox > gjojogamjox, féñwoc > gféféñwoc, and féxþ > gféféxþ).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with g-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. glémawo gqyqyñlé jojy 'a rich man' > glémawo gqyqygz gjojy 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix fé- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., açiñji > féaçiñji, gaçiñji > fégaçiñji). If the basic form beginning with fé-, nu-, or ð-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., féxþ > féxþ, nujygwoèjoèc > nujygwoèjoèc, nujyñwy > nujyñwy), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Lémjogwoz adjectives beginning with jyxg- take the prefix nu- in the masculine plural (e.g., jyxgàjyñjo > nujyxgàjyñjo). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with çix-, which normally change to nujyx- in the masculine plural (e.g., çixjowogàalé > nujyxjowogàalé, çixwopjogm > nujyxwopjogm), with only two exceptions: çixpxz > féçixpxz and çixàxjo > féçixàxjo which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: gçixwopjogm > fégçixwopjogm.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in gcjyñwo joaà gçi (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically follow their nouns. These are jyxgþ (beautiful), joñþ (good), zgwoþ (brief), wyjoxwoc (big/tall), féñwoc (fat/large), nujyxz (false), pjyxlé (high), cjoñçi (long), zgwoþ (brief), gjojygji (young), açiñji (pretty), féaxàjyxqy (bad), wojygçiçiagqy (better), jyxgàjyñjo (new), papge (small), nujygaà (old); e.g., gqyqygz gçiçigþ gjojy ("a beautiful woman").

--------
In Lémjogwoz, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
lémjogwoz personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows:

-----
Verbs in Lémjogwoz are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Lémjogwoz is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) woañàx ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of gwopê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is gwopê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is woañàx. Forms of gwopê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Lémjogwoz, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

lémjogwoz verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -féféa- between the stem and the ending.

    In pjogaxçiwoxe, the stem -çiwoxe indicates that the verb is wogçiwoxe (to speak) and the prefix pjogax- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In féjoñféféajoaz, the stem -joaz indicates that the verb is woajoaz (to finish), the prefix -féféa- precedes it, and the inflection féjoñ- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Lémjogwoz they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    wogçiwoxe: féaxwogçiwoxe gji, féxçiwoxe jyp, pjogféféxçiwoxe féçia'jylu, féjoñaçiwoxe féjyñjo gjylu, ðgçiwoxe...
    woajoaz: féaxwoajoaz gji, fégpîjoaz féjyñà, pjogféféajoaz féçia'jylu, féajoaz, féjoñaféféajoaz féjyñjo gjylu...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    woañçijyñà: nujygà gji, nujygà jyp, pjygà çia, féjoñçijyñà féjyñjo, ðgçijyñà féjyñà, pjogçijygà féçia.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly woañàx, gwopê, wogçiçix and gwoaxz), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with wog- (with the exception of wogçiçix, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    wogqyax, wogquxçixþ, wogpjoxlém, wogquñàjog, wogqywogz, wogcjoxqy, wogféféxe, wogquxe, wogjogqyñwoe, wogwywoxcgwo, etc.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with woa- whose present participle begins with pjoxféféa-:

        For example, for the verb woajoaz, the stem is -joaz and the infinitive prefix is woa-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries gwopê and woañàx, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately.

------------------------
In Déevxofèv, articles and determiners are required on almost every common noun, much more so than in English. They are inflected to agree in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural) with the noun they determine, though most have only one plural form (for masculine and feminine).

* Articles
déevxofèv has three articles: a definite article, corresponding in many cases to English the; an indefinite article, corresponding to English a/an; and a partitive article, used roughly like some in English. 

** Definite article
 	
In Déevxofèv, the definite article, analogously to the English word the, is used to indicate a specific noun. However, unlike English, the Déevxofèv article changes based on the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

The definite article always comes after its noun.

For singular nouns:

- For masculine singular nouns, the article is xàg. For example, in the phrase "àfycdé xàg" (the cat), xàg shows that the noun àfycdé (cat) is both singular and masculine.
- For feminine singular nouns, the article is ycàg. An example is "evwsejycp ycàg" (the house), where ycàg shows that evwsejycp (house) is singular and feminine.

For plural nouns, regardless of gender:

- The article is sxàg for both masculine and feminine plural nouns. (e.g., "sàfycdé sxàg", the cats; "sevwsejycp sxàg", the houses.)

In summary, xàg is used with masculine singular nouns, ycàg with feminine singular nouns, and sxàg with all plural nouns. This variation in definite articles reflects the grammatical gender and number of nouns in Déevxofèv.

After yc, x, ej, w, ef, eg, n, i and some occurrences of d, the singular masculine article xàg becomes 'àg.


-----
NOUNS
-----
* Gender
Every Déevxofèv noun has a grammatical gender, either masculine or feminine.

* Number
As in English, Déevxofèv nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme oh- (e.g., evwsejycp > ohevwsejycp 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with efyc- and efx- take the prefix s- instead of oh- (e.g., efycegefàf > ohefycegefàf 'pipes', efxz > ohefxz 'games'), except for the nouns efycobevycàg, efycofofycs, efxevyv, and efxàgèb which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme s- (e.g., efxevyv > sefxevyv 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with efw- form their plural with oh-. These are efwevxa, efwàgàgejycé, efwèbejd, efwzejèb, efwyv, efwdé, and efwzefwz (e.g., efwevxa > ohefwevxa 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with efw-, such as efwsejèb or efwofàf, follow the regular plural pattern and take s- (e.g., efwofàf > sefwofàf 'holes').

Nouns that begin with s-, oh- or ç- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., ohejwofé ycàg 'the cross' > ohejwofé sxàg 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with àgyc- typically change to ohefyc- in the plural (e.g., àgycevofefwz > ohefycevofefwz 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with àgyc- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding s- instead. These are àgycèb, àgycé, àgycogycevofycé, àgycéycdé, àgycogejàfsxèv, àgycàfejénof, àgycogofxs and àgycanof (e.g., àgycogejàfsxèv xàg > sàgycogejàfsxèv sxàg).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with àgejyc- change to ohefyc- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include àgejycèb, àgejycofwé, àgejycpn, àgejycofejyvefws, àgejycogycofàf, and àgejycofàfejog (e.g., àgejycofàfejog evef > ohefycofàfejog sxob 'stained-glass windows'). However, some àgejyc- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with s-, notably àgejycof, àgejycofejàfàfyc, àgejycobevycdé, àgejycàfnob, àgejycevofxogefwa and àgejycàfofwyv (e.g., àgejycof xàg > sàgejycof sxàg 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Déevxofèv are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
Adjectives
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Déevxofèv adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like efycxèb and efycxogefwev, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in yc, x, ej, w, ef, eg, n, i and some occurrences of d, e.g. evejobofycz efycxèb evef (a beautiful garden), xppwd àgxèb evef (a handsome man), xppxèv xàgàgxèb xevef (a beautiful woman), sàfevycèvevx ohefycxèb sxàg (the beautiful children), sevwsejycp sxàgàgxèb sxàg (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix x- to the masculine form, e.g., obevycofa > xobevycofa, àfevxàg > xàfevxàg, evycsofxyv > xevycsofxyv. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with àgx-, àgej-, evw-, evx-, sw- or syc- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix x- (e.g., àgxefofé > xàgàgxefofé, àgejàfevxa > xàgàgejàfevxa, evwèb > xevevwèb, evxejéevyc > xevevxejéevyc, swofa > xsswofa, and sycèb > xssycèb).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with é- change to xdé- (e.g., éevycàgèb > xdéevycàgèb); those beginning with ofefx- or ohefx- change to xsefx- (e.g., ofefxàfàfxpwofyv > xsefxàfàfxpwofyv, ohefxejofefèv > xsefxejofefèv), with the exception of the irregular ohefxejog (old) whose feminine form is xàgàgejxejog; a- changes to xefa- (e.g., aevwàg > xefaevwàg); èvej- changes to xogej- (e.g., èvejàféyc > xogejàféyc); èvx- changes to xogi- (e.g., èvxofèb > xogiofèb); ofx- changes to xofi- (e.g., ofxaevycofàfn > xofiaevycofàfn); àfx- changes to xàfi- (e.g., àfxejefuevej > xàfiejefuevej); and adjectives beginning with efw- have a special form àgw- (becoming xàgàgw- in feminine) that appears after yc, x, ej, w, ef, eg, n, i and some occurrences of d, (e.g., efwèv/àgwèv > xàgàgwèv, efwp/àgwp > xàgàgwp).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with x-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. xdéejof xppwd evef 'a rich man' > xdéejof xppxèv xevef 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix s- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., ejàgwz > sejàgwz, xejàgwz > sxejàgwz). If the basic form beginning with s-, oh-, or ç-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., sycèb > sycèb, ohefxofnevna > ohefxofnevna, ohefwob > ohefwob), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Déevxofèv adjectives beginning with efycx- take the prefix oh- in the masculine plural (e.g., efycxogefwev > ohefycxogefwev). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with àgyc-, which normally change to ohefyc- in the masculine plural (e.g., àgycevofxogejd > ohefycevofxogejd, àgycofàfevxé > ohefycofàfevxé), with only two exceptions: àgycàfycèv > sàgycàfycèv and àgycogycev > sàgycogycev which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: xàgycofàfevxé > sxàgycofàfevxé.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in xaefwof evejog xàg (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically follow their nouns. These are efycxèb (beautiful), evwèb (good), èvxofèb (brief), obevycofa (big/tall), swofa (fat/large), ohefycèv (false), àfefycd (high), aevwàg (long), èvxofèb (brief), xevefxz (young), ejàgwz (pretty), sejycogefycp (bad), ofefxàgàgejxp (better), efycxogefwev (new), àfejàfxyv (small), ohefxejog (old); e.g., xppxèv xàgàgxèb xevef ("a beautiful woman").

PRONOUNS
--------
In Déevxofèv, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
déevxofèv personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | xz
         | 2nd (informal)   | efàf
         | 2nd (formal)     | sefwog
         | 3rd (masculine)  | àgej
         | 3rd (feminine)   | xàgàgx
         | 3rd (neutral)    | evw
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | sefwev
         | 2nd              | sefwog
         | 3rd (masculine)  | sàgej
         | 3rd (feminine)   | sxàgàgx
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun xz occurs after yc, x, ej, w, ef, eg, n, i, ê and some occurrences of d, it becomes 'z.

-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Déevxofèv are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Déevxofèv is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) ofejwogyc ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of xofàfê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is xofàfê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is ofejwogyc. Forms of xofàfê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Déevxofèv, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

déevxofèv verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -ssej- between the stem and the ending.

    In àfevxejycàgofycyv, the stem -àgofycyv indicates that the verb is ofxàgofycyv (to speak) and the prefix àfevxejyc- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In sevwssejevejèv, the stem -evejèv indicates that the verb is ofejevejèv (to finish), the prefix -ssej- precedes it, and the inflection sevw- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Déevxofèv they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    ofxàgofycyv: sejycofxàgofycyv xz, sycàgofycyv efàf, àfevxssycàgofycyv sàgej'efu, sevwejàgofycyv sefwev xefu, çxàgofycyv...
    ofejevejèv: sejycofejevejèv xz, sxàfîevejèv sefwog, àfevxssejevejèv sàgej'efu, sejevejèv, sevwejssejevejèv sefwev xefu...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    ofejwàgefwog: ohefxog xz, ohefxog efàf, àfefxog àgej, sevwàgefwog sefwev, çxàgefwog sefwog, àfevxàgefxog sàgej.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly ofejwogyc, xofàfê, ofxàgàgyc and xofejycèv), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with ofx- (with the exception of ofxàgàgyc, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    ofxpejyc, ofxegycàgycèb, ofxàfevycdé, ofxegwogevx, ofxpofxèv, ofxaevycp, ofxssycyv, ofxegycyv, ofxevxpwofyv, ofxobofycaxof, etc.

        For example, for the verb ofxàgofycyv, the stem is -àgofycyv and the infinitive prefix is ofx-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with ofej- whose present participle begins with àfevycssej-:

    ofejevnèb, ofejàfycyvpwé, ofejyvofxefanob, ofejofefxàgèv, ofejobevycofa, ofïycd, ofejàfsxogevej, ofejàgwyv, ofejaefwof, ofejaefof, ofejàgycs, etc.

        For example, for the verb ofejevejèv, the stem is -evejèv and the infinitive prefix is ofej-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries xofàfê and ofejwogyc, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. xobofycaxof xz means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with ofx- (all verbs of the first group): x-, sx-, x-, sevw-, çx-, àfevx-.
    Verbs beginning with ofej- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): sej-, sej-, àfej-, sevwssej-, çxssej-, àfevxssej-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with xof- (part of the third group): s-, s-, - , sevw-, çx-, àfevx-.

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "sejycobofycaxof xz" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the ofx- prefix, e.g., ofxobofycaxof -> -obofycaxof.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the ofej- prefix plus the ssej- prefix, e.g., ofejsejwdé -> -ssejsejwdé. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: sejyc-, sejyc-, àfejyc-, sevwej-, çxej-, àfevxejyc-.

**Past participle

As in English, Xpoakcè nouns inflect for number, however they do so through prefixation rather than suffixation.

The plural is usually formed from the singular by adding the prefix morpheme zu- (e.g., olegàçvte > zuolegàçvte 'houses'). 

Nouns beginning with mv- and ma- take the prefix gà- instead of zu- (e.g., mvbàmcà > zumvbàmcà 'pipes', mawé > zumawé 'games'), except for the nouns mviovh, mvkkvgà, maoj, and mahne which form their plural by prefixing the morpheme gà- (e.g., maoj > gàmaoj 'tires').

Seven nouns beginning with mle- form their plural with zu-. These are mleoas, mlehhçvp, mleneçx, mlewéçne, mlej, mlexp, and mlewémlewé (e.g., mleoas > zumleoas 'knees'). All other nouns beginning with mle-, such as mlegàçne or mlekcà, follow the regular plural pattern and take gà- (e.g., mlekcà > gàmlekcà 'holes').

Nouns that begin with gà-, zu- or f- in the singular do not change in the plural (e.g., zuçlekp vh 'the cross' > zuçlekp gàah 'the crosses').

Nouns that begin with hv- typically change to zumv- in the plural (e.g., hvokmlewé > zumvokmlewé 'newspapers'). However, several nouns beginning with hv- are exceptions to this rule and form their plural by adding gà- instead. These are hvne, hvp, hvlàvokvp, hvpvxp, hvlàçcàgàacè, hvcàçpbuk, hvlàkagà and hvsbuk (e.g., hvlàçcàgàacè ah > gàhvlàçcàgàacè gàah).

Similarly, most nouns beginning with hçv- change to zumv- in the plural. Examples of this pattern include hçvne, hçvklep, hçvtebu, hçvkçjmlegà, hçvlàvkcà, and hçvkcàçlà (e.g., hçvkcàçlà om > zumvkcàçlà gàai 'stained-glass windows'). However, some hçv- nouns do not follow this pattern and form their plural with gà-, notably hçvk, hçvkçcàcàv, hçviovxp, hçvcàbui, hçvokalàmles and hçvcàklej (e.g., hçvk ah > gàhçvk gàah 'the rails').

* Case
Nouns in Xpoakcè are not inflected for any other grammatical categories. (However, personal pronouns are inflected for case and person.)

----------
ADJECTIVES
----------

An adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Xpoakcè adjectives therefore have four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, and feminine plural. A few adjectives, like mvane and mvalàmleo, have a fifth form, viz. an additional masculine singular form for use after a noun ending in v, a, ç, le, m, bà, bu, y and some occurrences of x, e.g. oçikvwé mvane om (a beautiful garden), atetelex hane om (a handsome man), ateteacè ahhane aom (a beautiful woman), gàcàovcèoa zumvane gàah (the beautiful children), gàolegàçvte gàahhane gàah (the beautiful houses).

The masculine singular, an adjective's basic form, is listed in dictionaries. Most feminine forms are formed by adding the prefix a- to the masculine form, e.g., iovks > aiovks, càoah > acàoah, ovgàkaj > aovgàkaj. 

Under certain circumstances, other minor changes occur in the formation of feminine forms. Specifically, masculine adjectives beginning with ha-, hç-, ole-, oa-, gàle- or gàv- double their initial consonant before adding the prefix a- (e.g., hamkp > ahhamkp, hçcàoas > ahhçcàoas, olene > aoolene, oaçpov > aooaçpov, gàleks > agàgàleks, and gàvne > agàgàvne).

Additionally, adjectives beginning with p- change to axp- (e.g., povhne > axpovhne); those beginning with kma- or zuma- change to agàma- (e.g., kmacàcàatelekj > agàmacàcàatelekj, zumaçkmcè > agàmaçkmcè), with the exception of the irregular zumaçlà (old) whose feminine form is ahhçaçlà; s- changes to ams- (e.g., soleh > amsoleh); cèç- changes to alàç- (e.g., cèçcàpv > alàçcàpv); cèa- changes to alày- (e.g., cèakne > alàykne); ka- changes to aky- (e.g., kasovkcàbu > akysovkcàbu); càa- changes to acày- (e.g., càaçmgéoç > acàyçmgéoç); and adjectives beginning with mle- have a special form hle- (becoming ahhle- in feminine) that appears after v, a, ç, le, m, bà, bu, y and some occurrences of x, (e.g., mlecè/hlecè > ahhlecè, mlete/hlete > ahhlete).

If an adjective's basic form beginning with a-, it does not change in the feminine (cf. axpçk atetelex om 'a rich man' > axpçk ateteacè aom 'a rich woman').

The plural is normally formed by adding the prefix gà- to the singular (masculine and feminine; e.g., çhlewé > gàçhlewé, açhlewé > gàaçhlewé). If the basic form beginning with gà-, zu-, or f-, an adjective does not change in the masculine plural (e.g., gàvne > gàvne, zumakbuobus > zumakbuobus, zumlei > zumlei), but its feminine plural form follows the rules detailed above. All Xpoakcè adjectives beginning with mva- take the prefix zu- in the masculine plural (e.g., mvalàmleo > zumvalàmleo). Distinctive plural forms occur with adjectives beginning with hv-, which normally change to zumv- in the masculine plural (e.g., hvokalàçx > zumvokalàçx, hvkcàoap > zumvkcàoap), with only two exceptions: hvcàvcè > gàhvcàvcè and hvlàvo > gàhvlàvo which follow the regular pattern. By contrast, the feminine plural is always formed according to the general rule: ahvkcàoap > gàahvkcàoap.

Adjective placement follows specific patterns. Most adjectives are placed before the noun they modify, and this is particularly true for colors, as in asmlek oçlà ah (the red wine). However, certain short, commonly used adjectives – those dealing with beauty, age, goodness, or size (sometimes remembered by the acronym "BAGS") – typically follow their nouns. These are mvane (beautiful), olene (good), cèakne (brief), iovks (big/tall), gàleks (fat/large), zumvcè (false), càmvx (high), soleh (long), cèakne (brief), aomawé (young), çhlewé (pretty), gàçvlàmvte (bad), kmahhçate (better), mvalàmleo (new), càçcàaj (small), zumaçlà (old); e.g., ateteacè ahhane aom ("a beautiful woman").

--------
PRONOUNS
--------
In Xpoakcè, pronouns are inflected to indicate their role in the sentence (subject, direct object, and so on), as well as to reflect the person, gender, and number of their referents. 

*Personal Pronouns
xpoakcè personal pronouns (analogous to English I, you, he/she, we, and they) reflect the person and number of their referent, and in the case of the third person, its gender as well. They also reflect the role they play in their clause: subject, direct object, indirect object, or other.

The personal pronouns change form to reflect the role they play in their clause. The forms used for subjects are called the subject pronouns, subjective pronouns, or nominative pronouns. They are as follows: 

**Subject Pronouns
------------------------
Number   | Person           | Subject Pronoun
------------------------
Singular | 1st              | awé
         | 2nd (informal)   | mcà
         | 2nd (formal)     | gàmlelà
         | 3rd (masculine)  | hç
         | 3rd (feminine)   | ahha
         | 3rd (neutral)    | ole
------------------------
Plural   | 1st              | gàmleo
         | 2nd              | gàmlelà
         | 3rd (masculine)  | gàhç
         | 3rd (feminine)   | gàahha
------------------------

Note: Whenever the subject pronoun awé occurs after v, a, ç, le, m, bà, bu, y, ê and some occurrences of x, it becomes 'wé.

*Relative pronouns

xpoakcè, like English, uses relative pronouns to link relative clauses to their head nouns, except that in Xpoakcè, as in Amharic for instance, the relative clause precedes its head and the relative pronoun, this is why we speak of "head noun" rather than of an "antecedent." The relative pronoun used depends on its grammatical role (such as subject or direct object) within the relative clause.

If the relative pronoun is to be the subject of the relative clause's verb, çmgé is ordinarily used: acàcàahpbàpçne vte buhlelà v çmgé atetelex'h ("the man who stole my bike"). Note that çmgé in this use does not change form to agree in any way with its head noun: gàabuhlelà bucàbu càole çmgé gàacàcàahpbàpçne gàah ("the bikes that were stolen").

If the relative pronoun is to be the direct object of the relative clause's verb, amgé (or 'mgé after v, a, ç, le, m, bà, bu, y, ê and some occurrences of x) is ordinarily used: abuhlelà v hç'mgé acàcàahpbàpçne vh ("the bicycle that he stole"). Like çmgé, amgé does not change form to agree with its head noun.


-----
VERBS
-----
Verbs in Xpoakcè are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Xpoakcè is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) kçlelàv ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of akcàê ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is akcàê, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is kçlelàv. Forms of akcàê are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Xpoakcè, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

**Stems and conjugation prefixes

xpoakcè verbs have a large number of simple (one-word) forms. These are composed of two distinct parts: the stem (or root, or radix), which indicates which verb it is, and the prefix (inflection), which indicates the verb's tense (imperfect, present, future etc.) and mood and its subject's person (I, you, he/she etc.) and number, though many prefixes can correspond to multiple tense-mood-subject combinations. In certain parts of the second conjugation there is also a prefix -gàgàç- between the stem and the ending.

    In càoaçvhkvj, the stem -hkvj indicates that the verb is kahkvj (to speak) and the prefix càoaçv- marks the third-person plural imperfect indicative. "Third person plural" meaning the subject of the verb is "they". The "imperfect indicative" being a tense.
    In gàolegàgàçoçcè, the stem -oçcè indicates that the verb is kçoçcè (to finish), the prefix -gàgàç- precedes it, and the inflection gàole- marks the first-person plural present indicative or imperative. The "first-person plural" is the "we" form of a verb. The "present indicative" being a tense and "imperative" being a mood, but in Xpoakcè they are indistinguishable without context.

These verb conjugations are coupled with a subject pronoun in order to convey who the subject of the verb is (i.e. who is doing the action).

***The principle of the fixed stem

The stem normally stays fixed in the first two conjugations:

    kahkvj: gàçvkahkvj awé, gàvhkvj mcà, càoagàgàvhkvj gàhç'mgé, gàoleçhkvj gàmleo amgé, fahkvj...
    kçoçcè: gàçvkçoçcè awé, gàacàîoçcè gàmlelà, càoagàgàçoçcè gàhç'mgé, gàçoçcè, gàoleçgàgàçoçcè gàmleo amgé...

In the third it is often modified, sometimes even between persons in the same tense:

    kçlehmlelà: zumalà awé, zumalà mcà, càmalà hç, gàolehmlelà gàmleo, fahmlelà gàmlelà, càoahmalà gàhç.

But such irregularities apart, the principle is that nothing is removed from the stem. 


**Conjugation prefixes

The conjugation prefix tells us:

    For all verbs, the mood and the tense;
    For finite verbs, the person and the number; and
    For the past participle alone, the gender and the number.

Apart from a few frequent verbs which are considered totally irregular (mainly kçlelàv, akcàê, kahhv and akçvcè), for each tense of each mood a series of six prefixes (one for each person singular and plural) is associated with a group or subgroup of verbs.


*Formation of simple tenses active

These tenses are not formed with an auxiliary, and their formation is discussed in the following section.

**Infinitive

A verb is normally named by its present infinitive. Starting from this infinitive, the conjugations can be classified into three different groups:

    The first group or first conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with ka- (with the exception of kahhv, which due to its numerous irregularities is usually classed as being in the third conjugation):

    kateçv, kabàvhvne, kacàovxp, kabàlelàoa, katekacè, kasovte, kagàgàvj, kabàvj, kaoatelekj, kaikvsak, etc.

        For example, for the verb kahkvj, the stem is -hkvj and the infinitive prefix is ka-.

    The second group or second conjugation. This contains the verbs with infinitives beginning with kç- whose present participle begins with càovgàgàç-:

    kçobune, kçcàvjtelep, kçjkamsbui, kçkmahcè, kçiovks, kïvx, kçcàgàalàoç, kçhlej, kçsmlek, kçsmk, kçhvgà, etc.

        For example, for the verb kçoçcè, the stem is -oçcè and the infinitive prefix is kç-.

    The third group or third conjugation. This contains all the other verbs.
    
Note that the auxiliaries akcàê and kçlelàv, although they would naturally seem to belong to the third conjugation, are traditionally classed separately. 

**Present indicative

The present indicative is the form of the verb used to describe an action in the present e.g. aikvsak awé means "I watch".

The stem of the present indicative is not always regular and can vary (especially in the third conjugation) and there are three main sets of prefixes:

    Verbs beginning with ka- (all verbs of the first group): a-, gàa-, a-, gàole-, fa-, càoa-.
    Verbs beginning with kç- (all verbs of the second group and most of the third): gàç-, gàç-, càç-, gàolegàgàç-, fagàgàç-, càoagàgàç-. But there are numerous irregularities, especially in the third group.
    Verbs beginning with ak- (part of the third group): gà-, gà-, - , gàole-, fa-, càoa-.
    
    Example:

-------------------------------
Person         | Singular             | Plural
-------------------------------
1st person     | aikvsak awé         | gàoleikvsak gàmleo
2nd person     | gàaikvsak mcà        | faikvsak gàmlelà
3rd person     | aikvsak ole/ahha/hç | càoaikvsak gàahha/gàhç
-------------------------------

-------------------------------

-------------------------------

2nd person     | gàçgàçlexp mcà         | fagàgàçgàçlexp gàmlelà
3rd person     | càçgàçlexp ole/ahha/hç | càoagàgàçgàçlexp gàahha/gàhç

**Imperfect indicative

The imperfect indicative is a past tense describing states and actions that were ongoing in the past, e.g. "gàçvikvsak awé" means "I was watching".

    The stem of the imperfect indicative is always invariant for a single verb. It is derived in various ways depending on the verb group.
    For the first group, the stem is the infinitive minus the ka- prefix, e.g., kaikvsak -> -ikvsak.
    For the second group, the stem is the infinitive minus the kç- prefix plus the gàgàç- prefix, e.g., kçgàçlexp -> -gàgàçgàçlexp. 
    And for the third group, the stem is derived from the first person plural of the present indicative.

    The conjugation prefixes of this tense are for any of the three groups always: gàçv-, gàçv-, càçv-, gàoleç-, faç-, càoaçv-.

2nd person     | gàçvikvsak mcà         | façikvsak gàmlelà
3rd person     | càçvikvsak ole/ahha/hç | càoaçvikvsak gàahha/gàhç

3rd person     | càçvgàgàçgàçlexp ole/ahha/hç | càoaçvgàgàçgàçlexp gàahha/gàhç
-------------------------------



    Verb akcàê : the stem is -càbu, endings are the same.
    

**Future

The future prefixes correspond to the present indicative of the verb kçlelàv. They are always regular: çv-, gàv-, v-, gàole-, fa-, càole-.

    The future stem is simply the infinitive (dictionary form). In other words, to form the future tense these prefixes are added to the infinitive:

**Past participle

Past participles, unlike present participles and gerundives, may be inflected to show gender and number by adding a- and gà- prefixes, as with a normal adjective. Hence, "càçcèolep càçmkcè om", "acàçcèolep akçlej aom", "gàcàçcèolep gàcàçmkcè gàai", and "gàacàçcèolep gàakçlej gàai."

The plain (masculine singular) form of a past participle begins with bu- for the 1st group verbs, and with ç- for the 2nd group verbs. Third group verbs have more diverse prefixes : m- (akioacàoa mioacàoa, akçlene mne, akçh mh, etc. and kçlelàvgà mgà, kçlelà mlà, kçlelàmlej mj), gàç- (akcàcàate gàçte, akioakj gàçkj, etc.), gàm- (akmhpoç gàmhpoç and akmhpak gàmhpak and only these verbs), càç- (akçimvte càçimvte, akçi càçi, etc.), cà- (verbs in akioç- : akioçaj càoçaj), càka- (kçklàmle càkalàmle, kçklàmlep càkalàmlep, kçkcècèle càkacècèle and kçkcècèmlegà càkacècèmlegà), or ma (kçlelàv ma). 

*Compound Tenses

xpoakcè compound tenses are verb forms that combine an auxiliary verb (either kçlelàv or akcàê) with the past participle of the main verb. These tenses are used to indicate actions that are completed or relate to another point in time. There are several compound tenses in Xpoakcè, each serving a specific purpose and adding nuance to the timeline of events.

**Compound Past

The compound past is perhaps the most commonly used compound tense in Xpoakcè. It is used to describe actions that have been completed in the past and is translated by the English simple past. The auxiliary verb is either kçlelàv or akcàê in the present tense, preceded by the past participle of the main verb. For example, "busovte çv'wé" (I ate) or "bulàçkkv càgàa hç" (He arrived). kçlelàv is used with most verbs, while akcàê is used with a specific group of verbs, particularly those indicating movement or change of state, and with all reflexive verbs. When in doubt, kçlelàv should be used by default.

-----
Verbs in Kwdûæef are conjugated to reflect the following information:

    a mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, or conditional)
    a tense (past, present, or future, though not all tenses can be combined with all moods)
    an aspect (perfective or imperfective)
    a voice (active, passive, or reflexive)
    Nonfinite forms (e.g., participles, gerunds, infinitives)


Verbs in the finite moods (indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional) are also conjugated to agree with their subjects in person (first, second, or third) and number (singular or plural). As in English, the subject must be included (except in the imperative mood); in other words Kwdûæef is neither a null-subject nor a pro-drop language.

Auxiliary verbs are combined with past participles of main verbs to produce compound tenses, including the compound past. For most main verbs the auxiliary is (the appropriate form of) æzuœîh ("to have"), but for reflexive verbs and certain intransitive verbs the auxiliary is a form of ûæehv ("to be"). The participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is ûæehv, and with a following direct object (if any) when the auxiliary is æzuœîh. Forms of ûæehv are also used with the past participles of transitive verbs to form the passive voice.

*Morphology

In Kwdûæef, a verb is inflected to reflect its mood and tense, as well as to agree with its subject in person and number.

The past participle is used in three ways in Kwdûæef: as an adjective, in the passive construction, and in the compound tense constructions. When it is used as an adjective, it follows all the regular adjective agreement rules. In passive constructions, it always agrees with the passive subject.

A. The auxiliary verb is æzuœîh.

    If there is no direct object (the verb is intransitive) or the direct object appears before the past participle, then the past participle does not agree (i.e., it takes the default masculine singular form).

        (direct object before verb) egûdzûafîhâf ijûb jœ îh ûæzîhafw. ("ûæzîhafw saw two whales.")
    If there is a direct object and it appears after the past participle, then the participle must agree with it. Three cases:

        (relative clause linked by ûjt) egûjœ îh ûæzîhafw ûjt egûdzûafîhâf ijûb egûaf ("the two whales that ûæzîhafw saw")
    The above rule is one of the most difficult in Kwdûæef.

B. The auxiliary is ûæehv, and the verb is not reflexive. The past participle agrees with the subject:

C. The auxiliary is ûæehv and the verb is reflexive. The agreement rules are in fact the same as those for structures with æzuœîh in A, keeping in mind that the reflexive pronoun corresponds to either the direct object or the indirect object of the verb.

    There is no direct object, or the direct object appears before the past participle → no agreement. In these cases, the reflexive pronoun expresses the indirect object.
